3.1 Introduction
3.1.1 Cultural Relationship Between the Xia and Shang and
the Zhou Dynasty
The Zhou Dynasty comprised the Western Zhou and Eastern Zhou.
Described here is mainly the ceramic culture and history of the Western
Zhou, which began when King Wu of Zhou overthrew the Shang Dynasty
and made Fenghao (modern name for the twin city formed by the Western
Zhou capitals of Haojing and Fengjing; also called Zongzhou) its capital
and ended when King Ping of Zhou moved eastward to Luoyi, lasting for
about 300 years from 1046 to 771 BCE.
   The first half of the Zhou Dynasty, the Western Zhou, included twelve
kings. Its powerful national strength and the submission of surrounding
nationalities to its rule made it the “Golden Age of China” as seen by
Confucius, who once proclaimed: “Developed on the rituals of the Xia and
Shang dynasties, how complete and splendid are Zhou rituals! I would
certainly follow Zhou rituals”. Confucius held the Western Zhou as an
exemplary model for Chinese politics, a period that later generations should
emulate. But from the first year of the Gonghe regency (841 BCE), as the
king’s rule diminished and the well-field system was abolished, northern
and western rival forces, namely the Quanrong and Qiang nomads, exerted
frequent military pressure on the Western Zhou, and in 770 BCE King Ping

was forced to forsake his traditional base camp, migrated eastward, and
established a new capital in Luoyi. After this the strength of Zhou waned.
The second half of the Zhou Dynasty was called the Eastern Zhou, which
experienced eighteen kings, but in fact during this period lands under direct
Zhou rule were much smaller than those during the Western Zhou.
   The Zhou Dynasty was of great significance for the development of
Chinese culture because many of China’s ancient laws, regulations and
customs, including Confucianism, originated during this time. The Western
Zhou perfected the tradition of succession by the eldest son of the wife, a
basis for the Zongfa system (descent line system, or extensive stratified
patrilineage), thus laying a solid foundation for the social and governing
systems centered on family, a system which contributed to the relatively
stable progress of Chinese civilization over the millennia. The eldest son of
the wife was the legitimate successor and the representative of the family’s
sacrificial activities, while the sons of concubines and mistresses would be
given a lower status. Families were the basic units of societal constitution
and statelets were an extended form of families. The Zhou kings, called
Sons of Heaven, form the main line of descent and political authority of all
fiefdoms, or the “grand line” (dazong) of the kingdom. They were owner
and representative of all subjects and lands and commanders-in-chief of all
the kingdom’s vassals and armies. Under the king, large fiefdoms were
given to princes and smaller principalities were given to brothers farther
removed. These Zhuhou (princes) and Dafu (officials) of the same family
name established new lineages of lesser authority, called lesser lines
(xiaozong).1
   The ritual vessels, rites and music used in sacrifices were different for
the grand and lesser lines. The king used nine ding, while Zhuhou and Dafu
used seven, five or three according to their rank. For music and dance, the
king used 64 performers, Zhuhou 48, Dafu 32 and Shi (a social stratum in
ancient China between senior official and the common people) 16.
Traditions of the family system, ancestral worship and sacrifice to Heaven
and Earth, were integrated into one to serve as rules of social behavior and
guidelines for administrative organization. The principles behind the entire
system, also the basis of the later Confucianism, were social harmony and
balance between man and nature.
   The many deities worshipped during the Shang Dynasty were simplified
into a single “Heaven, or “supreme god” as termed by the Shang Dynasty.

The creed of Heaven was the “Tao“(the Way), which was crystalized as
rites and music, in effect a complete set of laws governing society. The Son
of Heaven, namely the kings, as the grand line, should set an example for
all in respecting the rites and music, which was considered to be
“De”(moral), so that all citizens would emulate and follow the rites and
laws. The Son of Heaven was believed to return to Heaven after death to
become a god or deity. Sacrificing to the ancestors and to Heaven therefore
became an important part of the rites and laws. The establishment of official
kilns in later dynasties was also related to the fact that ceramic ritual objects
were required for these sacrificial activities. All citizens of the kingdom
apart from the Son of Heaven were ranked according to the five cardinal
relationships (ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, brother
and brother, and friend and friend) and were assigned clear rights and
duties. Such rules regulating interpersonal relationships helped reduce
friction and promote social harmony.2 All of these later became important
components of the Confucian thought system.
   As was the case in the Shang Dynasty, the political organization of the
Zhou was affiliated to family sacrifices, with its military and religious
functions intermingled. After overthrowing the Shang, the Zhou practiced
the system of enfeoffment, which was based on the ranks of family
sacrifices. The highest rank was the king and the ancestral sacrifices of the
royal house. The king was deemed to be performing the duties of the
supreme god and thus only the king had the right to sacrifice to the supreme
god. The capital in the Wei River valley was the sacrificial center of all
statelets in the kingdom and the residence of the ancestral temple of the
ruling house.
   The political authority of each statelet was in the hands of a powerful
family, whose strength was manifest in the number of war chariots,
religious privileges (the right to stage certain sacrificial rites, enjoy certain
dances and sing certain special anthems), its history and relationship with
the royal family, and the wealth (bronze, jade, lacquerwares, gold and silver
wares) in its possession. Among these, pottery was comparably crude and
porcelain had not yet matured. Thus, the two were not really symbols of
wealth. Nevertheless, pottery was brilliantly applied to architecture thanks
to its unique advantages.

3.1.2 The Nobility and the Workers

The adoption of the enfeoffment system encouraged new developments in
the politics, economy and culture of Western Zhou. Areas directly
controlled by Western Zhou and those subject to its influence were also
significantly wider than those in the late Shang. The overthrow of the Shang
regime brought large numbers of handicraft slaves to Zhou, creating
conditions for the development of the handicraft industry. As a result,
handicraft production during the Western Zhou witnessed remarkable
development.
   To satisfy the luxurious lifestyle of the royal court and nobility, the
Western Zhou rulers gathered skilled craftsmen in various trades to the
capital from around the kingdom to make exquisite vessels. These slaves
engaged in handicraft production were called “Workers of 100 Varieties”.
Archaeologists have found sites of Western Zhou workshops for various
handicrafts in areas near modern-day Yuntang Village in Fufeng County,
Shaanxi Province, and have unearthed large numbers of bronzes, pottery,
primitive porcelain, stone wares and bone tools there.
   Apart from daily utensils, the pottery unearthed also included a large
number of building components such as plain tiles, semicircle-shaped tiles,
eave tiles and waterpipes.3At Fenghao, capital of the Western Zhou, which
is in modern-day Chang’an, Shaanxi, building remnants and remains of
various workshops for firing pottery, smelting bronze and making bone
tools have also been found. Remains unearthed at pottery workshops
indicate that the firing of daily-use pottery and architectural pottery were
already separated. The large number of plain pottery tiles, semicircle-
shaped tiles and eave tiles found at various sites from the period indicate
that new development and progress was achieved in architectural pottery
during the Western Zhou Dynasty.
   The Western Zhou did not see new pottery vessel varieties. Pottery
vessels were merely further spread and improved based on the Shang
varieties. Developing particularly rapidly was architectural pottery. In fact,
architectural pottery already appeared back in the Shang Dynasty and more
varieties were developed and evolved by the Western Zhou. No particular
achievement was witnessed in porcelain development either. This was all
partly due to the introduction and development of vessels made from
bronze, gold, silver, lacquer and jade, materials that were far more valuable
than ceramic materials; it was also related to the preference of the royal
court and the nobility at the time.

During the Western Zhou, white pottery waned. Gray pottery was also
declining but was still produced widely as everyday vessels. Making further
progress were imprinted hard pottery and primitive porcelain. Production of
these was still concentrated in the southeast coastal areas as in the Shang
Dynasty. Yet primitive porcelain of the Western Zhou has been unearthed in
notably wider regions than in the late Shang, from modern-day Guangzhou
in the south to Beijing in the north and from the coast in the east to Shaanxi
in the west. In addition, the primitive porcelain gui (簋) unearthed in a
Western Zhou tomb in Luoyang had a shape design that has not been seen
in regions south of the Yangtze River, which indicates that apart from
southern areas continuing to produce primitive porcelain in large quantities,
other regions of the country were also making it and it had gradually
become one of the more widely used daily vessels of slave-owners and
nobles in the kingdom.

3.2 Gray Pottery
After its peak during the mid-Shang Dynasty, gray pottery started declining
in the latter years of the Shang and declined further in the Western Zhou.
Daily vessel varieties made from gray pottery were not as numerous as
those in the Shang Dynasty, nor was the workmanship as fine, which was
probably due to the large number of bronzewares, primitive porcelain wares
and lacquerwares used by slave owners in the Western Zhou in their daily
lives.
    Nevertheless, certain advantages of gray pottery, namely, that it was
cheap, practical, sturdy and durable, helped maintain its position and
production volume among the cooking, drinking, food and containing
vessels of the time. Hence in the Zhou Dynasty, practical pottery was still
dominated by gray sandy and clay pottery, complemented by some red
sandy pottery, red clay pottery and black clay pottery. Shaping was still
mostly by the potter’s wheel.
   The gray pottery in the central plains, the center of Zhou rule, was
developed on the one hand by inheriting local pre-Zhou pottery making
techniques, and on the other by assimilating the techniques of the Shang
ruled areas of the late Shang. Thus, some of the gray pottery wares of the
early Western Zhou preserved some characteristics of pre-Zhou pottery. By
the later years of the Western Zhou, the varieties and shape designs of

pottery in different parts of the kingdom, while maintaining some local
features, had by and large become the same, forming a pottery system of the
Zhou Dynasty featuring bag-shaped feet, circular feet and flat bottoms.
   Gray pottery cooking vessels of the Zhou Dynasty mainly included li,
yan and zeng, with li the most commonly used. With the appearance and
development of the stove, the shape design of pottery li underwent obvious
changes, mainly the lowering of the crotch and feet. In the early Zhou the
crotch of pottery li was elevated. Most were arc shaped and some were
shaped like included angles. The feet had pointy tips. By the late Zhou
Dynasty, the crotch was considerably lower, the included angle in the crotch
was almost gone, and the bag-shaped feet lost their pointy tips to become
short and plump. There were also oblate-bellied li with fei-leng ridges
featuring the same shape design with contemporaneous bronze li. The
crotch was almost flat, and the feet were cylindrical with flat bottoms. The
main food vessels in the Zhou were gui and dou. By the late Zhou Dynasty
pottery gui had disappeared. Pottery dou of the early Western Zhou mostly
had short circular feet. Some had relatively high circular feet with cross-
shaped holes. That of the late Western Zhou was mostly high-stemmed bell-
shaped dou, with a ridge protruding on the thin middle section of the stem.
    In the Western Zhou, drinking vessels (wine vessels) that were popular
back in the Shang Dynasty were seldom found or no longer found at all,
because alcohol was banned during the Zhou Dynasty. The Zhou people
believed the Shang was conquered because their rulers indulged themselves
so much in alcohol that even Heaven was enraged. “Admonition against
Alcohol (jiu gao)”in the Book of Documents (the Shangshu) states: “For
group drinking, thou shalt arrest every one of the drinkers and take them
back to the capital, and I shall have them killed”. Thus, wine vessel making
that was once advanced in the Shang Dynasty gradually declined during the
Zhou. For instance, jue were still produced in the early years of the Western
Zhou and the design was the same with those in the late Shang Dynasty, but
they were no longer to be found by the later years of the Western Zhou; jia
were seldom found in the Zhou Dynasty; similar gu to those in the late
Shang were still found in the early Western Zhou, but were replaced by a
new type of cup by late Western Zhou; wine containers such as zhi and you
had all disappeared by the later years of the Western Zhou. The pot was the
only drinking vessel that remained and there were many varieties. Slim pots
with pierced lugs were prevalent in the early Western Zhou, while in the

later years of the Western Zhou pots with lids that could also serve as a cup
when removed became popular for their practicality.
   The main containers were lei, jars, urns, basins and yu, of which pottery
yu appeared only in the later part of the Western Zhou. Pottery lei in early
Western Zhou basically continued the shape design of those in the late
Shang, that is, with two knobs on the shoulder, while by late Western Zhou
pottery lei were mostly without the knobs. Pottery urns developed from
ones with small mouths, straight collars and round shoulders in the early
Western Zhou to ones with a small mouth, rolled rim and slanting and
rounded shoulders.
   Apart from the varieties introduced above, the gray pottery of Western
Zhou also included small numbers of large zun with open mouths, ding with
shallow bellies, circular bottoms, and three drill-shaped feet, jue with folded
shoulders, thin waists and bag-shaped feet, vessel lids with bell-shaped
knobs and plates with circular feet. In addition, pottery emulating
bronzewares was also found in some regions.
   The surface decoration of Western Zhou gray pottery was
predominantly relatively thick rope patterns, and some carved and scratched
marks, comb patterns, string patterns and carved triangle patterns. Li (Fig.
3.1), yan, jars, urns, basins and lei were fully covered with rope patterns,
complemented by some carved lines and string patterns. Gui and lei were
decorated with rope patterns on the lower part and carved with triangles and
comb patterns on the upper part. Additional stacking patterns were rarely
used. Beast face patterns were still used on some gray pottery, emulating
bronze ritual vessels, such as the Gray Pottery Li with Beast Faces, a
collection in the National Museum of China. A gray clay pottery ware from
the early Zhou Dynasty, it has an outwardly extended mouth, narrow neck,
plump belly, high crotch, and three bag-shaped feet. The belly is decorated
with three sets of beast face patterns against a mat pattern background. The
beasts, with bulging eyes and huge horns, were vivid and awe-inspiring,
quite like those on bronzewares. Previous beast face patterns were mostly
set against the background of the yunlei pattern, yet this ware used a mat
pattern as the backdrop. It is still to be investigated whether this difference
was related to changes of theocratic thought in the Zhou Dynasty.

3.3 Imprinted Hard Pottery and Primitive
Porcelain
Imprinted hard pottery originated in the Shang Dynasty and reached
maturity in the Zhou Dynasty. Large numbers of imprinted hard pottery
pieces have been unearthed in many cultural sites and tombs of the Zhou
Dynasty in modern-day Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Jiangxi in the lower reaches
of the Yangtze River and Fujian and Guangdong in the coastal areas.
Common varieties included urns, crocks, and bu (small urns), all elegantly
shaped and highly practical containers. The urns and crocks are large and
tall with plump bellies. Some reach a height of 99 cm. The shoulders and
bellies are orderly sectioned into different parts which are respectively
stamped with yunlei, checks, square spirals, zigzag patterns, rhombuses,
waves, or kuilong. Many of the wares have two or three pattern types. The

imprinted hard pottery jar with handle unearthed in Guangdong has a big
mouth, straight neck, folded shoulder, shallow belly, flat bottom, and one
handle arching over the rim and shoulder. The shoulder is decorated with
string patterns. The body is light brown and the firing temperature was
high. Crocks and bu with beast-shaped lugs also appeared. One example is
the imprinted hard pottery crock with beast-shaped lugs unearthed in the
Tudun Tomb in Lishui, Jiangsu in 1978. The body is hard and purplish gray.
The ware has a straight mouth, short neck, deep and swelling belly, flat
bottom, and a pair of beast-shaped lugs on the shoulder. Four symmetrical
fei-leng ridges divide the ware surface into four sections which are stamped
with zigzags and square spirals. The patterns are shallow and sparse.
Another representative ware is the imprinted hard pottery bu with beast-
shaped lugs unearthed in Wuxi, Jiangsu in 1955. The body is hard and
brown. The ware has a straight mouth, short neck, broad shoulder, round
belly, big flat bottom, and symmetrical beast-shaped lugs on the shoulder.
The ware surface is stamped with zigzagging square spirals. The patterns
are extremely clear, obviously emulating bronzewares. Before this period
beast-shaped lugs were only used on bronzewares and were seldom found
on pottery. The appearance of beast-shaped lugs on imprinted hard pottery
was largely attributable to the influence of bronze ornamentation. In later
periods beast-shaped lugs gradually became an important ornament of
pottery wares.
   Scant imprinted hard pottery has been found in the middle and lower
reaches of the Yellow River, probably due to the heavy use of bronze in
these regions. It may therefore be said that during the Zhou Dynasty
imprinted hard pottery was still as popular mainly in the middle and lower
reaches of the Yangtze River as during the Shang Dynasty.
    Primitive porcelain developed side by side with imprinted hard pottery.
(Figs. 3.2 and 3.3) They used the same forming technique (coiling), were
fired at the same temperature (instances of primitive porcelain and
imprinted hard pottery being fired in the same furnace have been found at
some sites), and featured many similarities in decorative method. Besides,
both were mostly containers. So, the two could be said to be sister products
closely related to each other. Like imprinted hard pottery, primitive
porcelain made further progress in firing skills during the Western Zhou,
building on the experience of the late Shang Dynasty, and was produced
across a much wider area. It has been found in some of the cultural sites and

tombs of the Western Zhou in modern-day Beijing, Hebei, Shandong,
Henan, Shaanxi, Anhui, Hubei, Jiangsu, Jiangxi and Zhejiang. Common
varieties included dou, lei, pots, urns, li, bowls, jars, yu, zun, and he. In
general, the size of primitive porcelain wares was smaller than imprinted
hard pottery and the varieties were richer. Apart from containers, there were
also food vessels and drinking vessels, of which dou accounted for a large
portion. The body color is dominated by grayish white, and the glaze is
mostly bluish green or pea green, and sometimes yellowish green or bluish
gray. For surface decoration, apart from plain surfaces, there are underglaze
geometric patterns such as checks, basket patterns, yunlei, mat patterns, leaf
vein patterns, teeth-shaped patterns, scratched marks, string patterns, “S”-
shaped patterns, bump patterns, circles and zigzags.4 (Fig. 3.4).

3.4 Architectural Pottery
Although in the production of daily utensils and ritual vessels, the Western
Zhou did not make particularly notable progress, it saw remarkable
development in architectural pottery. Architectural pottery appeared in
China back in the Shang Dynasty, when the change in people’s living
conditions and the need of slave owners and the nobility to demonstrate
their luxurious lifestyle brought forth new requirements in architecture. In
order to enhance their authority, the nobility spent a great deal of resources
building palaces, courtyards and mansions, and these required materials
entirely different from previous architectural materials. One of these new
materials was pottery. In the Shang Dynasty architectural pottery had just
emerged and so boasted few varieties. In fact, pottery was used almost
exclusively to make water pipes, which were made mostly from gray clay
pottery with the occasional red clay pottery. The body texture was crude
and formation was mostly through a combination of coiling and hand
kneading, followed by the use of the wheel to trim the shape. Some were
formed with the potter’s wheel and model. Pipe surfaces were decorated
with rope patterns, scratched marks or string patterns. The rope pattern on
the end of some pipes was erased so that two pipes could fit tightly together.
Lots of pottery water pipes of the late Shang Dynasty have been found at
Yinxu in Anyang, Henan. The pipes may be divided into three groups,
based on their shape. The first is cylindrical with one end bigger than the
other. The second is cylindrical with two ends of the same size. This type,
made of gray clay pottery, had even pipe mouths and were decorated with
rope patterns and string patterns on the surface. When used, two pipes were
connected by the even mouths and then buried in the earth. The third type is
“T”-shaped, which was the same as the second type except for an additional
section on the side whose diameter was the same as the main pipe. Its
function is the same as today’s three-way pipes, that is, to connect pipes
perpendicular to each other.
    Architectural pottery experienced unprecedented development in the
Western Zhou. While the production of pottery water pipes continued, there
also emerged plain tiles, semicircle-shaped tiles, and eave tiles for building

roofs of large-scale palace buildings, as well as architectural pottery for
other purposes such as tile nails and bricks, a major achievement in the
history of Chinese architecture. Since then bricks and tiles have become
important building materials and firing them became a major part of pottery
production.
   Many semicircle-shaped tiles from the Western Zhou have been found
in modern-day Shaanxi. The tiles were decorated with interlacing rope
patterns on which there are exquisite cloud patterns carved in double lines.
Some of the tiles have cylindrical or conical tile nails in between. There
were also plain tiles decorated on the outer surface with rope patterns and
various eave tiles in the shape of a half circle. Semicircle-shaped tiles
installed with eave tiles were also attached with cylindrical tile nails.5
   The shaping of semicircle-shaped and plain tiles was an advance on the
crafting of pottery water pipes in the Shang Dynasty. Firstly, the coiling
technique was used to build a cylindrical greenware with one end bigger
than the other just like the waterpipes. The greenware was then perfected
with the potter’s wheel and stamped with rope patterns. Then it was cut
from the inside into two halves and thus two semicircle-shaped tiles with
one end bigger than the other was achieved. The same procedures were
used to make relatively larger cylindrical greenware, which were then cut
into three equal pieces to make three plain tiles with one end wider than the
other. The tile greenware was then attached with conical tile nails. Eave
tiles, used to cover the smaller ends of semicircle-shaped tiles, were in the
shape of a circle or semicircle. Eave tiles in the Western Zhou were mostly
plain, while some were decorated with simple images. These semicircle
tiles, plain tiles and eave tiles were almost all made of rough gray clay
pottery. Some were red and others yellowish gray. The tile surface was
mostly decorated with thick rope patterns. Some also had various scratch
marks on top of the rope patterns.6 From the large size of the tiles we may
infer that the architecture of the Western Zhou was already huge.

3.5 Conclusion
3.5.1 Collapse of Primitive Religious Patterns
The Zhou Dynasty represented an essential transition period during which
Chinese society moved from primitive totem worship, dance, music and

sorcery rites to feudal patriarchal law and a ritual system. Over this period
the ancient Chinese synthesized and standardized various totem taboos and
ritual celebrations left over from primitive clan society and transformed
them from primitive unwritten customary law into written codes and
regulations featuring strict hierarchical ranks. People stepped away from the
intuitive worship of gods and a fanatical fear of ghosts towards worshipping
ancestors, loyalty to the monarch, and filial piety to parents.
   With such a change in cultural values and social trends, the shape design
and decoration style of ritual objects and daily vessels also underwent
changes. Ceramics were no exception. Pottery emulating bronze ritual
vessels in the beginning of the Western Zhou still had animal patterns like
those on Shang Dynasty bronzewares—such as taotie and kuilong. But the
patterns were no longer as mysterious, deterring or ferocious as those of the
Shang Dynasty. Instead, they were more beautiful and exquisite as a form
of decoration. Thus, the beast patterns had lost their religious meaning and
served only as decorations. One example is the Gray Pottery li with Beast
Faces mentioned above, a collection held in the National Museum of China.
A clay gray pottery ware from the early Zhou Dynasty, it has an outwardly
extended mouth, narrow neck, and a belly decorated with three sets of beast
face patterns, one of which resembles a goat’s face. Though it has bulging
eyes and large horns like the others, the eyes are mild, and the expression is
pleasant. The large horns are carved with exquisite patterns. In addition,
most beast face patterns of the Shang Dynasty are set against a background
of yunlei patterns, yet this ware uses mat patterns as the backdrop. Yunlei
has strong symbolic and religious connotations while the mat pattern is
mostly only a background, a decorative form. These all point to the
conclusion that the Zhou Dynasty was transforming from primitive rule by
deities in the Shang to rule by man in the early stages of feudalism.
   By the mid-Western Zhou, mysterious beast patterns typical of the Xia
and Shang dynasties such as taotie and kuilong gradually disappeared, and
geometric patterns including qiequ, double circle patterns, yunlei, circles,
zigzags, checks, basket patterns, mat patterns, leaf vein patterns, teeth-
shaped patterns, scratch marks, string patterns, “S”-shaped patterns, and
raised bumps became the mainstream. Such geometric patterns, with their
soft, mellow, orderly and elegant style, embodied the significance of rites
and the spirit of music that were unique to the Zhou Dynasty.

3.5.2 Drinking Vessels and Dou as Sacrificial Ware
The Zhou Dynasty prohibited alcohol since they believed the Xia and
Shang had lost their regime due to drunken indulgence. There were thus
few varieties of drinking vessels in the Zhou Dynasty, and instead the
number of dou, an ancient food vessel featuring a shallow plate with a high
stem, increased, because drinking vessels were also sacrificial wares and
their place had to be taken by some other. The literal meaning of the
Chinese character for rites, 礼 (or in traditional Chinese: 禮), is to put sacrifice
in a dou to offer to the deities in order to win their blessing. Thus, at the
time, the dou was not only a type of food container but also an important
sacrificial vessel. The Book of Rites (the Liji) states: “Those above 60 shall
be seated and those in their fifties shall stand to show respect to the elderly.
Those in their sixties shall use three dou, those in their seventies shall use
four, eighties five and nineties six, so as to demonstrate the importance of
providing for the aged”. This shows that respect for the aged was an
important part of the “rites, and that the number of dou owned by an
individual was an indication as to their position and status. Similarly, only
the king was allowed to use nine ding. In the early years of the Western
Zhou, pottery dou mostly had short circular feet, while by the end of the
Western Zhou most were bell-shaped with long stems and the thin middle
section of the stem had a raised ridge. It is understood now that pottery dou
became more and more prescribed towards the end because it was used as a
ritual vessel.

3.5.3 The Rites of Zhou and Its Aesthetics
The Western Zhou was an important link in the history of Chinese arts and
culture. During this period the power of the king and the power of clans
were closely connected to build a national patriarchal regime with the
Zongfa system as its basis, putting down roots and setting the norm for the
development of Chinese society for thousands of years to come.
Meanwhile, the cultural and artistic values established in this period were
also to influence the Chinese literatis aesthetic preferences for thousands of
years to come. The image of the truly virtuous man held high by the rites of
Zhou has been the ideal image pursued by Chinese men of letters for
thousands of years. Although ceramic art itself did not witness any notable
achievements during the Western Zhou, the aesthetic pursuit established in

this period would continue to influence the highest aspirations and
standards of Chinese porcelain, namely, the pursuit of a jade-like color.
   Jade wares were already important ritual objects back in the time of the
Liangzhu Culture. Jade was considered the essence of the sun and moon
and a medium for communication with deities. Thus, it was made into jade
cong and jade bi (round flat pieces of jade with a hole in the center) to
represent the power of clan leaders. Many jade ritual objects and ornaments
have been unearthed at Shang sites. By the Zhou Dynasty, while the values
previously attached to jade were preserved, as Zhou people advocated high
spiritual and moral qualities, jade also became associated with a noble,
elegant and perfect character. Hence, drawing an analogy between jade and
virtue has since become a unique trait of Chinese culture. The Book of Rites
speaks of jade in the following terms: “Men of noble character compare
virtue to jade. The mellow luster of jade is benevolence, its solid texture is
wisdom, its square yet harmless corners are righteousness, and its weight is
rites; when struck, it gives a clear and echoing sound, which is music;
minor flaws do not impair its perfection, and that is loyalty”. This
description bestows an extremely high regard to the color, sound and
texture of jade, and in a personified manner. The color and texture of jade
later became the aspiration of Chinese porcelain. Though this quest was not
fulfilled in the Zhou Dynasty, in later dynasties jade-like celadon and white
porcelain with diverse hues and textures have been the mainstream of
Chinese porcelain. The trend reached a climax in the Song Dynasty when it
found perfect expression in the azure porcelain of the Ru kilns, the crab
blue porcelain of the Guan kilns, the light greenish blue and plum green
porcelain of the Longquan kilns, and the qingbai (bluish white) porcelain of
the Jingdezhen kilns. Apart from the color and luster, the warm and mellow
texture and the luscious appearance of jade are also aesthetic standards of
porcelain making that were followed generation after generation.
   The ceramic history of China is like a vivid and dynamic stroke in a
traditional Chinese painting, which, accomplished with one sweep of the
brush, might skip in places, but the energy remains. The Zhou Dynasty was
an incubation period for ceramic art. It was like the part of that ink stroke
that was seemingly discontinued but was in fact preparing for denser ink, a
more spectacular future.

4.1 Introduction
4.1.1 An Era of Cultural Transformation
The Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods were a time of so-
called “shattered rites and destroyed music”. It was a time of crisis for the
aristocratic society, its system and beliefs. Prior to the Spring and Autumn
period, war had been an aristocratic activity—war chariots, horses and
bronze weapons were owned by only a small number of people, and battles
were fought on open plains, where aristocratic families measured their
bravery and strength against each other and infantry, made up of peasants,
played only a minor role. But since the Warring States period, with the
decline of traditional rites and the patriarchal order, the nature of war
changed, and battles became bloodier. Now war was no longer a means of
demonstrating strength or expressing leniency to win repute when
necessary. Instead, it became a means of defeating the enemy and
conquering lands. Previously, practicing martial arts was a tradition of the
nobility, like sacrificial rites. War and religion were at one. Yet from the
Warring States period, commanding warfare was no longer a job for the
nobility, but the full-time role of tacticians and strategists. War and religion
began to separate and the sacrificial rites that used to accompany warfare

began to disintegrate. Such change inevitably brought sweeping
transformation to society, customs, the economy and to thought. The
appearance of ironware and coin casting brought revolutionary changes to
the social life of the time as well. The penetration of the northern and
western nomadic peoples and their cultures onto the central plains, bundled
with the emergence of large numbers of new thoughts and ideas about
revitalizing the kingdom by various schools greatly stimulated the
handicraft and fine arts industry that had stagnated in the Western Zhou.
Metal smiths and lacquer craftsmen of the Spring and Autumn period
created many new varieties that were suited to the time.
   Under the impact of such a revolutionary era, the ceramics industry also
acquired great vigor. With the progress of manufacturing and commerce,
the expansion of cities, and the development of commodity exchange,
ceramic production during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States
periods became more concentrated and specialized. The widespread use of
various iron tools enabled the production of more exquisite and diverse
ceramic handicrafts. Previously only bronzewares had inscriptions, while at
this time inscriptions also started appearing on pottery and were called
pottery inscriptions. Some pottery inscriptions indicated the wares were
produced by the government while some wares were engraved with names,
which differed from the marks of official workshops. The name
inscriptions, square, rectangular or circular, were in seal script and cut in
intaglio. Products from the same workshop were inscribed with different
names, indicating the workshop was run by a group of independent
craftsmen. This shows that from the Spring and Autumn period, social
organizations in different states turned from a clan-based management
system into a family-based system, and thus lots of private ceramic
workshops run by families came into being.
   Many pottery wares unearthed in Linzi were inscribed with place names
such as “Taoli” and “Douli”, with the latter mostly found on dou with
shallow plate. This indicates that some places were specialized in the
production of certain varieties of pottery. Pottery inscriptions were mostly
stamped onto the surface with a seal. The seals, apart from some bronze
ones, were mostly also made of pottery. The characters of the seal mostly
carried the birthplace and name of the craftsman. The inscriptions are of
inestimable value for the study of the Chinese written language, geography

and ceramic workshops of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States
periods.

4.1.2 Frontier Expansion and Diversification of Ceramic Types
During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States, China further expanded
its frontier and became a multi-ethnic country. Vast differences in
geographic environment, tradition and life customs from one place to
another meant that the ceramic products in different places were bound to
be different. The southeast coastal areas were pervaded by gray pottery,
imprinted hard pottery and primitive porcelain while other regions mainly
used clay gray pottery and, less frequently, sandy pottery. By the later years
of the Warring States period, with the intensification of economic and
cultural exchanges, commonalities of ceramic products among all regions
began to appear. For instance, substituting bronze burial objects with
pottery ding, dou and pots became a common practice in all states, and a
sort of thin-collar spherical-bottomed jar with thin rope patterns was found
in all seven major states. While cultural uniformity was strengthened,
different parts of the country retained their own characteristics in the
production of daily use ceramics.
   While existing ceramic types including gray pottery, imprinted hard
pottery, primitive porcelain and architectural pottery were retained and
developed, a new ceramic type—obscure pattern pottery—appeared in
modern-day Henan, Shanxi, Shandong, and elsewhere. Obscure pattern
pottery emerged after the Shang and Zhou dynasties as rope pattern pottery
declined. It began production in the Spring and Autumn period and
achieved greater development in the Warring States period.
   Another new ceramic type was painted pottery, which originated first in
the central plains and then spread to modern-day Hunan, Jiangxi, and
Guangdong south of the Yangtze River as well as to northwest and
northeastern areas. Its popularity reached much wider regions than the
obscure pattern pottery. Painted pottery was mainly used as burial objects,
and its rise was attributed to the funeral practice of replacing bronze burial
objects with pottery ones in the Warring States period. At the same time,
pottery figurines, serving as burial objects as a substitute for living persons,
pottery models of various objects, and animal pottery sculptures were also
developed, laying the foundation for the appearance of large quantities of
pottery figurines and sculptures in the Han Dynasty.

While new ceramic types developed, white pottery that was once in
vogue in the Shang Dynasty declined during the Spring and Autumn period
due to its time-consuming production process and low output and the
development of alternatives such as imprinted hard pottery and primitive
porcelain, never to step back onto the stage of history again.

4.2 Gray Pottery in the Spring and Autumn and
Warring States Periods
4.2.1 Gray Pottery and Daily Life
Gray pottery in the Spring and Autumn period was mainly clay pottery,
followed by sandy pottery. There were also sandy red and sandy brownish
gray pottery. Varieties mostly featured flat bottoms and three feet, or at
times a circular foot. Owing to changes in people’s lifestyles, vessels for
daily use were different from those of previous dynasties and continued to
change constantly. Common cooking vessels of the time included li, fu and
zeng, with li being the most numerous. In the early Spring and Autumn
period, li had large, plump bag-shaped feet and there was oblate belly
pottery li with fei-leng ridges emulating bronze li. Towards the end of the
Spring and Autumn period the bottom of pottery li became almost spherical
and only three slightly raised small bag-shaped feet were left in the middle
of the base. In the end, li evolved into fu with a spherical bottom. Food
vessels included dou, yu, and plates. Pottery dou also underwent some
changes. In the early Spring and Autumn, the part connecting the plate and
the stem had ridges on the outside and angles on the inside and by the later
years of the period the angles on the inside had disappeared. The bell-
shaped base under the stem also grew taller. Pottery dou in the central
plains during the Spring and Autumn period were mostly carved with words
and marks on the inside. Used at the time to contain vegetables, the dou had
either deep or shallow plates, but all had long stems which suited the habit
of having meals whilst seated on the ground. For pottery yu, the change was
in the belly which evolved from a round shape to a folded one. Containers
included urns, jars and basins. Pottery urns mostly had small mouths, high
collars, round shoulders, deep bellies and flat bottoms. Pottery jars
developed into high collar jars. Pottery basins once had slanting horizontal
rims and slightly swollen vertical bellies, but they now evolved into slightly

raised rims and round plump bellies, which offered easier sealing and a
larger capacity. These were highly practical and economical wares for daily
use.
    In the Warring States period gray pottery was widely used in all the
states and ethnic minority ruled areas. Varieties were many, including daily
use vessels, production tools, sculptures and burial objects.
   The shape design of daily use pottery in the early Warring States period
was almost the same as that of the late Spring and Autumn period, and only
underwent notable changes in the middle of the Warring States period.
Pottery products were still dominated by sandy gray and clay gray pottery,
complemented by some sandy red and brown pottery. Daily use wares were
mostly made of clay pottery. Only cooking vessels like fu were made of
sandy pottery. Gray pottery, fired at high temperature, was hard and mostly
light gray or blackish gray in color. Sandy pottery, fired from clay that was
mixed with coarse sand, had a crude and loose texture.
   Of all daily use wares, cooking vessels went through the biggest
changes. By the Warring States period, almost all cooking vessels were
replaced by fu. In the central plains, the shape design and surface
decorations of pottery fu were basically the same as those of the late Spring
and Autumn period, except that even the three small bag-shaped feet
disappeared. That pottery li evolved into pottery fu was obviously related to
the widespread use of the stove. Of particular practical use was a set of
cooking utensils composed of a fu, a zeng and a basin that was popular in
the Qin state. When used, the basin was put on top of the zeng as a lid and
the zeng was placed on the fu. All three matched in size to make a complete
set of tightly fitting cooking utensils. The fu had a short neck to strengthen
the weight bearing capacity of the mouth. The zeng, in the shape of an
upside down basin, had a narrowing lower belly so that it could be used on
fu of various sizes, and had a flat, broad upper rim so that the folded-belly
basin could be securely placed on it without slipping.1

4.2.2 Gray Pottery and Burial Objects
Using pottery instead of bronze burial objects started becoming popular in
the Spring and Autumn period. Archaeologists have recovered practical
pottery such as li, jars, dou, yu and burial objects of similar design in some
Spring and Autumn tombs on the central plains. In tombs of late Spring and
Autumn in modern-day Zhengzhou, archaeologists also found pottery burial

objects emulating bronze ding, lei, yi (gourd-shaped ladles), plates and
more. In tombs south of the Yangtze River gray pottery wares emulating
local imprinted hard pottery have been found, such as zeng and straight-
collar jars. Pottery burial objects of the Warring States period differed from
place to place in terms of variety and shape design due to differences in
geographical location, lifestyle and customs. Some Warring States tombs in
the central plains had ding, dou and pots, some had ding, cases and pots,
and some had additional burial objects such as plates, yi and long-stem
small pots. Some tombs even had painted pottery ducks. Regarding surface
decoration, obscure pattern and colored painting were the most popular. For
instance, pottery burial objects found in tombs of the Warring States period
in modern-day Shandong were mostly a set of ding, dou, pot, plate, yi, and
dui (grain receptacle); those found in tombs of the Chu state in the middle
reaches of the Yangtze River were mostly a set of ding, fu (簠, square grain
receptacle used at sacrificial ceremonies in ancient times), and pot, a set of
ding, dui and pot, or a set of ding, case and pot, and a few tombs also had
pottery fang (square-mouthed wine vessel). (Figs. 4.1 and 4.2).

Fig. 4.2 Pottery gui (簋),

    Pottery burial objects of the same variety differed in design from place
to place. For instance, the pottery pots of the Han state had long necks and
flat bottoms, sometimes with small circular feet; pottery pots of the Qin
state mostly had flat bottoms without circular feet; pottery pots of the Chu
state were slender with tall circular feet or fake circular feet under their
bottoms; pottery pots of the Yan state had short circular feet and standing
knobs on their lids; pottery pots of the Zhao state often had lotus flower
petal decorations on their lids; and the pottery pots of the Qi state had tight
mouths and swollen or oval bellies, while some had movable rings on their
shoulders. For pottery dou, those of Han and Wei had plates resembling
open-mouthed basins, short bell-shaped bases, and bell-shaped knobs on
their lids; those of Chu mostly had shallow plates, long stems and small
bell-shaped bases; and those of Qi mostly had semicircle-shaped plates,
thin, long stems, bell-shaped bases and round knobs on their lids. For ding,
those of Han and Wei mostly had tight mouths, short, plump feet, and
round, swelling lids; those of Qi had oblate oval bodies and lids, and short
feet; and those of Chu had straight bellies, tall feet, and square knobs with

flowery rims on their lids. The shape of other pottery varieties also
displayed local characteristics. (Fig. 4.3).

4.2.3 Modeling and Decorations of Gray Pottery
It can be seen from previous descriptions that while pottery burial objects
increased in the Spring and Autumn period, pottery for daily use decreased
dramatically to the extent that there were less than 10 common varieties,
including li, fu, yu, basins, dou, urns and jars.
   Most of the clay gray pottery wares were shaped with the potter’s
wheel, and some were shaped by model or by hand. Big wares like urns
were first shaped with the coiling technique and then the bottom was added
to the body. Some of the wares reached especially large sizes. Urns could

reach 82 cm in height, 41 cm in top diameter and 90 cm in belly diameter,
and fu could reach 55 cm in height and 88 cm in top diameter. Successful
firing of these large pottery wares during the Warring States period
indicates China’s pottery making techniques had made further progress,
which laid a good foundation for the emergence of high-quality large
pottery sculptures such as the pottery warriors and horses of the Qin
Dynasty.
    In terms of surface decoration, ornamental patterns in the Spring and
Autumn were simpler than those in the Western Zhou, primarily including
only two main patterns, imprinted thick rope pattern and tile whirling
pattern. Rope patterns were mostly applied to the belly of li, fu, jars, basins,
zeng and urns and tile whirling patterns were mostly applied to the shoulder
of li and fu and on the upper belly of basins. Dou and yu mostly had plain or
polished surfaces. Pressed pattern has been found on the shoulder of some
spherical-bottomed jars. Additional stacking pattern is found only on a few
large-sized li, presumably for the purpose of solidifying the ware. Checks
and mat patterns have been found on the belly of some urns and jars in
regions south of the Yangtze River.2 By the Warring States period most
gray pottery wares still had plain or polished surfaces, and fu, jars and urns
were still mostly decorated with rope patterns. Yet additional decorations
like string patterns, scratch marks and obscure patterns were applied to
pottery with plain surfaces or imprinted rope patterns. (Fig. 4.4).

   Apart from the daily use vessels and burial objects mentioned above,
gray pottery of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods also
included some production tools such as spindle whorls, bats and molds, and
small numbers of sculptures such as pottery fish, pottery ducks, pottery
horse heads and pottery tigers.

4.3 Imprinted Hard Pottery
During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, imprinted hard
pottery and primitive porcelain was used in vast areas covering present-day
Jiangsu, Shanghai, Zhejiang and Jiangxi in the middle and lower reaches of
the Yangtze River, present-day Fujian and Guangdong along the southeast
coast, and present-day Guangxi and southern Hunan, and was especially
popular in present-day Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Jiangxi. As important daily
utensils for people living in these areas at that time, imprinted hard pottery
and primitive porcelain accounted for a high proportion of all ceramic
production in regions south of the Yangtze River, especially during the
Warring States period. Yet imprinted hard pottery was still rarely found in
the central plains to the north.
   Imprinted hard pottery of the Spring and Autumn period basically
inherited the features of the Western Zhou. Common varieties were urns,
crocks, bu and fu. Though strong and endurable, imprinted hard pottery had
a coarse texture and was therefore not suitable as drink or food vessels.
They were therefore mostly used as containers and receptacles. Geometric
patterns stamped on the wares included yunlei (Fig. 4.5), leaf veins, small
checks, zigzags, mat pattern and square spirals inherited from the Western
Zhou, along with new patterns including big checks and textile patterns.3

Fig. 4.5 Pot with yunlei pattern, beast head and hoop handle,
Spring and Autumn, top diam.: 7.2 cm, height: 19.8 cm, in the Jiangxi Provincial Museum

   The clay material for imprinted hard pottery of the Spring and Autumn
and Warring States periods usually contained small quantities of impure
substances and sand particles. The firing temperature was high so that the
body was fully sintered and gave off a sonorous sound when struck. Some
wares had a thin layer of transparent matter on the surface. Due to the high
iron content of the clay, the resultant body was usually purplish brown or
reddish brown, the former usually fired at higher temperatures and having a
harder texture and the latter usually fired at relatively lower temperatures
and having a relatively looser texture. The shaping method was still the
coiling technique as in previous dynasties.
   There were not many varieties of imprinted hard pottery in the Warring
States period since they were only containers like urns, crocks, bu, jars,
bowls and yu, yet the decorative patterns varied greatly. Patterns with
religious connotations like qiequ and yunlei that were common in the
Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn periods were no longer commonly
seen. Replacing them were “米”-shaped patterns (米 is the Chinese character
for rice, pronounced /mi/), checks, linen patterns, square spirals, rice sieve
patterns and other such purely decorative patterns that only express textural

diversity and aesthetic appeal. Decorative patterns were chosen based on
the shape and size of the pottery ware to better match it. Urns, crocks and
large jars were often stamped with relatively rough patterns such as “米”-
shaped patterns, checks, rice sieve patterns and rough linen patterns, while
smaller vessels such as yu, bowls and small jars were usually stamped with
more elaborate and finer patterns like the fine linen pattern.
   Small vessels including jars, bowls and yu of the Warring States period,
influenced by contemporaneous bronze and lacquer wares, had exquisite
shapes, very thin walls, stamped fine linen patterns that were neat and
appealing, and often swirl patterns and “S”-shaped stacking patterns stuck
onto the shoulder. The shaping and decorative techniques were much more
advanced than in the Spring and Autumn period. Imprinted hard pottery
was widely used. Differences in geographical environment and social
customs resulted in different varieties, shapes and local characteristics of
imprinted hard pottery in different places. For instance, in modern-day
Zhejiang and Jiangsu, jars and crocks were produced in the greatest number,
followed by bowls, yu, and so on; in modern-day Guangdong and Guangxi,
urns, bu, jars, crocks, vats and gourd-shaped flasks were produced. The big
gourd-shaped flask with four small ears and a flat bottom4, the double-
handled crock with three feet, and the basin with three feet and lid
unearthed in Guangdong had distinct local features.

4.4 Primitive Porcelain
Production zones of primitive porcelain in the Spring and Autumn and
Warring States periods overlapped with production zones of imprinted hard
pottery, namely, the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River,
southeast coastal areas, and modern-day Guangdong and Guangxi.
Primitive porcelain was produced especially in modern-day Jiangsu,
Zhejiang and Jiangxi, i.e., areas that belonged to the Wu, Yue and Chu
cultures of the time. Primitive porcelain saw new development during the
Spring and Autumn period. Compared with that of the Western Zhou,
primitive porcelain produced in modern-day Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Jiangxi
had a finer texture, neater shape, and thinner and more even walls. The
shaping method changed from coiling to the potter’s wheel. Circles of fine
and elaborate swirl patterns started appearing on the inner bottoms of
bowls, plates and yu, and a series of cutting marks appeared on the outer

bottoms. Compared with the Western Zhou, processing of greenware was
more meticulous and the firing skills also improved, greatly raising the
quality and efficiency of primitive porcelain production. The wares had a
thin layer of lime glaze applied, and most appeared blue or yellowish blue
after firing. Some of the glaze was even in thickness and some was
concentrated in sesame-like dots. In modern-day Guangdong, Guangxi and
southern Hunan, the body of primitive porcelain, similar to local imprinted
hard pottery, was mostly purple or grayish red; for glaze color, apart from
yellowish-brown and yellowish green, there were also blackish green and
other hues, albeit all belonging to the blue glaze system with iron the main
coloring agent. These production zones of primitive porcelain were still all
located in southern China. Primitive porcelain from the time has not been
found in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, except for a
tight-mouthed deep-bellied flat-bottomed jar with underglaze check
patterns.5 (Fig. 4.6).

Fig. 4.6 Primitive porcelain cylindrical jar with carved pattern,
Spring and Autumn, top diam.: 19.5 cm, height: 27 cm, in the Palace Museum

    Primitive porcelain of the period began to distinguish itself from
imprinted hard pottery. While imprinted hard pottery still used the coiling
technique, primitive porcelain started adopting the potter’s wheel for
shaping. While imprinted hard pottery was mostly for making containers
due to its rough texture, primitive porcelain was mostly made into drinking
and food vessels and ding, zun and he emulating bronze ritual wares
because of its fine texture, thin walls and blue surface glaze, which allowed
easy contact with people’s mouths and lips and made them easier to clean
with water.
   Drink and food vessels at the time included bowls, plates, zhong
(handle-less cups), saucers and ding. Plates and ding had many designs.
Bowls were made in sets of the same size. Many products including wine

zhong adopted straight cylindrical shapes with an appropriate height and
thin rims, making them light to hold and convenient to use. Pottery ding
emulating bronze ones were varied and exquisite. Pottery he emulating
bronze ones normally had three hoof-shaped feet, a beast-head-shaped
spout and a semicircular hoop handle. The handle was decorated with raised
patterns to symbolize the body of a dragon. There were shallow holes
around the mouth. But the holes did not connect with the belly. Thus, the
wares were probably burial objects. Another representative ware was the
handled cup with blue glaze and a string pattern, now in the collection of
the Shanghai Museum. With a thin layer of bluish yellow glaze and
exquisite, neat, fine string patterns all over the body, the cup indicates that
the pottery making technology with the wheel at that time had reached a
very high level. (Fig. 4.7) In summary, primitive porcelain of the Spring
and Autumn and Warring States periods, with bright, clear glaze color,
delicate, exquisite shape, and neat, beautiful decoration, had distinct
features unique to the time.





Fig. 4.7 Handled cup with blue glaze and string pattern,
Warring States, top diam.: 4.4 cm, height: 11.2 cm, in the Shanghai Museum

During the Warring States period primitive porcelain was often fired in
the same kilns as imprinted hard pottery, although the clay materials,
shaping methods and suitable firing temperatures of the two were not
entirely the same. As a result, the greenware for primitive porcelain, which
required higher temperature, was frequently not fully sintered, while
imprinted hard pottery, which required relatively low temperature, was
appropriately fired to reach full sintering or in some cases even over-fired
such that the body collapsed and the mouth and bottom stuck together.
    Primitive porcelain continued to make advances throughout the 1,000
years from the Shang Dynasty to the Warring States period. Yet by the late
Warring States period primitive porcelain production in areas around
Zhejiang suddenly stopped, probably due to the destruction brought about
by the Chu State’s conquest of Yue and the ensuing wars, while modern-day
Hunan and Guangdong continued their production. It was not until the end
of the Warring States period and the beginning of the Qin and Han
dynasties that ancient potters created a new type of primitive porcelain
different from previous types in terms of shaping, decoration and glazing.
From that time onwards, primitive porcelain continued to develop under
new historical circumstances, until the successful making of porcelain in the
real sense in the Eastern Han Dynasty.

4.5 Pottery with Painting and Other Pottery
Burial Objects
A new pottery type sprang up during the Warring States period, namely,
pottery with painting. Different from painted pottery, which was made by
first painting the greenware and then firing it, pottery with painting was
made by firing plain greenware and then painting on the fired ware. No
further firing was performed after the painting. Thus, the colorings were
prone to fading or peeling off, making such wares pure burial objects, not
suitable for daily use. Pottery with painting appeared early in the late
Neolithic, and was produced in the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties as well
as the Spring and Autumn period. It reached its highest prominence during
the Warring States period, to a large extent due to changes in the funerary
system of the country—from the early and middle Warring States period the
nobility started replacing bronze vessels with pottery ones as burial objects,

leading to the rapid rise of pottery burial object production, and pottery with
painting was a type of funerary ware exclusively used for burial with the
dead.
    In the artifact and fine arts field at the time, not only was bronze
production advanced with a number of new techniques such as gold and
silver decoration, inlay, and line carving, lacquerware making was also
highly developed with diverse production techniques, which all benefited
the development of pottery craftsmanship and brought many new
approaches and varieties to the production of pottery burial objects. Various
decorative means for emulating bronze and lacquer wares emerged and
developed rapidly, including burnishing, obscure image, red painting and
powder painting. Pottery makers hoped to accurately imitate the appearance
of lacquerware and bronzeware through these means, and it was against
such a background that pottery with painting rapidly rose to the occasion.
There were two painting approaches, red painting and powder painting.
Firstly, greenware, coated or polished, was fired in the kiln, then after
firing, decorations of different colors were painted onto it. Red painting
refers to directly applying red coloring on gray, grayish black or brown
pottery. The color is bright, strong and warm. Powder painting mostly used
three colors, red, yellow and white, or black, white and red. Some used two
colors, e.g. red and yellow. Sometimes the colorings were directly applied
to the ware surface. Sometimes red, black or yellow colorings were painted
on a white or yellow background.
    Pottery with painting displayed strong local characteristics, and often
exhibited the influence of other art forms in the same area. For instance, the
Chu state was famous for its exquisite lacquer work, and pottery with
painting unearthed there mostly had signs of lacquerware. The lacquered
pot painted with the panchi (a sinuous dragon/lizard) pattern unearthed in
the Chu state tomb in Yunmeng County, Hubei in 1978 was a typical
example. Made from clay gray pottery, the pot was coated all over with
black lacquer. The neck is encircled by the panchi pattern painted by
drawing small dots with red coloring and then outlining them with gold
powder. The shoulder and belly each have two raised string patterns,
between which the panchi pattern was painted using red coloring and gold
powder. The lower belly was painted with a cloud pattern. Such techniques
—applying lacquer coating, painting images with red coloring and gold
powder—all came from lacquerware decorative practices of the time. The

pot is now in the collection of the Yunmeng County Museum. Unearthed at
the same site and time was also a lacquered pottery lidded dou with the
panchi pattern. Similar to the aforementioned pot, the ware is also an
imitation of bronzeware and its decorative style also demonstrates the
influence of lacquerware. It also had black lacquer applied all over and then
painted with the panchi pattern, cloud pattern and square spirals in triangles
with red coloring and gold powder.
   The pottery pot with red painting, unearthed at a Warring States period
tomb in Songyuan, Changping, Hebei and now in the collection of the
Beijing Capital Museum is also a typical pottery ritual object emulating
bronzeware. The complexity and exquisiteness of its shape design is rarely
seen in pottery wares pre-dating it. It has a rectangular neck, round belly,
and circular foot. There is a pair of handles on the neck in the shape of
beasts turning their heads ready to leap, and a pair of rings with a beast-
head base on the other two sides of the neck. The lower part of the neck and
the belly each have four clearings in the shape of triangles and ovals,
similar to the clearings frequently seen on painted porcelain of the Ming
and Qing dynasties, and red paint is applied to the clearings. (Fig. 4.8).

Fig. 4.8 Pottery pot with red painting,
Warring States, top diam.: 20 cm, height: 71 cm, in the Beijing Capital Museum

   Decorative patterns of pottery with painting were mostly drawn on the
neck, shoulder and belly of pots, dou, high-stem pots, plates, yi, etc.
Common decorative patterns included band or stripe patterns, line patterns,
rhombus checks, ripple patterns, yunlei, dragon and phoenix patterns,
persimmon calyx patterns, double curve patterns, rectangle patterns and
panchi patterns. On pottery buried with the dead in tombs of the Zhao state
during the Warring States period, there are detailed images of hunting,
animals, fish, tortoises, etc. meticulously sketched using the line carving
technique. The decorative images on these burial objects, painted and
carved alike, obviously imitated the decorative patterns of bronze and
lacquer ware. Such decorative methods assimilated from other

contemporaneous arts enriched the artistic expression of pottery at the time.
Though pottery with painting had no practical value, its rich expressive
means and masterly craftsmanship gave it an important position in the
history of Chinese ceramics. It is a real pity that, because the wares were
not fired after painting, they mostly lose the bright colorings painted onto
them when unearthed.
   Apart from pottery with painting, there was another type of pottery
burial object during the Warring States period. That is obscure pattern
pottery, another great creation of the potters of the time. They gently
pressed tools with smooth ends on the surface of half-dried gray clay
greenware to make string patterns, rhombus checks, ripple patterns, “S”
patterns, flower petal patterns, etc. When pressed, the density of the
greenware wall increased. Thus, after firing, patterns of bright blackish gray
color emerged.
   Another type of burial object was pottery figurines. Pottery figurines of
the period were relatively small, some only five centimeters tall and the
largest no taller than 15 cm. The firing temperature was poor, the handicraft
rough, and the figurines had tool marks all over them. During the Warring
States period, burying living persons with the dead was rare compared with
the Shang and Western Zhou, and instead burying wooden or pottery
figurines with the dead as a substitute for live persons had become popular.
There were also pottery animal sculptures as burial objects, some of which,
vividly designed with brilliant colors, were among the best pottery
sculptures of the time, such as the painted pottery duck found in Erligang,
Zhengzhou, the duck zun unearthed in Xingtai6 and Handan7, and the flying
bird on a pillar in a plate8 discovered in the Zhongshan State Mausoleum in
Pingshan County, Hebei. In addition, pottery models of chariots, oxen, he,
etc. have been found in Warring States period tombs in modern-day Shaanxi
and Gansu, predecessors of various pottery models frequently found in Han
dynasty tombs in later years.

4.6 Architectural Pottery
Architectural pottery during the Spring and Autumn period was similar to
that of the Western Zhou, being dominated by pottery water pipes and
various tiles. Yet compared with the Western Zhou, they were much thinner
and lighter and had more delicate and complex decorations. Smaller and

thinner plain tiles, semicircle-shaped tiles and eave tiles lightened the
pressure on roofs, a major improvement in architectural pottery at the time.
   During the Warring States period the states were all busy putting up
buildings in their capitals. The construction of cities and palaces pushed
architectural pottery toward rapid development. While tiles and tile nails
continued to be produced and further developed, various bricks for paving
and wall building were invented. It can be said that at the time, most of the
bricks and tiles used in architecture in China were already created and had
reached a relatively high technical level.
   The brick is an important architectural material in China. Most brick
varieties were invented during the Warring States period. Yet at that time
they were mostly used for paving or wall tiling and did not seem to be used
for building walls. There were two types of paving bricks. The first type,
collectively called square bricks or rectangular bricks, were small, thin
bricks shaped by compression molding and decorated with patterns on the
surface. The other type was large hollow rectangular bricks over one meter
in length and two to three centimeters in wall thickness. Large, strong, even
and visually pleasing, such hollow bricks were often used to pave floors and
stairs in large architectural endeavors, adding magnificence and loftiness to
the buildings. They were ideal building materials and could also be used to
replace wooden boards to make outer coffins.9 Also invented during this
period were rectangular frog bricks and special bricks with a “几(ji)”-shaped
longitudinal section. The latter was relatively widely used during the period
for it has been found in modern-day Yixian, Xianyang, Linzi, and
elsewhere. With mortise and tenon on both ends, the bricks could be joined
together and were probably used on house ridges. A type of balustrade brick
was found at the site of the Secondary Capital of Yan. Some of the bricks
were carved with beast patterns on both sides. The crouching beasts with
lowered heads and raised tails were very vivid. Such bricks are the earliest
balustrade building material found in China to date. Figure 4.9 is a
patterned brick from the Warring States period. Made of clay gray pottery,
it is a floor brick imprinted with square spirals in rhombuses. Its strong
texture and exquisite pattern indicate that at that time the pottery firing
technique and decoration workmanship had reached a high level.

Fig. 4.9 Patterned brick,
Warring States, length: 43.5 cm, width: 31.5 cm, in the National Museum of China

    Tiles appeared in the Western Zhou, achieved a certain development in
the Spring and Autumn period, and further matured during the Warring
States with more varieties and practical functions. Eave tiles developed
particularly well during the Warring States. Compared with those of the
Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn periods, eave tiles, now with more
varieties and more exquisite decorative patterns, were both building
materials and artworks. Installed at the end of rows of tiles, eave tiles
facilitate drainage from rooftops, protect the edge of eaves, and add to the
aesthetic appeal of buildings. Eave tiles during the Warring States were
mostly semicircular. Later round ones were introduced. They were mold
imprinted with decorative patterns that differed from place to place. The
semicircular eave tiles of the Yan state were particularly exquisite and the
patterns were dominated by taotie (Fig. 4.10), complemented by “山”-shaped
patterns (山 is the Chinese character for mountain, pronounced /shan/), beast
pairs, bird pairs, window bar patterns, etc. Those of the Qi state were
mostly imprinted with tree and double beasts or tree and double eyes,
besides which there were also tree and double riders (Fig. 4.11), tree and
“田”-shaped patterns (田 is the Chinese character for field, pronounced /tian/),
ripple patterns, double birds, dragon patterns, and beast face patterns. The

Qin state generally used round eave tiles whose patterns were dominated by
various cloud images, complemented by deer, birds, insects, lotus flowers
and sunflower patterns.
