    In the Warring States period the design of pottery water pipes was also
more mature than before. Water systems composed of pottery pipes of
various forms were adopted, some for water conveyance and some for
drainage, which not only provided convenient drinking water for city
residents at the time, but also discharged sewage and waste water to ensure
the cleanliness and sanitation of the city. The discovery of large numbers of
pottery pipes in the ruins of ancient cities all over the country fully
demonstrates that the Chinese people were mindful of water use and
drainage in city buildings as early as the Warring States period, and solved
it properly by burying water pipes.

4.7 Conclusion
4.7.1 Tendency Towards Secular Preferences in Ceramic Types
The Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods witnessed China’s
transition from slavery to feudalism and was a period of great upheaval and
change. The appearance of ironware greatly promoted the growth in
production rates, gave birth to new production relations and new thought,
and posed considerable challenges for old production relations and ideas. In
such an era of reformation in all fields, ceramics, as both daily use vessels
and a carrier of cultural concepts, was no exception.
   The introduction of ironware led to great progress in the handicraft
industry in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. As has been
mentioned in the introduction to this chapter, pottery inscriptions unearthed
and archaeological excavations of handicraft workshop ruins indicate the
handicraft industry at the time was run by both the official sector and the
private sector. Official handicraft production undoubtedly served the
government, while private handicraft production served the market. It was
for commerce and exchange. The existence of private pottery workshops
indicates that at the time there was already an exchange market for
ceramics. Inscriptions on pottery of the Qin state contained not only the
place of residence of the maker, but also “Xian Market”, “Xian Pavilion” or
in abbreviation “Xian” before the address to indicate the market
membership of the maker (the capital of the Qin State was Xianyang). It
was the same with pottery inscriptions of the Qi state, some of which were

stamped with official seals indicating their market membership. The pottery
unearthed at Shuihudi, Yunmeng County in Hubei was mostly printed with
“Anlu market pavilion”. Mr. Qiu Xigui pointed out that only those with
market membership were allowed to formally engage in commerce and the
handicraft industry or the so called “peddler business”, and were required to
pay tax to the state.10 In other words, the market was the place where
commercial transactions were conducted, and market membership was a
license artisans had to obtain in order to conduct transactions. The market’s
administrative organ was the “market pavilion”, which on the one hand
maintained the order of the market and on the other hand collected taxes on
merchants and turned them in. Handicraftsmen taking products to the
market to sell or trade had to pay taxes as well.
   The emergence of a ceramics market not only promoted ceramics
production, but also led to the diversification and secularization of ceramic
products. The diversification was driven by the demand to meet the needs
of different classes and groups. Secularization refers to the increase in
purely aesthetic pursuits in the shape and decorative patterns of ceramics in
addition to the religious and practical values that had dominated their
design earlier. In other words, beauty and visual appeal had become an
important aspiration in ceramic decoration, which brought a series of
changes to the shaping and decoration of ceramics. Of course, apart from
changing values and needs, such changes should also be attributed to the
evolution of tools and technology and to the mutual influence of
contemporaneous art forms.

4.7.2 Changes in Shape Brought by a New Lifestyle
Owing to the change in the people’s lifestyle, many old varieties, such as li
and yan, decreased in popularity, and some such as jue and gu disappeared
altogether. At the same time new varieties, rarely found in previous times,
came into being, such as fang, dui, zhong and saucers. Compared with
previous times the vessels were lighter, thinner, more delicate and more
exquisite, a style consistent with contemporaneous bronzeware and
lacquerware. Following social trends, ceramic design moved on from the
thick, heavy and unsophisticated styles featuring primitive simplicity that
dominated the field from primitive times to the Shang and Zhou dynasties
to form a more refined style which was to influence China’s ceramic art in
later periods. Another change was the introduction of lids for most of the

vessels, especially dou, ding, pots and dui. The wide use of lids helped keep
the contents of the vessels warm or clean, and added to the aesthetic value
of the vessels. The knobs on the lids were often three vivid and interesting
animals, such as oxen, ducks and birds, or just three straight supports.
When placed upside down, such lids could also be used as dou or plates.
These accessories were on the one hand knobs or supports, and on the other
hand ornamentation with characteristics of the historic period.

4.7.3 Increases in Decorative Subject
Considerable changes in pottery decoration took place in terms of the
theme, image and composition of decorative patterns. The themes were
richer than before and the more popular included panchi, dragons, phoenix,
birds, deer, fish, tigers, clouds and swirls. Though many of the animal
patterns had already appeared in the Shang and Zhou dynasties, they were
mostly used on bronzewares at the time and not on ceramic vessels. During
the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods they started to be
applied to pottery, though mostly on various pottery vessels with painting
and not on other pottery types. Some traditional animal patterns such as
taotie and kuilong became rare and were replaced with panchi and panhui
(sinuous snake), which in fact evolved from the kuilong pattern. In terms of
image types, while abstract geometric images continued to occupy an
important position, pictographic images of natural objects increased
dramatically, especially realistic portrayals of some animals. Still, most of
the natural objects portrayed were in silhouette and were composed of
simple lines. Compelling evidence of the common understanding that
Chinese calligraphy and painting share the same origin, the design of
animal images during the Warring States period highly resembled the
structure of Chinese characters in the bronze inscriptions and seal script of
the time, both featuring squares and circles encircling each other with
smooth and changeable curves. In terms of composition, metrical patterns
following certain rules and forms, such as dual continuous patterns,
quadruple continuous patterns and patterns confined to a frame, which were
heavily used from the time of primitive painted pottery, continued their
prevalence during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. But
decorative languages were richer and more diversified than before as free
composition began to be adopted. Not restricted by metrics or the size of a
frame, free composition allowed animals and landscape to be arranged in

the same picture and were suitable for depicting relatively complex scenes.
The approach was used more prominently on lacquer and bronzewares, on
which there emerged large-scale pictures depicting people’s lives and
production scenes, such as mulberry leaf harvesting and silkworm breeding,
attacks and occupation on land and water, chariots and horse hunting and
music and dance banquets, all of which have been found on bronzewares of
the Warring States period. Such complex life scenes and expressive
approaches were never seen in previous times and were made possible by
free composition, which broke the confinement and restrictions of
traditional decorative patterns and brought new vigor to the decorative style
of the vessels.
    Naturally, such complex scenes as portrayed on bronzewares did not
really appear on ceramics at the time, but since contemporaneous art forms
always exert some influence on each other, similar scenes could be found
on ceramics, especially on pottery with painting, firstly because painting
with brush on lacquer coating allowed much higher expressive capacity
compared with other ceramic types of the same period, and secondly,
because pottery with painting, such as burial vessels, strived to imitate the
decorative approaches of the then more exquisite bronzeware and
lacquerware. As a result, pottery with painting closely resembled
lacquerware in painting style. Lacquerwares of the Warring States period
were dominated by black and red, complemented by golden, white, reddish
brown, yellow, grayish green, and more, and pottery with painting also
mainly used these colors. It was also like lacquerware in subject matter and
decorative method.
   Since the painting on such pottery was not fired, the pictures faded and
blurred as time passed. But from the remnant images surviving today we
can imagine how brilliant and stunning they must have been when the
vessels had just been made. Although pottery with painting was only a kind
of burial ware, its remarkable painting craftwork laid the foundation for the
development of ceramic painting in later times. (Figs. 4.12 and 4.13).

   To summarize, a tolerant and active academic atmosphere, a maturing
commodity market and the introduction of ironware elevated the ceramic
art of the Warring States period to a new level. Its aesthetic boundary went
beyond the mysterious and awe-inspiring beauty representing kingship of
the Xia and Shang dynasties and beyond the metric, moderate and peaceful
beauty of the Western Zhou to create a much richer beauty full of
associations with bronze inscriptions and seal script, drawing the art form a
step further from primitive mythology towards realistic humanity.

5.1 Introduction
5.1.1 Transition from Aristocratic Society to Plebeian Society
In 221 BCE, the Qin State conquered all of the other Warring States and put
an end to the turbulence which had lasted over 500 years from the Eastern
Zhou. Though the newly unified Qin Dynasty lasted only 15 years (221 to
207 BCE), its founder, Qin Shi Huang (literally “First Emperor of Qin”),
turned the page on the history of China and the world by establishing a new
country based on a new “nationality”, i.e., the China we see today. This was
also why the King of Qin called himself the “First Emperor”, that is, the
first monarch of a large country with all of China as its territory.
   The new country ruled over a wide area with a clear geographical
boundary—the Great Wall in the north, the coastline in the southeast and
the mountain ridges in the southwest. It not only integrated the many ethnic
groups down from the Xia and Shang dynasties to the Zhou Dynasty into
one new “nationality”, but also, with the power of a centralized monarchy,
fused local cultures in different parts of the country into a unified
civilization with the central plains culture at its center, thus establishing a
new unified country with Confucianism as its base.
   Before Qin unified China, the three “central” dynasties in the central
plains adopted a placatory style of rule and did not exercise strong control
over vassal states who paid allegiance to the common sovereign. In fact, the

relationship between the sovereign and the states was somewhat akin to that
of the previous alliance of chieftain states during the Neolithic period. In
times of political crisis or celebration, the Zhuhou responded to the call of
the king to offer military support or to have an audience with the king.
These states included forces beyond the rule of the Zhou Dynasty, areas
called “ethnic minorities or “barbarians” in the later feudal era.1
   Emperor Qin Shi Huang set up a new imperial system of centralized
power. He abolished the Zhuhou and states, replaced them with a non-
hereditary bureaucratic system supported by a payment system, and formed
a new administrative system comprised of four central and local levels: the
central government, the prefecture (state), the county and the township.
   Qin consolidated the multiple ethnic groups and newly conquered states
into one unified country, and standardized the writing system, measurement
units, length of cart axles, and currency. A national transport system
comprising eight roads connecting the capital with major regions of the
country including the southwest and the south and canals linking the east,
west and southwest was built to facilitate transportation of people and cargo
within the country. The biggest public works project of the Qin was the
unification, with about 400,000 laborers, of diverse state walls erected
during the Warring States period into a single Great Wall of China that
extended 2,250 km along the northern border. The Great Wall was to be the
most important line of defense for China through later dynasties. It also for
the first time effectively separated the agricultural and nomadic civilizations
in the territory of China, forming a distinction between “Han” and “non-
Han” and giving birth to a new “ethnic group” south of the Great Wall with
the agricultural civilization of the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties at its core.
The new ethnic group gradually developed different views on the ethnic
groups outside the Great Wall and came to regard them as barbaric
foreigners. Thus, during the Qin and Han dynasties the territory of the “Han
ethnic group” and the concept of “Han Chinese” first appeared in the
history of China.2
   The establishment of the Qin Dynasty declared an end to the chaotic era
of the Warring States. China entered a feudal imperial age, where the
unification of politics, the economy and culture further consolidated the
centralization of power. The Han Dynasty inherited the centralized imperial
system of the Qin. The unified country and the vast territory greatly
enhanced the strength of the Qin and Han dynasties, especially the Han

Dynasty, a golden age of Chinese civilization during which feudal rule was
solidified and the development of Chinas politics, economy and culture
reached an unprecedented zenith.
   Qian Mu argues that in the Qin and Han dynasties China began its
transformation from an ancient aristocratic society to a plebeian society.
The Qin Dynasty was a preparatory period for such a transformation and by
the Han Dynasty China began to become a simple peasant society. In
ancient China the political power was in the hands of aristocrats down to
the Spring and Autumn and Warring States. By the middle and late Warring
States, freelance scholars started participating in the organization of the
political regime, which was the precursor to civilian scholar participation in
politics. Scholars since the Warring States period represented civilians, yet
most of them still lived off the support of the aristocratic class. Then in the
Han Dynasty the “Five Classics Doctoral system” was established. The
government provided education where “doctoral students” graduated after a
one-year study program and were assigned positions by the government.
Most of those who achieved first degree examination results worked as
bodyguards and court officials of the emperor, while those who achieved
secondary degrees and lower were designated positions in local
governments, mainly in their respective native places. Thus, over time local
government official positions were gradually taken by young graduates of
these state-run universities.3
   The formation of this system had a very direct relationship with the
emperors of the day. Emperor Gaozu of Han (Liu Bang), born to an
ordinary peasant family, believed the Confucian concept “Mandate of
Heaven” and the idea of governance by virtue were beneficial to enhancing
his rule. Emperor Wu of Han broke the convention of the older-generation
noble class’ hold on the nation’s levers of power by appointing the
grassroots scholar Gongsun Hong as prime minister. He also appointed the
Confucians Dong Zhongshu and Tian Fen as prime minister. The
engagement of Confucian scholars in government services created a new
bureaucratic class made up primarily of scholars, the Shi class. Emperor Wu
promoted Confucian doctrines exclusive of any other school of thought and
in effect revered and elevated Confucianism as the national philosophy so
as to build a new national administrative system based on it. State power
worked jointly with Confucian officials and rediscovered, collated and
compiled a large number of Confucian classics. The Imperial College and

county-level schools across the country were set up to teach and promote
Confucianism. The central government issued nationwide edicts selecting
officials at all levels according to Confucian moral standards and their
mastery of the Confucian classics, with the criteria being filial piety,
honesty, ability, uprightness, literature, etc. These “Shi”, deeply influenced
by the core Confucian beliefs, carried a strong sense of responsibility and
need for social stability, which made them the perfect candidates as
government officials.4 The implementation of this official selection system
transformed the government, formed by royal family members and military
aristocracies, into one comprised mainly of selected intellectuals. This was
the first “government by literati” in Chinese history.5
   The new social landscape described above contributed to the
development of the ceramics industry. Under the umbrella of national unity,
commercial prosperity was only natural and commercial prosperity was
bound to bring prosperity to the handicraft industry. Amid the tides of
booming commerce emerged fabulously wealthy families that
simultaneously engaged in agriculture (grain or rice production, animal
husbandry, fishing, etc.), manufacturing (textiles, iron casting, and
lacquerware), trade and other industries, and that therefore commanded a
large labor force,6 which brought great progress to ceramics production.
During the Qin and Han dynasties great achievements were made not only
in ceramic art and craftsmanship, but also in the clearer division of labor
among ceramic workshops. The ceramic industry in the Qin and Han
dynasties may be classified into three sectors: workshops directly controlled
by the central government, those run by local governments, and those run
by private individuals. These workshops with different natures produced
different products to serve the needs of different classes. In other words, the
common prosperity of the royal court, local governments and private
workshops jointly promoted the development of the ceramics industry at the
time.
   The prosperity of the handicraft industry and commerce, especially the
rapid development of the salt and iron industries, led to the appearance of
big businessmen. If this trend had continued, China would have become a
commercially advanced country. But the traditional Shi of China, either
Mohist, Taoist, Legalist or Confucian, all condemned luxury and
unnecessary consumption when it is the nature of commercial behavior to
induce and promote unnecessary consumption. This led to social

disparagement of businessmen which was reflected in government
regulations setting restrictions on various aspects of the life of businessmen,
including the residence and utensils they were allowed to occupy or use
when alive and the tombs they were allowed to occupy after death. For
instance, one regulation stipulated that “businessmen shall not wear silk or
take a carriage”. Thus, businessmen might be wealthy but were not
considered honorable, while poor peasants that studied to become scholars
were respected. Once the latter were celebrated, their social status was
much higher than that of businessmen. Hence, businessmen who had made
enough fortune to support their family were all in a hurry to change the
family’s profession by asking their offspring to leave the market and to
attend school, even seeking a distant teacher, and study Confucianism. The
status of businessmen sunk even lower when it came to the Eastern Han. As
described by Qian Mu, “the society of the Eastern Han was centered not on
the nobles, not on the military, and not on the rich, but on the Shi or
intellectuals”.7 In fact, this tradition, i.e. “to be a scholar is to be the top of
society while all other occupations are inferior” was not only a tradition of
the Han dynasty, but continued throughout the history of China.

5.1.2 Ceramic Production Within the New Cultural Context
I believe the tradition of “to be a scholar is to be the top of society while all
other occupations are inferior” was closely associated with the development
of Chinas ceramics industry. More specifically, I believe one reason for the
fact that primitive celadon appeared so early in China and matured during
the Eastern Han when no other country had invented porcelain lay in the
high regard for scholars and the restriction of the luxurious lifestyle during
the Han Dynasty. Before the Han Dynasty Chinese society was centered on
the nobility who led extremely luxurious lives and used bronze and lacquer
wares. Ceramic wares, on the other hand, were of little significance in their
lives and only served as daily utensils or ritual objects of the common
people, and therefore their development received little attention from the
government. Yet when it came to the Han Dynasty, especially the Eastern
Han, the life of the rich was restricted and naturally the use of luxurious
objects was no longer called for. This created an occasion for the simple yet
noble porcelain, which also accorded with the aesthetic preference of the
Chinese literati with its warm and mellow jade-like texture, to rise to the
occasion. Primitive porcelain was mainly used to make burial objects. As

the firing technique matured, it was used more and more for daily life and
had subsequently become the most important material for daily utensils in
the history of China. Ceramic products could be found in every corner of
Chinese people’s lives, imperial nobles and common people alike, and
became an integral part of the cultural activities and everyday lives of the
Chinese. This shows that besides the technological, there were cultural
reasons behind the rise of ceramics.
   The Qin and Han dynasties marked the important transition from
primitive porcelain to porcelain in the real sense. Primitive porcelain
appeared in China in the Shang Dynasty, developed further during the early
and middle Warring States period, then was seriously damaged by warfare
when the Chu State conquered Yue, and so primitive porcelain production
came to a temporary halt in areas around modern-day Zhejiang. Luckily,
during the late Warring States and the Qin Dynasty it was revitalized and
then enjoyed rapid growth over the 300 years from the Western Han to the
Eastern Han, and finally evolved from primitive porcelain to proper
porcelain in the middle and late Eastern Han. The birth of porcelain in the
real sense was a major leap forward in the history of Chinese ceramics and
made China the earliest country in the world to invent porcelain. The
primitive porcelain of the Qin and Han dynasties was mostly ritual objects
emulating bronzewares and was rarely made into daily utensils. It was not
until the later years of the Eastern Han that mature porcelain vessels started
being used in people’s everyday lives.
   The trend against luxury and promoting simplicity was expressed not
only in daily utensils but also in burial objects. One rule at the time was that
burial objects “shall all be earthenware, and no gold, silver, bronze or tin
decoration shall be used”. So large quantities of pottery burial objects
emerged, of which various sculptures exhibited particularly outstanding
craftsmanship. From the slave society in the Xia and Shang dynasties to the
Zhou Dynasty it had been popular to bury living persons with the dead. In
the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods it was encouraged to use
pottery figurines as substitutes for real people, and by the Qin and Han
dynasties it had become a common custom to use pottery figurines for
burial.
   When it comes to pottery sculptures of the Qin and Han dynasties, the
first examples that spring to people’s minds are the magnificent Terracotta
Army guarding Qin Shi Huang’s Mausoleum and the many vivid painted

pottery figurines in Han dynasty tombs, (Fig. 5.1) which represented a
zenith in the history of China’s ceramic sculpture art. The figurines, with
perfect artistic form and vivid lifelike expressions, describe the
physiological features, psychological characteristics and even the inner
spirit of people from different regions and different classes at the time. The
figurines were evidence of the long-standing realist tradition and the bright,
concise, profound and grand style of Chinese sculpture art. The pottery
sculptures made in large quantities as burial objects are the most vivid and
authentic material for us to understand the social life back in the Qin and
Han dynasties thanks to the richness and extensiveness of their subject
matter and detailed description of the scenes and customs of people’s lives
at the time.

Fig. 5.1 Sitting female servant,
Han Dynasty, height: 65 cm, in the Shaanxi History Museum

   Another representative of pottery art of the Qin and Han dynasties was
the characteristic painted bricks for tomb building. With a wide range of
subject matter and rich content, the bricks were famous for their bas-relief
and intaglio. Painted bricks in the Han Dynasty were mostly used for
building coffin pits and so are also called tomb bricks. The images on the
bricks were often based on the life experience and personal philosophy of
the tomb owner. Many such brick images collectively constitute vivid

portraits of the customs and habits, lifestyle, production and labor, urban
construction, commerce and trade, transportation, dance, music and
acrobatics, myths and legends, and other scenes and features of the society
at the time, and are therefore comprehensive historical data for people today
to study the culture, art and political system of the Han Dynasty.

5.2 Gray Pottery
5.2.1 Types
Clay gray pottery vessels were still the most widely used pottery in the Qin
and Han dynasties. Sandy pottery was rare during this period. Clay gray
pottery wares could be further categorized based on texture, color and
hardness into clay gray pottery, clay red pottery, clay black pottery, sandy
pottery, sandy red pottery, clay hard pottery and clay soft pottery. (Fig. 5.2)
The differences resulted from different handling of the clay (some was
mixed with sand and some not, etc.), different iron oxide content, different
firing temperature, and different flame type so as to create diverse product
vessels for different functions.





Fig. 5.2 Pottery measuring vessel,
Qin Dynasty, height: 34 cm, top diam.: 39.6 cm, in the Cultural Activity Group of the Ju Ud League
(present Chifeng) in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region

Since the Qin Dynasty lasted for a very short time, in most regions it is
difficult to tell whether the unearthed pottery was from the Qin Dynasty.
Wares that are confirmed to have the typical characteristics of the Qin
Dynasty are mostly found in the Guanzhong area. The shape and design of
some of these wares were similar to, and retained some of the features of
those in the late Warring States period. The wares mainly comprised three
types, namely cooking vessels such as fu, li and zeng, food vessels like
bowls, and containers such as urns and pots. There were two types of pots.
One was the cocoon pot, a representative pottery variety of the Qin Dynasty
that is also called a duck egg pot because of the shape of its belly. The other
type, with a long thin neck and round belly, is called garlic pot due to its
garlic bulb shaped mouth. Surface decorations include imprinted rope
patterns, scratch marks, string patterns and color painting. All pottery wares
were wheel made, apart from the large and special shaped vessels such as
large cocoon pots, some of which were shaped with the coiling technique.
(Fig. 5.3).





Fig. 5.3 Cocoon pot with color painting,
Western Han Dynasty, height: 28 cm, top diam.: 13.5 cm, in the Henan Museum

Gray pottery in the Han Dynasty included daily use wares and burial
objects, though most of those found were burial objects because excavation
of city sites and human settlement remains from the period was less. As the
whole country was further unified during the Han Dynasty, pottery wares in
different parts of China, daily wares and burial objects alike, tended to be
similar in quality and design, though local features were retained to
different degrees.
   Daily use pottery wares of the Han Dynasty were nevertheless
comprised of three types, namely cooking vessels, mainly sandy fu with
spherical bottoms as well as zeng with big-mouths, slanting walls, flat
bottoms and through-carved holes, food and drinking vessels, such as open-
mouthed bowls, double-eared cups, and dou with long stems and shallow
plates, and containers, such as jars, urns, pots, basins and vats decorated
with rope patterns, string patterns and scratch marks. Gray pottery started
declining during the Han Dynasty. It was used less and less in people’s lives
and production was dominated by burial objects. (Fig. 5.4).

Fig. 5.4 Pottery zeng with color painting,
Western Han Dynasty, height: 37 cm, top diam.: 34 cm, in the Henan Museum

5.2.2 Development of Gray Pottery Burial Objects in the Han
Dynasty
Pottery burial objects of the Han Dynasty were extremely rich and highly
advanced. The number and variety of burial objects found in Han tombs far
exceeds those in previous dynasties. They include ritual vessels emulating
bronze and lacquer wares, figurines, sculptures and painted wares. Most are
gray pottery for it is widely available, cheap, easy to shape, simple to fire
and suitable for coloring.
   The funerary and burial customs of the Han Dynasty were quite
different from previous dynasties. The changes did not occur overnight.
Rather, they took place slowly and gradually, a process that is reflected in
the change of the burial pottery ensemble in the tombs of the Han Dynasty.

Take burial objects found in the central plains for example. In the early
Western Han, most tombs contained a set of ding, dui, fang and pots, or a
set of ding, dui and pots, mostly emulations of sets of bronze and lacquer
ritual wares. By the middle of the Western Han, most tombs contained a
collection of ding, dui, pots, grain containers, stoves, jars, and urns,
sometimes also with basins and bowls. The collections were still dominated
by emulations of bronze and lacquer ritual wares, but grain containers and
stoves were new. By the late Western Han, apart from ding, urns, jars, dui,
pots, grain containers and stoves, there also appeared pottery wells, lamps,
incense burners, fu, zeng, and plates. By the early Eastern Han, traditional
ritual objects such as ding and dui decreased dramatically or only dui but
not ding was buried with the dead. Pottery imitating then popular daily
utensils such as cases, earrings and spoons also appeared in tombs. By the
middle of the Eastern Han, ding or dui were no longer found in tombs,
while sculptures of livestock and fowl increased. Pottery objects of varying
subject matter rarely found before also appeared, such as sculptures of
music and dance scenes, of acrobatics, and of pavilions, houses, castles,
barns, mills, storehouses, warehouses, and paddy fields, and even pottery
chickens, sheep, pigs, dogs, cattle, horses and other livestock along with
pottery models of the enclosure for raising these animals. (Figs. 5.5 and
5.6).





Fig. 5.5 Pottery barn,
Han Dynasty, height: 22 cm, top diam.: 27.6 cm, in the Shaanxi History Museum

Fig. 5.6 Pottery incense burner,
Western Han Dynasty, height: 12.5 cm, top diam.: 13 cm, in the Hunan Museum

   The flourishing of pottery burial objects during the Han Dynasty was on
the one hand due to the rule that burial objects “shall all be earthenware,
and no gold, silver, bronze or tin decoration shall be used”, and on the other
hand due to the rejection of the social ethos that “people regard elaborate
funerals as a virtue and disdain plain burying”. The popularity of burying
many objects with the dead was on account of the common belief that after
death people would continue to live in another world as they did when
alive, so would need everything that they owned when alive. This gave rise
to the amazingly rich variety of burial objects that covered almost every
aspect of people’s lives. They are not only art works of high aesthetic value,

but also rich, vivid and precious materials for modern scholars to study the
culture, history and lifestyle of the Han Dynasty.

5.2.3 Decoration of Gray Pottery in the Han Dynasty
Decorative means of gray pottery in the Han Dynasty mainly included
string patterns, scratched patterns, rope patterns, imprinted patterns, relief
fashioned with mold, coloring and painting. Of these, string patterns were
used the most extensively. They may be classified into broad string and thin
string patterns or raised string and dented string patterns. Thin string
patterns were sometimes applied on their own or in combination with other
patterns, especially with continuous scratch marks. Scratched patterns
included rhombus checks, disconnected lines, connected rings, dots, fish
patterns, comb patterns and carved animal images. Two types of tools were
used to scratch or carve the patterns. One was a small, thin, hard tool with
one round end, and the other had comb teeth-like structures on one end that
was used to impress linear patterns (comb patterns) onto wares. Imprinted
patterns included square spirals, arcs, tree patterns, triangles and bear-
shaped sculptures, which were all imprinted one by one onto greenwares
with molds of different patterns. Relief fashioned with mold could be
ornamental parts made with molds that were then stuck onto wares. It might
also be directly imprinted onto a ware’s surface, such as the relief on
building bricks. Relief fashioned with mold was often used on pottery
stoves, brandreths, and the feet and ears of vessels. One typical example are
the rings with beast-headed bases that were often stuck on the bellies of
vessels.
   Coloring and painting were mainly used in the decoration of pottery
burial objects, i.e. gray pottery that was first fired and then painted, which
was introduced earlier but which only became more popular in the Han
Dynasty because of the social fashion of burying many objects with the
dead. Back in the Warring States period painting on pottery developed
mainly under the influence of bronzeware and lacquerware, especially the
latter, and this influence continued into the Han Dynasty. Nevertheless,
compared with the Warring States period, more colors were now used.
Apart from the original red, yellow, black, and white, additional colors
including orange, reddish brown, blue, green, gray and brown were also
used. Moreover, instead of using only one color on one ware, multiple
colors were applied to the one vessel so that the decoration was richer, more

harmonious, and more artistically appealing. Pottery pots with painting at
the time are particularly distinctive. The mouths and rims were colored
black. The surface from rim to belly was partitioned with red or black lines
into sections which were then respectively painted. The belly was often
painted with the Azure Dragon, the White Tiger, the Vermilion Phoenix or
cloud patterns, or sometimes the image of a dragon, tiger and phoenix
chasing each other in clouds. With bright colors and smooth lines, the
paintings were vivid, lively, intense and full of imagination. (Fig. 5.7) There
were also food vessels emulating lacquerware and other daily use utensils
such as ding, goblets and lidded jars, all vessels that people hoped could be
of use to the deceased in their life in the netherworld. (Figs. 5.8, 5.9, and
5.10) The decorative patterns on some of the vessels have rich connotations.
For instance, the “lidded pottery jar with paintingshown in Fig. 5.11 depicts
a vivid scene of a blue beast attacking a horse-riding shooter with its tusks,
and on the other side of the jar is a striding tiger with a long body. The blue
beast represents Sirius, and the shooter is the personification of its neighbor
Sagittarius. The white tiger on the other side represents a western
constellation and is connected with Sirius and Sagittarius at night. Sirius,
considered an evil star that governs theft and robbery, symbolized the tribes
fighting the Han people on the northern border of China. It was said that
when the color of Sirius changed, bandits would attack, and when Sirius
moved away from its usual position, the Huns would attack. Fortunately,
there was also Sagittarius, who knew who was evil and was always on the
alert to punish any rebel. It perpetually points its arrow at Sirius and passing
through it is a host of ominous meteors. Sagittarius was often associated
with the Eurasian nomads. Considered to be Chinas guardian, it had the
connotation of repelling the Huns.

5.3 Lead-Glazed Pottery of the Han Dynasty
5.3.1 Origins
Lead-glazed pottery featured low-fired lead glaze that is brown and green in
color. The glaze was made of glassy materials such as quartz stone, with
copper oxide and iron oxide added as colorants. Lead compounds were used
as the basic fluxing agents so the glaze would start to melt at about 700
degrees Celsius, making it a type of low-temperature glaze. The successful
production of lead-glazed pottery was one outstanding pottery-making

achievement of the Han Dynasty. Such pottery first appeared in the
Guanzhong area but was still rarely found in tombs during the reign of
Emperor Wu of Han. Lead glaze technology started to develop at a quicker
pace following Emperor Xuan of Han and comparatively more remains
from the period have been found in modern-day Henan. During the Eastern
Han, lead-glazed pottery experienced significant development and became
popular across a wider area. It has been unearthed in Gansu in the west,
near the Great Wall in the north, Shandong in the east and Hunan and
Jiangxi in the south.
   The origin of lead-glazed pottery in China is still a somewhat
controversial subject in academic circles. Some scholars believe that low-
fired lead-glazed pottery appeared in the Han Dynasty due to the
introduction of foreign lead glaze technology. They include Japanese
scholars who believe that low-fired lead glaze was first invented by the
Egyptians, then introduced to the Mediterranean coastal areas. It then
gradually spread to Persia and the Western Regions (a Han Dynasty term
for the area west of Yumenguan, including what is now Xinjiang and parts
of Central Asia), and finally spread to Han Dynasty from the Western
Regions.8 But other scholars pointed out that there was every reason to
believe that Chinese craftsmen invented lead-glazed pottery on their own in
the Han Dynasty because as early as the Xia and Shang dynasties Chinese
artisans had had a certain understanding of copper, tin, lead and gold in the
practice of metal smelting, and by the Han Dynasty they had accumulated a
deep understanding of and rich practical experience in lead and lead
compounds.9
   Lead-glazed pottery used the same clay as gray pottery and was also
wheel made. As the firing temperature was low, the ware was usually quite
thick to make sure it was strong enough. The glaze was yellowish-brown or
green, the former fired in an oxidizing flame with iron as the colorant and
the latter, also fired in an oxidizing flame, but with copper as the colorant.
Low firing temperature and an oxidizing flame led to relatively large pores
and the shortcoming of poor impermeability. These coupled with a high
lead content made it unsuitable for containing food or liquid. Therefore,
lead-glazed pottery vessels were used only as burial objects and not for use
in daily life. To reduce costs, the outside of the vessels only was usually
glazed. (Fig. 5.12).

Fig. 5.12 Green glaze pottery mirror case,
Han Dynasty, height: 15.6 cm, top diam.: 20.4 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Lead-glazed pottery appeared in the early Western Han. At first there
was only yellowish-brown glaze. Green glaze appeared later in the mid-
Western Han, but it immediately won people’s favor, soon surpassed
yellowish-brown glaze pottery in output and became the mainstream lead-
glazed pottery. The instant popularity of green glaze was due to the fact that
such smooth, glossy and beautiful glaze with a bright, clear green color had
never been seen before while the yellowish-brown color started to be used
for pottery decoration as early as the Neolithic painted pottery and
craftsmen had long known about using iron as a colorant.

5.3.2 Types and Features
Lead-glazed pottery found in tombs of the Han Dynasty include bronze-
imitating ritual objects such as pots, handleless cups, bu, ding, cases, eared
cups, plates, mirror cases, and incense burners, and various models such as
barns, stoves, wells, livestock enclosures, water power tilt hammers, mills,
workshops, pavilions and ponds. Decoration was mostly relief fashioned
with mold, and themes were mostly mythological stories and animals
roaming in sacred mountains, heavenly palaces, running water and flowing
clouds. (Fig. 5.13) For example, the green glazed pottery mirror case,

collected by the Palace Museum, is a funerary object imitating the
lacquerware of the time. It is decorated with relief patterns, mainly animals
such as deer, tigers, rhinos, bears, monkeys and lions, running freely in the
mountains, which decorated the band shaped middle section of the belly
bordered by two raised lines. Another example is a yellow glazed pottery
zun unearthed in Baotou, Inner Mongolia in 1981. The ware is cylindrical in
shape and has a Boshan (sacred mountain in the sea) style lid. Its belly is
covered with various reliefs, including myths, auspicious birds and animals,
armored warriors, dances and operas. There are altogether 47 images of 29
types, which can be divided into six groups. The first group is the Jade Hare
pounding medicine in a mortar, a goddess, Queen Mother of the West, a
monstrous spirit and a three-legged bird. The second group is an armored
warrior, a winged horse, a female pig, a toad, and a singled-horned sheep.
The third group is Yi (name of a master archer), a mulberry tree, the moon,
a three-legged crow, a long snake and a sinuous dragon. The fourth group is
a human figure with the head of an ox and a human figure with a rooster’s
head. The fifth group is an image of monsters having a feast. And the sixth
group is a nine-tailed fox. The reliefs, realistic and somewhat exaggerated,
are amazingly rich. The composition is rigorous and clear. There is also a
jar with a mountain-shaped lid from the Han Dynasty, a wine container
imitating bronzeware that was placed in a tomb. The jar was imprinted with
molds when the clay was still moist, and every detail of the relief can be
seen through its lustrous green glaze. The mountain is full of mythological
animals, demonstrating the important Taoist idea that mountains are places
where you might meet spirits and gods.

Fig. 5.13 Green glazed mirror case with Boshan lid,
Han Dynasty, height: 24.7 cm, top diam.: 22 cm, in the Shanxi Provincial Museum

    In most cases green glaze and yellowish-brown glaze were used
separately, but there were rare cases where yellowish-brown glaze patterns
were applied to a green glaze backdrop, or green glaze patterns were
applied to a yellowish-brown glaze background. When the two types of
glaze were used to decorate one ware, the green glaze was often the less
stable and was prone to peeling off as time went by. Remains of green glaze
wares that have been found now have all experienced differing degrees of
glaze thinning or peeling. Some even demonstrated “silvering”, which
refers to the layer of silver-white matter with a metallic luster that is
sometimes seen on the surface of lead-glazed pottery unearthed from tombs
of the Han Dynasty. People often call the matter “silver glaze”, which is
more often found on lead-glazed pottery unearthed from tombs with
relatively high humidity. The so-called “silver glaze” was actually formed
by crystallization in certain conditions at the glaze surface and cracks of

dissolved substances that were eroded from the glaze through reaction with
water and the atmosphere together with soluble salts that were in the water
in the first place. As such erosion and crystallization continues to take
place, the sediment on the surface of the ware thickens, and when it reaches
a certain thickness, the ware takes on a silver luster due to the interference
of light. The phenomenon has also been observed on the tricolor glazed
porcelain of the Tang Dynasty (Tang Sancai). But it occurrs only on the
surface of the copper green glaze and not on the iron yellow glaze or the
cobalt blue glaze, which indicates that copper green glaze is easily eroded
by water and atmosphere, while iron yellow glaze and cobalt blue glaze are
not. For example, a green glazed container with a kuilong-shaped handle
has mostly turned “silver” except for parts of the mouth and handle that
remain green. (Fig. 5.14).





Fig. 5.14 Green glazed container with kuilong-shaped handle,
Eastern Han Dynasty, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S

   Low-temperature lead glaze is a good ceramic decorative material.
Advantages such as high refractive index, low viscosity at high
temperature, strong fluidity, and broad melting temperature range mean it
does not have the common defects of lime and alkali lime glazes, i.e.,
“pinholes” or the glaze looking like the skin of an orange. In addition, there
are no bubbles and few residual crystals. Thus, the glaze layer is clear,
transparent, and smooth. The appearance of lead-glazed pottery in the Han
Dynasty laid the foundation for the creation of the tricolor glazed porcelain
of the Tang Dynasty, and for the appearance of various colorful glaze types

later. The successful production of lead-glazed pottery was a great
achievement of the ceramics industry in the Han Dynasty. (Fig. 5.15).





Fig. 5.15 Green glazed pottery bear lamp holder,
Han Dynasty, height: 46.5 cm, in the Shanghai Museum

5.4 Primitive Porcelain of the Qin and Han
Dynasties
5.4.1 Development
During the Qin and Han dynasties primitive porcelain was produced mainly
in modern-day Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu, which were the main
production areas of primitive porcelain back in the Shang and Zhou
dynasties. Though production came to a temporary halt in the middle
Warring States period, kilns were rebuilt in the late Warring States and early
Qin Dynasty and production resumed. By the Han Dynasty primitive
porcelain experienced further development and lots of primitive porcelain
has been unearthed at tombs and sites of the Han Dynasty in modern-day
Zhejiang, Jiangsu and southern Anhui.
   The primitive porcelain of the Qin and Western Han dynasties differed
from that of the Shang, Zhou and Warring States periods in terms of the
iron oxide and alumina oxide content of the body material, in the procedure
and technique of applying glaze, and in the firing temperature. The former
had higher contents of iron oxide and alumina oxide than the latter. Higher
iron oxide content resulted in deeper body color after firing in a reducing
atmosphere, while a higher alumina oxide content enabled the clay to
withstand higher firing temperatures, which reduced the chance of
deformation during firing. But if the firing temperature was not high
enough, the ware could not be fully sintered, leading to a loose body
texture. In addition, primitive porcelain of the Qin and Western Han
dynasties had a thicker glaze than that of previous dynasties, and the glaze
contained more iron, resulting in a deeper glaze color. The differences
between the primitive porcelain of the two historical periods led some to
believe that the two were independent creations of their respective times
since no direct inheritance in terms of firing techniques could be observed
between them. However, the rejuvenation of primitive porcelain in the very
same place indicated the craftsmanship and influence of primitive porcelain
before the Warring States period had not entirely disappeared.
   The rejuvenation and further development of primitive porcelain in the
area of the old state of Yue, that is, modern-day Shaoxing, Ningbo, Shangyu
and Cixi of Zhejiang with Shaoxing at the center, should be attributed not
only to local tradition and inheritance, but also to favorable natural

conditions. Firstly, the area had fine porcelain clay. Secondly, dense forests
surrounding the area could provide both fuel for firing and wood for
building kiln houses and greenware sheds and for making wooden tools
such as jigger wheels and planks for holding greenware. Thirdly, rich water
resources could be used on the one hand to power tilt hammers to crush
porcelain clay (to raise the clay processing efficiency and to make finer
clay, treadle-operated and water-powered tilt hammers were widely adopted
at this time) and on the other hand to wash porcelain clay to reduce
impurities. In addition, as water transport was an important mode of
transport at the time, good waterways in the area enabled raw materials to
be easily shipped in from surrounding areas and enabled products to be
shipped outside for sale. All these natural and geographic advantages
coupled with previous tradition and experience rejuvenated the primitive
porcelain production in the area during the Qin and Han dynasties after the
temporary hiatus of the Warring States, and by the late Eastern Han the area
had become the birthplace of mature Chinese porcelain.
   The primitive porcelain of the early Western Han, following the custom
which had existed since the Warring States period, was still dominated by
burial objects imitating bronze ritual wares. Common varieties included
ding, dui, cases, fang, handleless cups, and bu. The shape design was grand
and dignified and the workmanship was fine and exquisite. The cover and
upper belly of ding, dui and cases were often had bluish green or yellowish-
brown glaze applied. (Fig. 5.16) With the changes in lifestyle and funerary
customs, the shape design of primitive porcelain experienced considerable
change by the mid-Western Han. Some varieties developed new features
while others were replaced by new ones. For example, by the middle of the
Han Dynasty, dui had been completely replaced by cases. The shape of the
cover of some vessels emulating bronze ritual objects, such as ding and
cases, was significantly different from those which were manufactured
earlier. The belly of ding became deeper and the feet became so short that
for some they were barely visible. Thus, the ding became almost
indistinguishable from cases. Meanwhile, glazed parts shrank, and some
were not glazed at all. The workmanship was not as exquisite or meticulous
as that at the beginning of the Han Dynasty. By the late Western Han, ritual
objects such as ding and cases almost disappeared and there was a surge in
daily use utensils such as pots, bu, jars, fang, mirror cases, washers, basins
and spoons. The craftsmanship placed more emphasis on daily practicality.

At the same time, ceramic burial models of cattle, horses and houses
appeared.





Fig. 5.16 Primitive porcelain ampule with ripple patterns and beast-shaped handles,
Western Han Dynasty, height: 32 cm, top diam.: 22.5 cm, in the Palace Museum

    Primitive porcelain in the Western Han Dynasty is generally decorated
with simple patterns such as strings and water ripples. Complicated
decorative patterns have not been seen. After the mid-Western Han, the
original dented strings that were carved were replaced by raised strings
fashioned by sticking thin, flat mud strips onto the ware. Between these
conspicuous raised strings, images of water waves, floral scrolls, rolling
clouds, and herringbone patterns were carved, among which the cloud
patterns were especially vivid and beautiful with soft, smooth lines and
mythical animals and birds amongst the drifting clouds. By this time
dipping had begun to be used to apply glazes. Vessels were glazed almost
all over except for perhaps areas near the bottom. So decorative patterns
were often on the mouth rim, neck, shoulder and upper belly of the vessels.

5.4.2 Appearance of Mature Porcelain at the End of Eastern
Han

Following its appearance in the Shang Dynasty, Chinese primitive porcelain
did not evolve into true porcelain until the Eastern Han. Porcelain made in
the Eastern Han contained fewer colorant impurities such as iron oxide and
titanium oxide. The firing temperature reached 1,310 degrees Celsius so
that the body was fully sintered and did not absorb water. With a dense,
hard texture, the vessels emitted a forceful and clear sound when struck.
The body also transmitted light well. The glaze layer was transparent and
glossy, and there was no peeling off, attaining the standard of modern
porcelain. These qualities indicate that the porcelain at the time was already
true porcelain in the modern sense. (Fig. 5.17) Archaeological
investigations have discovered abundant remains of the production sites of
primitive porcelain from the Eastern Han in modern-day Ningbo, Shangyu
and Yongjia of Zhejiang Province and Yixing in Jiangsu Province.
Therefore, this area could be said to be the birthplace of China’s earliest
mature porcelain. In all these places primitive porcelain had previously
been fired in the same kilns with imprinted hard pottery. By the end of the
Eastern Han, most kilns in the area were devoted to firing celadon and thus
became porcelain kilns in the real sense. Since then pottery and porcelain
became two distinct entities and porcelain production became a new
independent handicraft industry.

Fig. 5.17 Primitive porcelain jar with double lugs,
Eastern Han Dynasty, height: 32.2 cm, top diam.: 12 cm, in the Palace Museum

   The porcelain of the late Eastern Han may be divided into two types
according to glaze color. One is blue glazed porcelain and the other black
glazed porcelain, and they are respectively called celadon and black
porcelain. Celadon constituted the majority. Black porcelain was less
prevalent and was mostly fired in celadon kilns. The Yue kilns were the
most famous porcelain kilns at the time and were especially renowned for
their celadon.
   Most early celadon of the Yue kilns was adequately sintered at an
appropriate temperature and atmosphere, resulting in a fine, hard, solid
body that was grayish white in color with a relatively low iron oxide
content. The glaze layer was even and tightly stuck to the body. Glaze
peeling rarely occurred. Early porcelain wares inevitably bore similarities to
primitive porcelain in terms of shape design and decorative style since they
had evolved from it. Common varieties were bowls, small cups, basins,
washers, pots, handleless cups, bu, plates, cups with handles, tiger-shaped
chamber pots, water pots and incense burners. There were also small
numbers of inkstones, spittoons and five-linked jars. (Fig. 5.18) Bowls
came in two designs. One type had thin mouth rims, deep bellies, arced
walls and flat bottoms. The other type had tightening mouths, slightly
swelling upper bellies, narrowing lower bellies and flat bottoms. The
second type was smaller and basically the same as the bowls of the Warring
States period. The plates were similar to primitive porcelain plates and were
usually used as saucers for cups with a handle. The basins had straight
mouths, folded rims, straight upper bellies and narrowing lower bellies with
obvious fold lines in between. There were many varieties of jars, including
double-lugged jars, pickle jars and four-lugged jars, all with straight mouths
and spherical bellies. The first two jar varieties fully inherited the shape
design of primitive porcelain, while the last one, the four-lugged jar, was
new and the most prevalent. It had a rounded lip, swollen belly, flat bottom,
raised shoulder and four (a few had six) equidistant horizontal lugs on the
shoulder. The piercings of the lugs were too small to pass ropes through, so
the wall opposite the lugs was often dented to make the piercings bigger.
(Fig. 5.19) The jars were often decorated with string or ripple patterns on
the shoulder and imprinted linen patterns on the belly. Some were plain all
over. Pots have also been unearthed in large numbers. Their shape design

continued to resemble that of primitive porcelain pots, except those fully
covered with thick string patterns on the belly had become rare, and the
plate-shaped mouth was shallower than before. The early porcelain of the
Eastern Han was mostly common household utensils, namely, food vessels
like bowls and small cups, containers like jars, pots with plate-shaped
mouths, handleless cups, and sanitary utensils including water pots,
spittoons and tiger-shaped chamber pots.





Fig. 5.18 Five-linked jar,
Han Dynasty, height: 10 cm, top diam.: 4.8 cm, in the Museum of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous
Region

Fig. 5.19 Four-lugged jar with textile pattern,
Eastern Han Dynasty, height: 22.6 cm, top diam.: 14.5 cm, in the Cultural Relics Management
Committee of Cixi County, Zhejiang

   The decorative elements of the early blue glazed porcelain were the
same as those commonly seen previously, i.e., string patterns, water ripple
patterns, rings with beast-headed bases, feet in the shape of a beast’s head,
etc. String patterns were usually found on the mouth and shoulder of
vessels, but thick string patterns were also found on the belly of pots with
plate-shaped mouths and of jars. The three feet of washers were often
shaped like the head of a dragon, tiger or bear, and there were often rings
with a beast-headed base on the belly so that the washers look dignified. In
summary, the decorative patterns and techniques of early porcelain were
similar to primitive porcelain, even with imprinted hard pottery. For
instance, some bu and lei formed using the coiling technique were stamped
with linen patterns, window bar patterns, net patterns, fir leaf patterns,
triangles, checks and butterfly patterns, basically the same decorative
patterns as imprinted hard pottery. This indicates that the porcelain of the
Eastern Han had obviously inherited a lot from primitive porcelain and
imprinted hard pottery. Meanwhile, the porcelain of the period was also
influenced by the shape design and decoration of other contemporaneous art
forms. For instance, the large jar shown in Fig. 5.20 was fired by the Yue
kilns. The three groups of animal patterns carved on its surface were

associated with lacquerware decoration of the same period, while the design
of the broad, flat handles on the shoulder came from early bronzewares.





Fig. 5.20 Green glazed storage jar,
Han Dynasty, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S

   Apart from celadon, craftsmen of the Eastern Han also produced black
porcelain. Both used iron as the main colorant and the production
technologies were basically the same. What sets them apart is the content of
iron oxide in the glaze material. Glaze material with less than 3% iron oxide
would make celadon and that with 4 to 9% or even more would make black
glaze. The primitive porcelain of the Eastern Han already used two glaze
types, namely, bluish yellow glaze with a lower iron content and caramel
glaze with a higher iron content. After the middle of the Eastern Han, as the
firing technology improved, craftsman had better control over kiln
atmosphere and developed a deeper understanding of the color of different
glaze materials after firing, creating the conditions for the successful firing
of celadon and black porcelain at the same time.
   The body texture of black porcelain was usually not as fine as that of
celadon. Yet the body texture also differed based on the function of the
ware. Food, drink and wine vessels such as bowls, washers, and handleless
cups and pots had a relatively finer body that was grayish white or light
gray, while larger vessels such as bu and lei had a coarser body that
contained sand particles or quartz and more pores and was deeper in color,

i.e. gray or dark gray. Most black porcelain wares could be adequately fired
because they were made of porcelain clay that could be fully sintered at a
relatively low temperature, namely, 1,200 to 1,240 degrees Celsius.
   Few black porcelain wares were fully glazed. Most were unglazed near
the bottom, exposing the purple body. The glaze was uneven in thickness
and strips of extra glaze like candle guttering often gathered into thick
layers in dented parts near the ware bottom. Thin parts of the glaze were
lighter in color and looked greenish brown or yellowish-brown, while
thicker parts were darker, looking blackish brown or black. Some vessels
were bright black like charcoal and were extremely shiny and beautiful.
Glaze peeling has been observed, but is quite rare, which indicates that
black porcelain workmanship had reached a high level in the Eastern Han.
Even when celadon and black porcelain were fired in the same kiln, the
celadon was often of fine body texture while the body texture of the black
porcelain was coarser, which suggests that at that time potters were already
able to skillfully select and prepare raw materials, adopting high-quality
fine clay to make a celadon body and coarser clay material for black
porcelain. Black porcelain differed from celadon in terms of glaze color, but
in this period the shape design and decorative patterns of the two were
basically the same.

5.5 Pottery Sculptures of the Qin and Han
Dynasties
5.5.1 Pottery Sculptures of the Qin Dynasty
The pottery sculptures of the Qin and Han dynasties occupy an important
position in the history of Chinese sculpture art. The magnificent, bold and
life-like Qin pottery sculptures and the vivid, lively and varied Han pottery
sculptures are both unsurpassed throughout history. Pottery sculpture
originated very early in China and can be traced back to the Neolithic. At
that time all the pottery sculptures seemed to be made as substitutes for
human sacrifices and thus were mostly burial objects. Therefore, when the
popularity of luxury funerals rose in the Warring States period, such pottery
sculptures also became popular as a result and their development reached a
new peak in the Qin and Han dynasties.

The Qin and Han dynasties saw China complete the great cause of
national reunification for the first time. The first emperor of Qin,
Yingzheng, called himself the first “Huangdi”, a new term coined from 皇
(Huang) and 帝 (Di), both titles of ancestral legendary rulers, to express his
pride in the expansive rule of the Qin Dynasty, a dynasty that had expanded
beyond the realm of all previous dynasties. In the eyes of the Chinese
people at the time, China was the whole world under Heaven. The Doctrine
of the Mean held that everywhere accessible by vehicles, boats and people,
everywhere covered by frost or dew, and everywhere illuminated by the sun
or the moon, were the same country where the axles of carts were of the
same length, the same writing system was used, and the same ethical code
of behaviors was followed. The ruler of such a kingdom naturally
commanded the feeling and bearing of “king of the world”, and the country
and the army under his leadership naturally also enjoyed unprecedented and
unstoppable momentum. This momentum embodied the spirit of the time, a
spirit that must have also found its expression in the arts of the time. It is
only that the short-lived rule of the Qin Dynasty left us too few artwork
remains to truly understand the state of many arts of the time.
    Luckily, the discovery of the terracotta warriors and horses opened our
eyes and introduced us to some of the charm of the ceramic art of the Qin
Dynasty. In the spring of 1974, the accidental discovery by local farmers
drilling a well near Qin Shi Huang’s Mausoleum turned out to be “a great
discovery of the twentieth century, a discovery that made archaeological
history”. Thirty years of continuous exploration and excavation brought to
our attention in succession the No. 2 and No. 3 terracotta warrior pits,
containing copper chariot and horse pits, stone armor pits, acrobatic
figurine pits, copper treasure poultry pits, and more. Pit No. 1, some 210 m
long and 62 m wide, is divided into 11 tunnels with rammed earth beams.
The tunnels are covered with green bricks on the bottom and contain nearly
6,000 terracotta warriors, horses and wooden chariots (more than 2,000 of
which have been unearthed). The whole pit is arranged in an eastward array
of 38 columns. The warriors and horses, shaped and sculpted as individuals
and arranged in tidy ranks, are of the same size as real horses and
individuals and make a spectacularly grand scene. They are a three-
dimensional reproduction of the irresistible, sweeping and grand Qin army
“with more than one million armored soldiers, thousands of chariots and ten
thousand horses”. It is no wonder that scholars call the terracotta figures the

epitome of the vast Qin Empire army and a miracle in the history of
Chinese sculpture, while foreigners call them the eighth wonder of the
world.10
   The thousands of life-sized terracotta warriors and horses stand in full
battle array, appearing to await orders to set out. Among them are warriors
acting as the vanguard, infantrymen, chariots and horses as the main body
of the army, and flanking guards on both sides. Strong horses, in groups of
four, tow well-equipped chariots. Armored warriors and soldiers in battle
robes carry an array of sophisticated weapons. The figures—warriors and
horses arranged neatly, infantrymen and chariots standing next to each other
—formed a Qin army in its entirety. They reproduce the magnificent
courage and strength of Qin Shi Huang to conquer all the land and unify the
whole country, and are also a concrete record of the mighty and powerful
Qin army. (Figs. 5.21 and 5.22).
