   Commonly used decorative techniques included engraving, scratching,
printing, sticking, stamping and comb scratching. Engraving refers to the
technique of carving patterns in relief on greenware with iron, bamboo or

bone blades, and then applying glaze and dispatching for firing. Scratching
refers to applying needle-like tools to the greenware to scratch out lines in
intaglio before glazing and firing. Printing refers to pressing decorative
images onto semi-dried greenware with a pattern-bearing molding tool.
Sticking refers to attaching ready-made sculptures onto the greenware body,
which creates a three-dimensional effect like a shallow relief.
    In terms of decorative patterns, Sui porcelain not only inherited some
plant patterns prevalent in the Southern & Northern Dynasties, but also
cleverly interpolated and replaced certain themes in image layout to create
new patterns. The shoulders and bellies of bottles and jars were usually
decorated with ribbons made of blossoms and rolled leaves. Plates and
bowls were often decorated in the center with a circular pattern composed
of individual blossoms or rolled leaves. The circular pattern might contain
one, three, five or seven layers based on the size of the ware. Main patterns
included flowers such as lotus petals, individual blossoms, honeysuckle,
blades of grass, and plum blossoms, and geometric patterns included
strings, ropes, waves, triangles, linked beads, double circles, mat patterns
and vertical lines. These flower and geometric patterns often formed
ribbons that decorated the neck, belly and outer side of the mouth rim of the
vessels or constituted circular decorations of one, three or five layers that
decorated the well of bowls or plates according to the shape design of the
vessels. Animal imageries included dragons, phoenixes, rooster heads, lion
heads, elephant heads, and monkeys. There were also human images. These
decorations were mostly first molded and then attached to the surface of the
vessels. In general, compared with those of the Wei, Jin, and Southern &
Northern Dynasties, the decorative porcelain patterns of the Sui Dynasty
featured less animal themes and more plant imageries. (Fig. 7.18).

Fig. 7.18 Blue-glazed lamp holder,
Sui Dynasty, height: 17.4 cm, top diam.: 5.4 cm, in the Hunan Museum

   Before the Sui Dynasty China’s porcelain was all fired with naked fire
and various propping tools were used to support the greenware in the kiln.
During the Sui Dynasty almost all northern and southern kilns still used
these propping tools, indicating that at the time porcelain was still mostly
fired with naked fire. Nonetheless, the craftsmen of the Sui Dynasty were
already able to adopt different kinds of propping tools according to the
wares to be fired. The variety of the propping tools was extremely rich. For
instance, up to nine types of propping tools were unearthed at the sites of
the Anyang kilns in Henan Province, including tooth-shaped props, trident-
shaped props, column-shaped props, cylinder-shaped props, supporting
cups, supporting rods, cushion cups, cushion pads and ring-shaped props.

The same type of propping tools came in different sizes. For example, the
trident-shaped props could reach up to 15 cm in height and the shortest was
only six centimeters. All these indicate that the Anyang kilns’ porcelain-
making technology had reached a fairly advanced level.
   Kiln furniture is important for studying porcelain firing techniques.
Although most kilns in the Sui Dynasty, northern and southern alike, still
used props, cylindrical saggers appeared in the Xiangyin kilns in Hunan,
indicating that in the Sui Dynasty saggers were already used to contain
porcelain wares for firing, a major innovation in kiln furniture. Before the
adoption of saggers, porcelain glaze was often troubled by sand grains
sticking onto it and impure color owing to the contamination of smoke, ash
and dust particles in the kiln vault and direct contact between the ware and
the flame during the firing process. Worse still, the use of propping tools
often left many nail marks on the inner sides of bowls, cups and plates,
which not only undermined the appearance of the objects, but also affected
their use. These drawbacks were avoided after the sagger was adopted.
Although saggers were not widely used at the time, they substantially
improved the quality of porcelain products and thus promoted the
development of China’s porcelain industry.

7.2.2 The Yue Kilns of the Tang and Five Dynasties
The center of the Tang dynasty porcelain industry were the Yue kilns
located near Shanglin Lake in Yuyao, Zhejiang Province (about 30 km
northeast of present-day Yuyao City). Shanglin Lake is a long north–south
natural lake with an area of 1,770,200 square meters. The Yue kiln sites,
over 700 in number, are lined along the east and west sides of the lake: from
Mugou Bay at the northern point to the Huangshan Mountain on the east
bank in the south, and then from Yanzikun on the west bank in the south to
Wujiaxi in the north. Strewn over hundreds of square kilometers, the sites
cover present-day Yuyao, Shangyu, Shaoxing, Huangyan, Ningbo,
Shengzhou, Fenghua, Zhuji, Cixi, Xianju, Linhai, Wenling, Yueqing and
other places. The Gong kilns which were famous for firing secret-color
porcelain in the late Tang and Five Dynasties were also near Shanglin Lake.
The porcelain output of the Yue kilns ranked first among the major kiln
systems in China and was sold both in China and to Central Asia and other
overseas markets. Its peak period was the late Tang and Five Dynasties,
evidenced by the large volume of Yue kiln celadon among the burial objects

in the tombs of the Qian family during the late years of the Tang Dynasty
and early years of the Wuyue Kingdom. The Yue kilns began to decline in
the early Northern Song Dynasty.
   The main raw material used in the Zhejiang kilns in the south was
porcelain clay with low aluminum (Al2O3) and high silicon (SiO2) content,
which turned into a high density porcelain body after being fired in a
temperature ranging from 1,200 to 1,270 ℃. From the Eastern Han
Dynasty to the Five Dynasties, high calcium lime glaze (calcium content
15–20%) was used for celadon making in both the north and south, and Yue
kiln celadon was no exception (it was not until after the Song Dynasty that
the content of calcium was reduced to less than 15% and high potassium
raw materials were introduced to make alkaline lime glaze). Unlike the
northern steamed bun kilns which could only perform slow heating and
cooling, the ability of southern dragon kilns to heat up and cool down
quickly allowed the firing of clear and transparent glass-like glaze from
high calcium lime glaze material with low fusibility and low viscosity.
   The characteristics of Yue kiln porcelain in the Tang and Five Dynasties
can be summarized in the following manner: (1) the similar composition of
both the ware body and the local porcelain stone indicates the ware body
was mainly made up of porcelain stone without kaolinite, but some “zijin”
(reddish purple) clay might have been added to improve the shaping
property of the clay; (2) the iron and titanium content was high; (3) over the
consecutive 1,000 years that the Yue kilns fired porcelain, the makeup of
the ware body and the glaze underwent little change—the glaze had always
been typical lime glaze made from a mixture of porcelain stone, limestone
and plant ash, inheriting the primitive glazing technology of the Shang and
Zhou dynasties with the recipe basically unchanged. This shows that
porcelain-making technologies had been passed down from generation to
generation. Iron gives glaze a green color in reducing atmosphere and a
yellowish green color in oxidizing atmosphere. The high iron content
determined the basic characteristic of the glaze color of Yue ware. (Fig.
7.19).

Fig. 7.19 Yue kiln four-lugged jar,
Tang Dynasty, height: 15.5 cm, top diam.: 6.95 cm, in the Shanghai Museum

    In the early Tang Dynasty Yue ware was characterized by limited
variety and shape design and a high glaze peeling rate. By the middle and
late Tang Dynasty the number of kilns increased, and the quantity and
quality of products improved significantly. The most famous kilns in the
country at the time were the Yue kilns in the south and the Xing kilns in the
north, forming the landscape of southern celadon and northern white. The
emergence of secret-color porcelain in the late Tang Dynasty marked an

unprecedented height of the Yue kilns’ technical levels. Secret-color
porcelain represented the highest level of southern China porcelain
production at the time and was a result of continuous progress in porcelain
production technologies over the previous one thousand years.
   Since ancient times, potters had been critically focused on the addition
or reduction of air–or oxygen to be more specific—that was put into the
kiln, and had tried every means possible to oxidize or reduce the coloring
metals in the glaze material. It took a reducing flame to fire fine celadon.
The higher the reduction ratio, the more ferrous oxide and the less ferric
oxide there is, resulting in better celadon glaze color, while a high oxidizing
ratio would do the reverse. To avoid an unfavorable oxidizing atmosphere,
fuel charcoal must be continuously fed into the kiln while maintaining good
ventilation, which was very uneconomical. Thus, firing celadon was both
difficult and costly. In spring and summer, the climate in eastern China was
humid, making kiln firing more difficult. Most kiln workers therefore had
developed the habit of only starting kiln firing when the air was drier after
the typhoon season, such as in late autumn or early winter when it was crisp
and cool. This technical experience could not be accumulated overnight and
the outstanding achievements of the Yue kilns in the Tang Dynasty were the
outcome of creative work on the basis of the knowledge of predecessors.
The Yue kilns also offered valuable experience and laid the foundation for
the emergence of famous later porcelains such as Longquan ware.
   What made Tang Dynasty Yue kiln celadon a famous porcelain down
through the ages and the leading celadon maker, surpassing many kilns of
the day, was not only its long production period, but more importantly, its
near perfect glaze color. The Yue celadon that has been passed down
through generations or unearthed, has a fully sintered and light gray body
with a dense texture. The glaze is opaque. The glaze color of early Yue
celadon was in fact a kind of dark blue, often with a tinge of yellow, like
pine or cypress leaves in winter. By the late Tang and Five Dynasties, the
glaze color was mostly lake green, lush and mellow, making Yue ware the
best. (Fig. 7.20).

Fig. 7.20 Blue-glazed phoenix-head pot,
Tang Dynasty, height: 41.3 cm, top diam.: 9.5 cm, in the Palace Museum

Yue ware in the Tang and Five Dynasties pursued both practicality and
beauty in terms of shape design. Daily life utensils were made into the
shapes of flowers, leaves, melons and fruit. The main products were bowls,
plates, pots, small-mouthed jars, bottles, jars, eared cups, saucers, powder
cases, water pots, spittoons, grease boxes, ceramic sculptures, pillows, and
oil lamps. These objects inherited the shape of previous dynasties, but also
took on new features. For instance, plate-mouthed pots turned into small-
mouthed jars with bell-shaped mouths and long necks (Fig. 7.21); the
bellies of bowls turned from deep to shallow, and bowls developed into two
types, namely those with jade bi bottoms and those with short circular feet.

Fig. 7.21 Yue kiln blue-glazed pot,
Tang Dynasty, height: 14.3 cm, top diam.: 6.1 cm, in the Palace Museum

   By the Tang Dynasty rooster-head pots disappeared and were replaced
by handled ewers. Many vessels from the late Tang Dynasty have exhibited
obvious signs of imitating gold and silver utensils. Bowls developed richer
varieties—apart from those with jade bi bottoms and those with tight
mouths, shallow bellies and flat bottoms, lotus flower bowls, lotus leaf

bowls, rhombus pattern mouthed bowls, crabapple flower bowls, sunflower
petal mouthed bowls, and more also appeared. (Fig. 7.22) As for plates,
some had flared mouths, slanting walls, and flat bottoms, some had open
mouths and jade bi bottoms, some had sunflower petal style mouths, and
still others were square. There were also various cups, lidded boxes and
saucers. The bellies of handled ewers were fashioned into the shape of
melon ridges. The mouth rims of bowls and plates were fashioned into the
shape of sunflower petals or lotus petals. Saucers were shaped like lotus
leaves. Lidded boxes were small and exquisite with the lid and box fitting
snugly and the lid surface carved with simple patterns. The utensils,
assimilating the shape design and decorative features of gold and silver
wares, were refined, exquisite, novel and beautiful. (Fig. 7.23).





Fig. 7.22 Yue kiln blue-glazed bowl,
Tang Dynasty, height: 8.1 cm, top diam.: 16.4 cm, base diam.: 8.3 cm, in the Palace Museum

Fig. 7.23 Yue kiln blue-glazed engraved small case,
Tang Dynasty, height: 3.4 cm, top diam.: 3.7 cm, base diam.: 2.8 cm, in the Palace Museum

   The early Yue celadon of the Tang Dynasty was rarely decorated,
merely impressing admirers with its “mountain green” glaze color. In the
late Tang and Five Dynasties, engraved patterns or words began to appear
on utensils. Carved patterns were often found on the wells of bowls and
plates, on the bodies of pots, or on the surfaces of box lids. These patterns
were relatively simple, the common ones being ruyi-head clouds, lotus
flowers, crabapple flowers and vine flowers and leaves. Such images
depicted through carving had smooth and simple lines. Often only a few
strokes could create a blooming lotus flower, a wind-blown rolled lotus
leaf, a crabapple flower in full bloom or a four-petal blossom with
symmetrical branches and leaves. Printed patterns were often found on
round surfaces such as the wells of bowls and plates. Common patterns
were dragons flying in clouds, longevity cranes, and flowers. Printed
patterns were mostly restrained and rigid, not as free and bold as carved
patterns. Apart from carving and printing, other decorative techniques
included underglaze painting and gold and silver inlay, the former being
used for painting brown images of clouds and lotus petals on small-

mouthed jars, bowls, incense burners and other vessels to make them more
solemn, dignified and magnificent, and the latter used on some palace
porcelains, giving them a particularly rich and luxurious look with gold and
silver edges.
   The premier product of Yue kilns during the Tang and Five Dynasties
was its “secret-color porcelain”. The earliest tributary porcelain in China
specially made for the royal family, it represented the highest craftsmanship
of Yue celadon. Treatise on Geography V of the New Book of Tang records:
“Governor’s office of Kuaiji County in Yuezhou. Tributes: … porcelain,
paper and pen”. Both archaeological data and documentary records
corroborate the fact that in the central Yue kiln area near Shanglin Lake, a
“tributary kiln” was set up in the Tang Dynasty to make porcelain for the
court. The inscription on a jar unearthed from a Tang dynasty tomb in
Wujiaxi, Shanglin Lake in 1977 clearly states the existence of a “tributary
kiln” in CE 887.
   Some of the tributary wares were inscribed with the characters for
“official” or “internal use”. The tributary kiln also produced large quantities
of bowls, plates, bottles and other wares for common use after completing
its tributary ware production tasks. Therefore, the tributary kiln was not an
official kiln in the real sense, that is, a kiln set up by the royal court and
devoted to firing imperial wares. Rather, it produced tributary wares only
when there were orders and was thus essentially still a folk kiln.

7.2.3 “Secret-Color Porcelain” of the Tang and Five Dynasties
Before 1987, the term “secret-color porcelain” only appeared in historical
records and no one had seen a real secret-color ware. In 1987, when
repairing a brick pagoda from the Ming Dynasty in Famen Temple, Fufeng
County, Shaanxi Province, people found an underground palace beneath the
base of the Tang Dynasty True Relic Pagoda and from the palace hundreds
of precious cultural relics were unearthed, including two white porcelain
wares, 12 celadon wares, and two yellow-glazed silver-ridged porcelain
vessels with gold and silver decorations, of which, according to the
inscriptions on stone tablets, 13 pieces were “secret-color” porcelain
granted by Emperor Yizong of Tang in the Xiantong 15th Year (CE 874).
Also unearthed from the underground palace was an eight-ridge long-
necked celadon vase, which was not recorded in the inscriptions but

according to research was also a secret-color ware made at Shanglin Lake.
(Fig. 7.24).

Fig. 7.24 Yue kiln secret-color eight-ridge porcelain vase,
Tang Dynasty, height: 21.7 cm, top diam.: 2.3 cm, base diam.: 7.9 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Archaeological and cultural circles have now reached the consensus that
the firing site of secret-color porcelain was located in the Shanglin Lake
area in Cixi, Zhejiang Province, where the “tributary kiln” was dedicated to
firing secret-color porcelain for the palace.
     It is estimated that the firing of secret-color porcelain for the court by a
“tributary kiln” began in the early ninth century, and its peak period was the
late Tang Dynasty and the reign of the Wuyue Kingdom of the Five
Dynasties.
   Though it is generally agreed that “secret-color” described the color of
glaze, no common understanding has been reached on the meaning of
“secret” since the only records we may refer to are some descriptions of
secret-color porcelain in a few poems of the Tang Dynasty. Some people
think “secret color” means rare color or that it literally means the glaze was
made from a secret recipe. Some believe it refers to a particular kind of
color, vanilla or a type of blue. Some say the so-called secret color was a
type of celadon only used as tributes, and to name them secret-color
porcelain was to distinguish them from regular celadon used by common
folk. Others believe secret-color porcelain refers to those for tributary
purposes produced by outstanding folk kilns yet under the supervision of
government officials.
   There were both folk kilns and official kilns near Shanglin Lake. Early
works of the official kilns featured a thick body with rough texture and
lusterless glaze, mostly dim yellow or blue, due to poor control of the
atmosphere in the kiln. From the Five Dynasties to the Northern Song
Dynasty, as the demand for products increased, the firing technology also
improved, ushering in the golden age of secret-color porcelain. Even wall
thickness indicated further improvement in skills with the potter’s wheel.
Advances in firing technology realized the burning of the iron-oxide-based
colorant into a bluish green color by changing the oxidizing flame to a
reducing flame. Secret-color porcelain had a high degree of vitrification,
jade-like luster, neat and full glaze application, and five irregular prop

marks at the bottom. Most of the unearthed vessels were daily life utensils,
such as plates, bowls, dishes, pots, bottles, boxes, saucers, water pots,
flagons, and washers. Most were small and exquisite with high artistic
attainment. All parts of the vessels, from the mouth, belly, bottom to the
corners and protruding ridges, were meticulously fashioned. Even the
circular feet of bowls, dishes, and washers were not simply dug out, but
were fashioned from several pieces and then polished with the wheel. Thus,
the circular feet extended slightly outward, appearing delicate and beautiful,
resembling gold and silver utensils. The shape design emphasized proper
use of lines, which, either long or short, straight or curved, all
complemented naturally and appropriately the vessel’s shape. Even the
weight and thickness of the body were in perfect harmony with the use of
the utensils. (Fig. 7.25) Exquisite Yue ware was often praised by literati and
poets. For instance, the Tang poet Pi Rixiu described Yue kiln teacups as
“round like a fallen moon and light like rising clouds,”extolling both the
neatness of the shape and the lightness of the body.

Fig. 7.25 Yue kiln secret-color long-neck porcelain vase,
Tang Dynasty, height: 22.4 cm, top diam.: 2.3 cm, base diam.: 7.3 cm, in the Palace Museum

    Secret-color porcelain widely assimilated and skillfully integrated the
decorative approaches of Tang Dynasty gold and silver ware, bronzeware
and lacquerware, thus forming its own unique decoration style. The
decorative patterns covered a rich range of themes, such as symmetrical
butterflies, parrots, phoenixes, flying cranes, swimming dragons, birds and
plants, and rabbits in grass. There were also various blooming flowers
sketched with only a few strokes, such as peony, lotus, chrysanthemum,
sunflower, water lily, and crabapple.13 The carved images were full of vigor
and vitality, richly dynamic and not at all confined to any conventional
pattern. A highly skillful carving technique produced smooth, powerful
lines. The composition was meticulous. The various human figures, birds
and animals depicted were both realistic, and made more vivid by
appropriate exaggeration, achieving artistic effects close to those of
painting.
    In addition, it has been found that products similar to those of the Yuyao
kilns were produced by both the Yinxian and Shangyu kilns. It can be
inferred that the Yuyao kilns alone could not meet the Wuyue Kingdom’s
needs to satisfy the court, to pay tribute to the central plains monarch, and
to expand overseas trade, and so for other well-established folk kilns in the
jurisdiction of Yuezhou, the Wuyue Kingdom also sent officials to supervise
their production. In this way the advanced technical strength and superior
equipment at the time was concentrated and mass production was made
possible under strict management and supervision. The secret-color
porcelain we see today is undoubtedly celadon produced in such “imperial
kilns.”14
    In recent years, with the discovery of more archaeological data,
especially with the unearthing of blue glazed bottles, bowls, plates, dishes,
etc. recorded as “porcelain of secret color” from the Tang Dynasty
underground palace in Famen Temple in Shaanxi Province in 1987, the
mysterious veil shrouding secret-color porcelain has been finally lifted.
Nowadays, researchers of ancient ceramics have basically reached the
consensus that secret-color porcelain was not necessarily fired in tributary
kilns, rather, it was more a general term for the best Yue celadon from the
Tang and Song dynasties.

7.2.4 Celadon Other Than Yue Ware of the Tang and Five
Dynasties
In the Tang and Five Dynasties, many other famous kilns besides the Yue
kilns were also firing celadon.

7.2.4.1 Wuzhou Kilns in Zhejiang Province
The Wuzhou kilns were another famous kiln cluster in Zhejiang Province.
They originated back in the Three Kingdoms period, reached their peak in
the Tang and Five Dynasties, and continued firing till the Song Dynasty,
lasting some 900 years. Products of the kilns were mainly celadon, which
ranked third in Lu Yu’s Book of Tea. From the Tang and Five Dynasties to
the Northern Song Dynasty, the Wuzhou kilns developed rapidly with a
continuous expansion of their production scale. The kilns were widely
distributed in various counties in Jinhua and Quzhou prefectures, forming a
unique porcelain kiln system of their own. Besides celadon, the Wuzhou
kilns also fired black glazed porcelain, colorful glazed porcelain and color
painting porcelain.
   Wuzhou kiln celadon had a dark body color, mostly dark gray or purple.
The glaze was rarely jade green. Rather, it was often green with a yellow,
yellowish-brown or beige tone. Jinhua and Quxian were red soil areas. To
change the body color, Wuzhou celadon started using engobe as early as the
Western Jin Dynasty and had widely applied the technology by the Eastern
Jin Dynasty. The glaze layer was uneven, often strewn with coagulated
sesame dots and small crystals that precipitated where the bonding between
body and glaze was not strong enough and where the glaze surface cracked.
Most products were roughly made, and the quality was not as good as Yue
ware. Nonetheless there were also many fine works. After the middle and
late Tang Dynasty, the Wuzhou kilns mainly produced daily use utensils for
the common people, such as bowls, plates, bottles, and jars. Common
funerary objects included small-mouthed dragon jars and multiple-horned
jars, the latter evolving from the granary urns of the Three Kingdoms and
Jin Dynasty. They were peculiarly shaped with pointy horns all over and
symbolized good harvest for all crops. In the Tang Dynasty, celadon
decorated with black and brown patches appeared among the products of
the Wuzhou kilns. The decoration was like that of the colorful glazed
porcelain in the north.

Besides celadon and blue-glazed brown-spotted porcelain, the Wuzhou
kilns in the Tang Dynasty succeeded in firing opaque glaze porcelain. All
the six Wuzhou kilns of the early Tang Dynasty that have been discovered
so far featured opaque glaze porcelain as their main products. These
porcelains were mostly pale blue, with some azure or sky blue. The glaze
was thick with an even, smooth surface. Major varieties included bowls,
pots, and jars. On these opaque glaze wares there were sometimes also large
round brown spots, mostly on jar lugs, bottle bellies or bowl mouths. This
opaque glaze porcelain was fired until the Yuan Dynasty.

7.2.4.2 Shouzhou Kilns in Anhui Province
The Shouzhou kilns were located in Shangyao Town in the Tianjia’an
District of Huainan Prefecture, Anhui Province. The sites are scattered in
the southern and northern suburbs of the town, on the east bank of Gaotang
Lake and the Yaohe River, and at the western foot of Mount Laogua. The
sites are arranged along a four-kilometer belt from Guanjiazui to Waiyao,
with the sites in Yujiagou being the most concentrated and those in
Guanjiazui being the earliest. The distribution and age of the kiln sites
indicate that porcelain firing expanded from north to south. Shangyao Town
sported a convenient water route—wooden sailboats could enter the Huaihe
River via the Yaohe River—and it was along this water route that Shouzhou
ware was transported to and sold in different places along the Huaihe River.
Yellow glazed porcelain wares from the Tang Dynasty have been unearthed
in an area hundreds of kilometers long along the Huaihe River, from eastern
Henan to northern Anhui and then to northern Jiangsu. A substantial part of
these yellow glazed wares was in all probability produced by the Shouzhou
kilns. It is credible that the Yujiagou kilns were in fact the Shouzhou kilns
which were famous in the Tang Dynasty because the main products of
Yujiagou were yellow glazed wares, coinciding with the record of Lu Yu’s
Book of Tea that “Shouzhou porcelain was yellow”.
   Shouzhou kiln porcelain featured yellow glaze of different shades.
Some were like the color of wax, some were the color of eels, and some
were yellowish green, with this last type being the finest. This yellow glaze
porcelain was actually a variant of celadon, in effect the outcome of
unsuccessful firing, that is, the yellow glaze was produced by insufficient
reducing of the iron molecules in the glaze material. Thus, this porcelain
should be included in the celadon system. The Shouzhou kilns also fired

black porcelain, some of which also carried printed patterns, but these were
relatively rare.
   The main utensils produced by the Shouzhou kilns were bowls, cups,
small cups, flagons, pillows and all kinds of children’s toys, with bowls and
small cups being the most numerous. The wares were thick and heavy,
mostly with flat bottoms and some with concave bottoms. The bottoms of
bowls and small cups were often trimmed with a knife, a feature similar to
the Xing white porcelain of the Sui and Tang dynasties. The body of
Shouzhou ware had a rough texture and a white color with a tinge of red.
Many semi-finished products coated with engobe but not glazed have been
found at the sites. This shows that some of the Shouzhou wares were first
fired without clay, then had a layer of white engobe applied, and then
glazed and returned to the kiln. During the works on Huaihe River in the
1950s, thousands of Shouzhou kiln wares were unearthed at a construction
site stretching hundreds of miles in northern Anhui, which indicates the
production scale of the Shouzhou kilns must have been quite large.

7.2.4.3 Ou Kilns in Zhejiang Province
The Ou kilns were distributed in Wenzhou, Yongjia and Rui’an in present-
day southern Zhejiang Province. The Ou kilns were famous celadon kilns in
Zhejiang in the Tang Dynasty similar to the Yue and Wuzhou kilns. Though
their production scale and porcelain-making achievements lagged far
behind Yue celadon and more Yue ware has been unearthed in various
places, the shape design of Ou kiln porcelain was more elegant and
beautiful than that of the Yue kiln products. In the late Tang Dynasty,
bowls, plates, pots, saucers and other utensils broke free from previous
conventional designs and assumed a variety of forms including imitating
the shapes of flowers and fruit, resulting in lightweight, attractive and
practical vessels. This modeling approach is similar to that of Yue ware in
the same period, reflecting a common aesthetic taste of the time.
  Ou kiln products had a loose body texture which was not as dense as
Yue ware, grayish white body color which was lighter than Yue ware, and a
neat glaze layer with better transparency than Yue ware. Ou kiln wares in
the early and middle Tang Dynasty inherited the legacy of the Southern
Dynasties with yellowish glaze that had ice crackles and was prone to
peeling. By the late Tang Dynasty there appeared a jade-like green glaze
that bonded well with the body and rarely peeled. The shape design became

lighter, richer and more delicate and porcelain-making technologies
improved significantly, making the late Tang Dynasty the peak period for
the Ou kilns that saw unprecedented development.

7.2.4.4 Qiong Kilns in Sichuan Province
The Qiong kilns, also called the Qionglai kilns, constituted a huge kiln
system in southwestern Sichuan. Originating in the Eastern Jin Dynasty,
developing in the Sui Dynasty, flourishing in the Tang and Five Dynasties,
and declining in the middle and late Southern Song Dynasty, the kiln
system lasted for nine centuries. Its greatest contribution was, inspired by
the Yue kilns in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River, the pioneering
firing of multicolored painted porcelain featuring brown, black and green
colors, which had a significant impact on the subsequent tricolor glazed
earthenware of the Tang Dynasty and the high-temperature painted
porcelain of the Changsha kilns. They are named “Qionglai” kilns because
the first and most representative sites were found in present-day Qionglai
County. The Qiong kilns mainly fired celadon and were the most famous
kilns in Sichuan during the Tang Dynasty. The kiln sites won the attention
of and were investigated many times by domestic and foreign researchers as
early as the 1930s but were also severely damaged by theft excavations.
After the 1950s, many investigations and small-scale excavations by the
Sichuan Cultural Relics Management Committee and the Qionglai Cultural
Relics Preservation Institute produced a preliminary understanding of the
history and distribution of the kilns. According to existing archaeological
excavation findings, there are 13 Qiong kiln sites from the Tang Dynasty,
which are widely distributed, mainly in four places in Qinglai County,
namely, Wayaoshan in Guyi, Jianshanzi in Xihe, Dayucun in Baihe, and
Shifangtang in Nanhe.
   The body of Qiong kiln porcelain was rough, thick and heavy. Most was
brown, dark brown or purplish red. There were several types of glaze, blue,
bluish gray, green, yellow, caramel, and so on. If the body was dark brown
or reddish brown, the glaze would mostly be green, greenish blue or
yellowish blue. If the body color was light, approaching grayish white, the
glaze would be bluish gray or whitish blue. The body of Qiong kiln wares
was mostly dark brown or purplish red because it was made of a type of
clay with a high iron content, so before glazing the ware surface had a layer

of white engobe applied to serve as a backdrop, and then was decorated
with printing and carving. (Fig. 7.26).





Fig. 7.26 Qiong kiln yellowish brown-glazed multiple-legged inkstone,
Tang Dynasty, height: 5 cm, top diam.: 11.4 cm, base diam.: 14.6 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Qiong kiln products included daily use utensils, stationery, toys, and
various kinds of sculptures. Daily use utensils included pots, jars, bowls,
plates, cups, dishes, small cups, lamps (Fig. 7.27), stoves, yi (gourd-shaped
ladles), dou, boxes, spittoons, and crocks. These utensils had distinctive
regional characteristics. The pots were generally high with thin bottoms,
long curved spouts, and “P”-shaped or “阝”-shaped handles. The handle and
spout were mostly flush with the pot’s mouth at the highest, with some
higher than the pot’s mouth. The shape design often imitated other artifacts.
For instance, there are cups decorated with an interlaced branch pattern that
imitated wickerwork, deep-bellied goblets that imitated gold and silver
ones, the same as cups produced by the Xiangyin kilns in Hunan and the
Fengcheng kilns in Jiangxi. There are also hoop handle jars imitating
wooden pails with mouths bigger than their bottoms and hoop handles on
their mouths. The shape of the hoop handle cups are the same as the hoop

handle jars. There are also various round boxes with printed patterns, whose
shape and decoration were also copied from similar gold and silver vessels.





Fig. 7.27 Qiong kiln green-glazed oil lamp,
Tang Dynasty, height: 3.7 cm, top diam.: 13 cm, base diam.: 6.8 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Ceramic sculptures fired by the Qiong kilns are lifelike, vivid and
attractive. There are chickens, ducks, lions, tigers, oxen, horses, monkeys,
dogs, cats, tortoises, fish, parrots and more. A single duck-shaped wine cup
unearthed from a site is adequate and clear proof of the Qiong kiln
craftsmen’s masterly shaping skills. The entire cup is shaped like a duck
lying on its stomach with its tail fanning out to form the cup mouth and its
head turned and reaching to grip the tail with its beak to form the cup
handle.
   Besides celadon, the underglaze painted porcelain of the Qiong kilns is
also quite distinctive. The Qiong kilns first invented and fired high-
temperature tricolor porcelain in the Sui Dynasty, and subsequently
produced multicolored painted porcelain. These colorful porcelains were
collectively known as “tricolor Qiong ware.”Initially black, brown and
green colorings or two of the three were used to paint on blue, beige white
or grayish white glaze. The patterns painted are simple and graceful, mainly
geometric patterns composed of linked beads and circles, black lines and

circles, or grass images, circles and linked beads. Such patterns are in some
respects similar to the linked circle pattern of brocade and also resemble the
joint circle and linked dot patterns commonly used in ancient Persia. The
Qiong kilns were among the first to fire Tang tricolor earthenware. In his
The Rise and Inheritance of Color Glazed Ware of the Qiong Kilns, Tang
Changpu introduced the view that the origin of Tang tricolor earthenware in
the north was through the influence of Qiong kiln ware in the south and
conjectured that it was Wu Zetian that brought the Qiong kiln tricolor ware
from Sichuan up to the central plains. It was perhaps thanks to the
patronage and promotion of Wu Zetian that tricolor ware became famous
after she took the throne.15
   By the Tang Dynasty, the colors evolved from black, brown and green
to yellow, green, brown, blue and white dominated by yellow, green and
brown, with occasional red patches here and there. In terms of patterns, the
circles and linked beads of the Sui Dynasty were inherited. There were
grass patterns, floral scrolls, auspicious clouds, lotus scrolls, and
composites of auspicious clouds and grass patterns, or of grass patterns and
vertical linked dots, painted with yellow, green and brown colorings. Still
more commonly seen were randomly painted patches and speckles, the
latter mostly green, and the former brown and green or green and yellow,
some round, some in the shape of the tip of the heart, and some in irregular
stripes. Sometimes three or two colors were randomly applied to the faces
and bodies of people or animals painted on the ware. The sintering
temperature was 1,270 ± 20 ℃. It is worth noting that the Qiong kilns also
produced low-temperature tricolor ware, which featured brown and green
paintings or printed patterns on yellow glaze. The body of high-temperature
tricolor ware was mostly grayish black, blackish red, reddish brown or
yellowish brown. A few were yellowish white or grayish white. Most of the
exposed body parts were blackish red in varying shades and very few were
yellowish white. The body of low-temperature tricolor ware, on the other
hand, was red or white, with exposed body parts being brick red or
yellowish white. Both high and low temperature tricolor ware had white
engobe underglaze applied,16 which was like the Changsha kilns’
underglaze painted porcelain, rich in local color with distinct characteristics
of the time.

7.2.4.5 The Hongzhou Kilns in Jiangxi Province

Hongzhou kiln sites were first discovered by the Jiangxi Provincial
Museum in 1978 in the Luohu area of Fengcheng in the south of Nanchang.
They were so named because back in the Tang Dynasty Fengcheng was
under the jurisdiction of Hongzhou. There were about 29 sites scattered in
an area covering some 400,000 square meters, with deposits reaching six
meters thick in some places. Archaeological excavations have proven that
Hongzhou kilns started firing porcelain in the Eastern Han Dynasty,
flourished in the Sui and Tang Dynasties, and declined in the Tang and Five
Dynasties, lasting for more than 800 years.
   The body of Hongzhou ware had a rough texture and brown or dark
brown color. To improve body surface texture, a layer of engobe was
applied before the wares were sent for firing. Most glaze was yellowish-
brown or caramel. Thus, in the Book of Tea Lu Yu notes, “Hongzhou
porcelain is brown”. Taking into consideration the entire history of the
Hongzhou kilns, we may note that although in general they are not able to
truly compare with Yue ware, from the Southern Dynasties to the early Sui
and Tang dynasties, Hongzhou ware was not inferior to Yue kiln celadon in
terms of shape, glaze color and decoration, nor was it inferior to the
products of the Wuzhou or Shouzhou kilns at the time either. The reason
why Lu Yu ranked Hongzhou ware sixth or last in the Book of Tea was in
fact because the Hongzhou kiln products he observed in this period were
yellowish brown vessels from the declining period of the kilns.
    In the Tang Dynasty, the Hongzhou kilns mainly fired bowls, cups and
plates. Other varieties included saucers, pots, long stem plates, spittoons,
inkstones and ding stoves. The shape of the wares was very distinctive.
   The decorative techniques of Hongzhou kiln porcelain included
printing, stacking and carving. One important decorative feature of
Hongzhou ware, and one rarely seen in the products of other famous kilns,
was a circle of swirl patterns printed on the outer mouth rim of vessels,
especially bowls, small cups and zhong. Hongzhou ware was rarely fully
glazed, exposing the body on the foot and bottom. Many Hongzhou vessels
were unearthed in Tang tombs in Jiangxi and other places.

7.2.4.6 Jingdezhen Kilns
Mr. Chen Wanli discovered a number of celadon shards on the highway of
Baihuwan and a hillside in Yangmeiting in 1953 during his inspection
around Hutian. The body was gray and thick. The bottom also had

yellowish blue glaze that was thin with very fine crackles applied. Plates
had wide rims with burn marks on them. The center of the plates had the
marks of propping tools and shallow bowls had dented marks on the
outside, which indicated the vessels were placed one on top of the other in
the kiln. Mr. Chen Wanli, concluding “all these are obviously Tang style”,
regarded the shards found in Yangmeiting and Baihuwan as products of the
Tang Dynasty.17 Later, archaeologists, after analyzing and studying the
shape design and firing techniques of the specimens unearthed from the
above-mentioned sites and comparing them to those unearthed from dated
tombs, believed they were products not of the Tang Dynasty but of the Five
Dynasties18. Thus, researchers have always believed the earliest kiln site
found in Jingdezhen was from the Five Dynasties period. Still later findings
have pointed to a different conclusion.
   At the end of December 2011, the brick factory in Jinxing Village of
Xianghu Town came across remains of ancient kilns when digging earth on
a back hillside (Wanyaowu). After learning about this, researchers of the
Jingdezhen Institute of Ceramic Archaeology immediately went to
investigate and found a large number of blue glazed porcelain shards and
kiln furniture exposed on the surface of the col. As the remains had been
damaged, the Institute immediately organized the teachers and students of
the School of Archaeology and Museology of Peking University and the
Jingdezhen Ceramics Institute to conduct archaeological investigations and
undertake rescue excavations at the kiln site. The excavations revealed a red
soil layer, possibly remnants of a kiln, and an ash pit, and unearthed lots of
specimens.
   The site is on the hillside of Wanyaowu in the northwest of Lantian
Village in Xianghu Town, 20 km to the east of Jingdezhen City. Objects
unearthed include blue glazed porcelain, white glazed porcelain, qingbai
porcelain, fishing net weights, porcelain whetstones, and kiln furniture, with
blue glazed porcelain accounting for nearly 90% of all shard specimens.
Specifically, the unearthed relics were described as follows: 1. The blue
glazed porcelain had yellowish blue glaze and a grayish brown body.
Varieties included handled ewers, jars, bowls, plates and dishes. 2. The
amount of white porcelain unearthed was very small. The main varieties
were bowls, plates and jars, with bowls and plates mostly with circular feet
and jars with decals on the shoulder. 3. The amount of qingbai porcelain
unearthed was also very small, mainly bowls and plates with circular feet

and simple carved patterns. 4. Unglazed porcelain fishing net weights came
in large and small sizes and more than 10 types. 5. Porcelain whetstones
were unglazed and disc-shaped with a round hole in the center. 6. Kiln
furniture included flat-bottomed slanting-walled saggers, sagger trays,
cushion columns, ring-shaped cushion pads, and kiln props.
   Previous archaeological investigations showed that there are more than
30 kiln sites from the Five Dynasties to the Song Dynasty in Xianghu
Town, where Wanyaowu in Lantian Village is located. From ancient times
Xianghu Town had enjoyed a flourishing economy and a wonderful
humanistic environment. The “Eight Sceneries of Xianghu” (Azure Dragon
Ancient Temple, White Tiger Long Bridge, Southern Pond Willows,
Northern Lane Flowers, Moon upon Stream, Double Peaks Shrouded in
Clouds, Fishing on Rocky Ledge, and Night Ferry) were recorded in the
Gazetteer of Fuliang County. The town was surrounded by hills, which
supplied abundant firewood, and enjoyed convenient water transportation
with the Nanhe River connecting to the Changjiang River. These offered
particularly favorable natural conditions for firing porcelain.
   Many objects unearthed in Lantian on this occasion had never been
found before in ancient Jingdezhen kiln sites. For instance, the bowls,
plates, pots and jars, all with blue glaze and flat bottoms, differed greatly
from previously discovered relics from the Five Dynasties in terms of body
and glaze quality and shape design. According to ceramics typology, these
blue-glazed flat-bottomed wares should be from prior to the Five Dynasties.
I had come across and purchased bowls and pots from the late Tang
Dynasty, mostly blue glazed with a rough body, in Jingdezhen’s ancient
ceramics market before, and after hearing of the excavation work in Lantian
Village, I went there to investigate personally. I came upon some porcelain
shards and kiln tools. The body quality of the shards was basically the same
as the late Tang ware I had purchased earlier. Porcelain in the late Tang
Dynasty was in general poorly made, and the glaze of many was unevenly
fired. (Fig. 7.28) The marks of propping nails on the wells of bowls were
also very obvious. (Fig. 7.29).

Fig. 7.28 Jingdezhen kiln celadon jar,
Late Tang Dynasty, in the Jiangxi Jingdezhen Folk Kiln Art Research Institute

Fig. 7.29 Jingdezhen kiln celadon bowl,
Late Tang Dynasty, in the Jiangxi Jingdezhen Folk Kiln Art Research Institute

   Kiln sites from the Five Dynasties in Jingdezhen were discovered
earlier. There were about 20 sites, mainly distributed on both sides of the
Nanhe River and in today’s Jingdezhen urban areas. On the two sides of the
Nanhe River there were Hutian, Yangmeiting, Sanbaopeng, Huangnitou,
Tongluoshan, Yingtian, Yueguangshan, Shihuwan, Xianghu, Shou’an,
Fengshushan, and others, and in the urban areas there were Luomaqiao,
Shibadu, Shegongmiao, Dongjiawu, Lijia’ao, and more. The accumulation
of relics at these sites had reached a certain scope and thickness, with an
average thickness of one to two meters.
    Varieties found at the above kiln sites are basically the same, mainly
celadon and white porcelain wares for daily use such as bowls, plates,
dishes, and handled ewers. The shape, body and glaze of celadon wares
shared the common style of celadon produced by southern kilns such as the
Yue and Changsha kilns. The white porcelain reached the standards of
modern porcelain with its spotless white color and fine texture. It was the
earliest white porcelain produced in southern China and represented the
finest porcelain quality in China at the time. This foreshadowed
Jingdezhen’s emergence as the country’s development center of qingbai
porcelain later in the Song Dynasty.19
   Jingdezhen products in the Five Dynasties were mainly daily use wares
that mostly featured plain surfaces without decoration, fine body texture,
thin walls, and neat shapes with some common modeling features such as
flowery mouths, melon-shaped bellies, flat bottoms with wide edges, and
short circular feet. Porcelain of this period was made from the single raw
material of porcelain stone and the calcium oxide content in the lime glaze

was 10.92%. Porcelain stone was mined, crushed (with a water powered tilt
hammer) and washed to make body clay. Preparation of the glaze material
also involved limestone mining, lime burning, and selecting porcelain stone
with a high potassium and sodium content and a low alumina content to be
crushed and washed into fine material. The relics found at the dozen kiln
sites from the Five Dynasties were all accumulated in compact places, and
the scale was not at all as extensive or thick as that of the Song Dynasty,
which indicates that in the Five Dynasties the greenware workshops and
kiln yards of Jingdezhen were in the same place although no greenware
workshops have been found to date.
   Greenwares were placed one on top of another with propping nails in
between and sent to kilns for firing. Since the height of the greenwares
overlaid together was limited, the kiln chamber could not be too high. Then
if the kiln was made short, the firing temperature and atmosphere would be
easily impacted, and the energy utilization rate would be low. To avoid this,
the kiln body had to be lengthened and the slope of the kiln bottom had to
be increased to an appropriate degree. Thus, it is presumed that dragon kilns
were the popular kiln form at the time. The wares were of limited variety,
rough craftsmanship, and primitive firing method. The large number of
defective goods at the kiln sites indicate that the ceramics industry had just
emerged and started developing. I once collected some porcelain shards at
the Huangnitou kiln site of the Five Dynasties in Jingdezhen and found that
there were both celadon and white porcelain in the same kiln. There were
also many porcelain fragments with obvious marks left by propping nails.
(Fig. 7.30).

Fig. 7.30 Jingdezhen kiln celadon and white porcelain shards,
Five Dynasties, in the Jiangxi Jingdezhen Folk Kiln Art Research Institute

7.2.4.7 Xicun Kilns in Guangdong Province
To date, some 138 Tang dynasty kiln sites have been found in 32 cities and
counties in Guangdong, of which the Xicun kilns in Guangzhou are the
most representative. Guangdong porcelain in the Tang Dynasty displayed
distinct regional characteristics. All the kilns fired celadon as the main
product and produced small numbers of yellow glazed and caramel glazed
vessels. Celadon produced in the early Tang Dynasty often had yellowish
glaze and a loose body texture. Varieties were limited, mainly daily use
utensils, the majority of which were semi-glazed and often troubled by
peeling due to insufficient bonding between glaze and body. By the late
Tang Dynasty, celadon glaze had become greenish and lustrous, most kilns
realized firm body-glaze bonding, and utensil varieties increased greatly.
Tang dynasty kilns in Guangdong were dominated by steamed bun kilns,
which developed there under the influence of northern steamed bun kilns.
For example, seven steamed bun kilns have been found and cleaned up in
modern-day Chaozhou, Foshan, Sanshui and Xinhui. Dragon kilns have
also been found in Guangdong but were small in number and from a later
period, mostly from the late Tang Dynasty.

7.2.4.8 Tongchuan Kilns in Shaanxi Province
The Tongchuan kilns, located in Huangbao Town, Tongchuan, Shaanxi
Province, originated in the Tang Dynasty, flourished in the Song Dynasty
and withered in the Yuan Dynasty. They were also called the “Yaozhou
kilns” because in the late Tang and Five Dynasties Yaozhou was set up in
Tongchuan, and Huangbao Town was under the jurisdiction of Yaozhou.
Huangbao Town was 20 km southwest of Tongchuan City and 15 km north
of the Yaozhou District. The kiln site is in the southwest of the town and
extends from the Xiaoqing River Stone Bridge to Xincungou. The ruins and
remains are scattered along both sides of the Xianyu Highway and both
banks of the Qihe River. The extensive size of the site and the richness of
the relics is rare in ancient porcelain kiln sites in northern China. In the
past, little Yaozhou kiln celadon from the Tang Dynasty was unearthed.
Large volumes of celadon were unearthed only in the 1980s. Varieties were
rich; in addition to daily life objects, there were also stationery, musical
instruments and religious utensils such as Kalasa (water vases).
Specifically, there were bowls, handled ewers, double-lugged bottles, plate-
mouthed bottles, basins, gourd-shaped bottles, Kalasa, fish-pair bottles,
cuspidors (Fig. 7.31), lamp holders, spittoons, double-eared jars, hoop
handled jars, saucers, etc. Some vessels were printed, carved, or engraved
with decorative patterns. The glaze layer was thin and had a good glass
texture, yet there were often shades of yellow or gray. During the late Tang
and Five Dynasties there appeared a small quantity of celadon with pure
glaze color, which, while its texture was not as good as the Yue celadon at
the time, laid the foundation for Yaozhou celadon’s rise to fame in the Song
Dynasty. (Fig. 7.32).

Fig. 7.31 Yaozhou kiln blue-glazed lotus style cuspidor,
Five Dynasties, height: 6.3 cm, top diam.: 7.3 cm, base diam.: 4 cm, in the Palace Museum

Fig. 7.32 Yaozhou kiln blue-glazed bowl,
Five Dynasties, height: 5 cm, top diam.: 11.4 cm, base diam.: 4.6 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Excavation data show that in the Tang Dynasty Yaozhou kilns were
steamed-bun-shaped inverted-flame kilns using wood as fuel. Because this
type of kiln could control the atmosphere within easily, its product types
were quite rich. In addition to blue glazed porcelain, there were also black
glazed ware, yellow glazed ware, white glazed ware, multicolor glazed
ware, tea-leaf glazed ware, white glazed ware with black painting, white
glazed ware with green painting, black glazed ware with color painting on
cleared ground, white glazed ware with brown painting, celadon with
brown painting, tricolor ware, unglazed ware with black painting and
unglazed plain ware.
   Like most porcelain kilns of the Tang Dynasty, the Tongchuan kilns
mainly fired daily use vessels such as bowls, plates, pots, boxes, bottles,
and cups, as well as some small porcelain figurines. Different from its
products later in the Northern Song, which were mainly celadon with
carved and printed patterns, Tongchuan kiln products during the Tang
Dynasty were dominated by plain items without decorative patterns, except
for white glazed ones which were often painted with simple black

decorations. Common patterns were flower and grass, clouds, speckles, or
round, long and heart-tip-shaped patches. A few used Chinese characters as
decoration. The shape design of the vessels had typical characteristics of the
Tang Dynasty.

7.3 White Porcelain of the Sui, Tang and Five
Dynasties
7.3.1 Xing Kilns
The landscape of “southern celadon and northern white” was a feature of
ceramic production of the Sui and Tang dynasties. Celadon production had
a longer history in China. The primitive porcelain of the Shang and Zhou
dynasties was already close to celadon and by the Eastern Han celadon
production had grown to be quite mature. In contrast, white porcelain
production started later, originating in the Northern Dynasties and realized
successful firing only in the Sui Dynasty. Porcelain workers of the Sui
Dynasty mastered the skill of controling the iron content in the body and
glaze material such that it remained under a certain level and so realized
firing of white porcelain with good and stable color. The Sui dynasty white
porcelain unearthed from tombs near modern-day Xi’an had attractive
shapes and bright glaze. Tests show that the content of ferric oxide (Fe2O3)
in the body is only 1.12%. (Figs. 7.33 and 7.34).

Fig. 7.33 White-glazed engraved double-lugged thin-neck bottle,
Sui or Tang Dynasty, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S

Fig. 7.34 White-glazed double dragon-handled plate-mouthed bottle,
Sui or Tang Dynasty, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S

   White porcelain-making technology was quite mature by the Sui
Dynasty, yet it took a long time to locate the site of the kilns. In May 1982 a
Sui dynasty white porcelain kiln site was found in Jiacun on the border
between Neiqiu and Lincheng. White porcelain vessels found at the site
included those with engobe applied to a grayish white body as well as
extremely exquisite items without engobe. Bowls all had deep bellies,
straight walls, and flat bottoms, the same as white porcelain bowls
unearthed from northern Sui tombs. The discovery of Sui white porcelain in
the area of the Tang dynasty Xing kilns indicated that white porcelain had
developed in the area prior to the Xing kiln white porcelain appearing later
in the Tang Dynasty. The discovery of a Sui dynasty white porcelain kiln
site in Jiacun provided evidence for the maturity of white porcelain firing
technology in the Sui Dynasty and for the first time provided an answer to
the location of the kilns that produced the Sui dynasty white porcelain that
had been unearthed.
   The appearance and production of white porcelain in the Sui and Tang
dynasties was an important event in the history of Chinese ceramics. If it
had not been for the birth and development of white porcelain, the
appearance of polychrome porcelains that came later, such as the Yuan blue
and white porcelain, the Ming wucai porcelain, the Kangxi wucai porcelain,
and the Yongzheng famille-rose porcelain, would all not have been
possible. White porcelain developed mature firing technology in the Sui
Dynasty, and reached a zenith in the Tang Dynasty. The most renowned
white porcelain kilns in the Tang Dynasty were the Xing kilns, whose status
in white porcelain production was like that of the Yue kilns in celadon
production. In fact, the porcelain production landscape of the Tang Dynasty
was mainly characterized by the celadon kiln system represented by the Yue
kilns in Zhejiang and the white porcelain kiln system represented by the
Xing kilns in Hebei. The white porcelain kilns of the Tang Dynasty were
mainly located in modern-day Hebei and Henan, specifically, the Xing,
Ding and Cizhou kilns in Hebei, and the Gongxian and Mixian kilns in
Henan. In addition, the Hunyuan kilns in Shanxi were also producing white
porcelain at the time.
   The Xing kilns were among the most famous porcelain kilns in the Tang
Dynasty and were of great significance in the history of Chinese ceramics,

but their sites were discovered relatively late. Li Zhao of the Tang Dynasty
recorded in his Guo Shi Bu that “white porcelain teacups from Neiqiu and
purple inkstones from Duanxi were used by the rich and the poor”, from
which it may be deduced that the Xing kilns were probably in Neiqiu. In
August 1980, multiple kiln sites were found in Ciyaogou on the border of
modern-day Lincheng and Neiqiu and in Chengcun, Xiecun, Chengdi, and
Gangtou in Lincheng County. Relics of the Tang Dynasty were found at the
site cluster in Gangtou. In Qicun and Shuangjingcun to the north of
Gangtou, kiln sites from the early and middle Tang Dynasty were found,
and the white porcelain produced by the Qicun kilns was the most typical of
Xing kiln white porcelain. In 1985 a few more sites were discovered in the
Chengguan area in Neiqiu County. The white porcelain produced there was
the same as that fired by the Qicun kilns, some with jade bi-shaped bottoms
carved with the Chinese character “盈”(ying). The discovery of Xing kiln
sites in Neiqiu provided evidence for the record of Li Zhao’s Guo Shi Bu.
(Figs. 7.35 and 7.36).





Fig. 7.35 Xing kiln white-glazed bowl,
Tang Dynasty, height: 4.7 cm, top diam.: 15.6 cm, base diam.: 6.7 cm, in the Palace Museum

Fig. 7.36 Xing kiln white porcelain handled pot,
Tang Dynasty, height: 12.5 cm, top diam.: 6.7 cm, in the National Museum of China

   Compared with common white porcelain of the same period, the body
of Xing kiln white porcelain had a lower Fe2O3 and TiO2 content, and a
higher Al2O3 content, which meant the firing temperature of Xing kiln
white porcelain would have been higher and the resultant whiteness better.
White porcelain of the late Tang Dynasty had a rough and gray body with
engobe applied, which gave the glaze a yellowish or grayish white color,
with some silver white.
   The most prominent feature of Xing ware was of course its “silver-like”
and “snow-like” glaze color as described by Lu Yu in his Book of Tea. The
poet Pi Rixiu in his poem Teacups, described Yue ware vividly as “round

like the fallen moon and light like rising clouds,”extolling the neatness of
the shape, the lightness of the body and the whiteness of the color.
   Though the main impression of Xing ware in most people’s minds was
its “snow-like white” color, as far as the shards unearthed at the Qicun and
Neiqiu sites are concerned, there are three glaze colors, namely white,
black, and brownish yellow. White ware can be classified into coarse and
fine, with the former making up the majority and the latter accounting for a
little. Xing ware was famous for its white color and previously no
additional decoration had been found. After the discovery of the Qicun
sites, however, it was found that Xing white porcelain production also used
many decorative techniques, such as printing, carving and dotting, which
offered a more comprehensive understanding of Xing white ware.
   Most Sui and Tang vessels and fragments unearthed at the Neiqiu sites
were pots, bowls, plates, jars, basins, pillows and other household utensils,
as well as small sculptures such as horse riders, white porcelain lions and
bird food receptacles. (Fig. 7.37) The Xing kiln fine white porcelain mainly
consisted of bowls, holders, leather-bag style pots, flagons, jars, and other
varieties, with the most common being shallow-bellied open-mouthed
bowls and shallow or deep tight-mouthed bowls. Some had a circular foot
and some had flat bottoms. Some of the bowls had mouth rims in the shape
of eight petals, four straight ridges on the outer walls, and a circular foot in
the shape of a four-petal crabapple flower and came with a disc-shaped
bowl tray with a short circular foot. Vessels unearthed included one leather-
bag style pot with a hoop handle, flat bottom, and raised lines resembling
leather stitching marks on both sides (Fig. 7.38), a water pot with a
spherical belly, short spout and curved handle (Fig. 7.39), and a jar with a
round lip, short neck and broad shoulder (Fig. 7.40). The vessels all had an
extremely white body and were glazed, and it is no exaggeration to describe
them as “white as snow”.

   Xing ware mostly featured a plain surface without patterns, except for
some vessels with carved or attached decorations. While this seemed not as
advanced as the renowned contemporaneous Yue celadon that featured
richer decorative patterns, white porcelain obviously required higher firing
technologies than celadon. The Xing kilns were the first to fire mature
white porcelain in the Sui Dynasty, and their products were sold widely not
only in China but also to overseas markets. In fact, Xing white porcelain
has been discovered in the ancient ruins of Iraq, Egypt, Pakistan, Japan and
Iran. (Fig. 7.41).
