7.6.2 Origin and Kilns
After Tang blue and white porcelain was discovered, researchers naturally
started investigating its kilns and origins. Tests on and analysis of several
blue and white porcelain shard specimens unearthed in Yangzhou and a
batch of Gongxian kiln white porcelain unearthed from the same strata
showed that the shape, body texture and glaze color of the two were highly
similar, as was the chemical composition of the body. Tests show that cobalt
oxide, the blue pigment for blue and white porcelain, was produced abroad.
In recent years, the Henan Provincial Institute of Cultural Heritage and
Archaeology carried out excavations of the Gongxian kiln site, where
samples of Tang blue and white porcelain and specimens similar to Tang
blue and white ware were found. The discovery provided an important
scientific clue for the further study of the kilns of Tang blue and white
porcelain.
   The findings concerning the kilns and raw materials of blue and white
porcelain provided important evidence for the study of its origin in China.
Since 2002, archaeological excavations in Shuichihe and Huangye Village

in the area of the Gongxian kiln site have proven that the area began firing
white porcelain back in the Northern Wei Dynasty and succeeded in making
fine white porcelain in the early to mid-Tang Dynasty. The production of
fine white porcelain in the Gongxian kilns laid the foundation for the
creation of Tang blue and white ware in terms of body texture. Besides
white porcelain, the Gongxian kilns were also famous for firing Tang
tricolor ware, which won people’s admiration with its colorfulness,
gorgeous decoration and vivid shapes, becoming the best-selling ceramic
products of the time at home and abroad, and were the most popular burial
objects found in the tombs of emperors and dignitaries during the peak of
the Tang Dynasty. The use of Tang tricolor pottery as burial objects was
also what enabled a large number of vessels to be preserved in their
entirety.37 With the long-term and large-scale production of tricolor pottery
in the Tang Dynasty, Gongxian kiln craftsmen accumulated rich practical
experience, including the mastery and application of the chemical
composition, preparation, coloring mechanism and firing technology of
various colorings and glazes. Especially significant was the mastery of the
properties and use of the cobalt blue pigment, which paved the way for the
creation of Tang blue and white porcelain. All these facts suggest that
Gongxian was probably one of the production sites of blue and white
porcelain in the Tang Dynasty. The emergence of Tang blue and white
porcelain was not only a reflection of China’s comprehensive physical and
chemical knowledge at the time, but also an affirmation of the leading
position and wide overseas dissemination of China’s science and
technology to the world.

7.6.3 Transportation of Exported Tang Blue and White
Porcelain
The Gongxian kilns were located at the junction of the Luoshui and Yellow
rivers, a water transport hub connecting most areas of northern China. From
the Gongxian kilns in the west, the Luoshui River reached the eastern
capital Luoyang and the capital Chang’an. To the east the Yellow River
reached Zhengzhou and Kaifeng, where one could enter the Grand Canal.
The Grand Canal connected northward to the North China Plain and there
one could reach Korea and Japan from Tianjin. It also connected southward
to Yangzhou, an important port and a domestic and international trade city
at the time. Then traveling from Yangzhou to the east along the Yangtze

River one could directly reach overseas regions including East Asia, South
Asia and the Middle East. On land, the Gongxian kilns were connected to
the capital Luoyang in the south through the Xuanyuan Pass. Luoyang was
the eastern end of the Silk Road, an important route for Gongxian kiln
products to be transported to the Western Regions and to Europe.38 These
provided necessary traffic conditions for the trade of blue and white
porcelain in the Tang Dynasty.

7.7 Export of Ceramics During the Sui, Tang and
Five Dynasties
7.7.1 Export Routes and Ports
The Tang Dynasty not only communicated and traded with the outside
world through the land-based Silk Road, but also opened maritime ceramic
trade routes. In the Tang Dynasty, maritime trade commissioners were
appointed and the positions were held concurrently by local officials or
transshipment commissioners. At that time, the maritime trade
commissioner of Guangzhou was the Lingnan Jiedushi (regional
commander). The main duties of the maritime trade commissioners were to
manage overseas trade affairs such as inspecting and releasing departing
foreign merchant ships, managing domestic merchant ships venturing
abroad, and implementing the court’s policies of encouraging foreign trade.
Initially a means of showing conciliation towards overseas people, the
primary purpose of appointing maritime trade commissioners was not to
increase foreign tax revenue through the management of merchant ships,
but to promote China’s national prestige and expand its political influence.
Maritime trade commissioners were also called “befriending
commissioners” because they were also responsible for foreign relations as
well as overseas trade affairs. The appointment of maritime trade
commissioners in the Tang Dynasty laid the foundation for the
establishment of the ancient maritime trade system in China and also
provided an excellent guarantee for the maritime ceramics trade of the
period.
   During the Tang Dynasty China’s ceramic products were not only for
the domestic market, but also exported in large numbers. There were mainly
two channels for this export. The land route, namely, the ancient Silk Road

which extended northwest through the Gansu Corridor and Western
Regions to reach Central Asia, Persia and Tianzhu (India), or traveled
northeast to reach Korea and then to Japan. However, due to the many
difficulties and high breakage rate in transporting porcelain by land, the
volume of porcelain exports in the early Tang Dynasty was small. After the
late Tang Dynasty, the development of the shipbuilding industry and
improvements in navigation technology created new conditions for the
large-scale export of porcelain and subsequently the export of China’s
porcelain was mainly by sea. There were two main sea routes. One, with
Guangzhou as the major port of departure, passed Southeast Asian countries
and skirted the Malay Peninsula to reach West Asian countries,
Mediterranean countries and regions, and Egypt. The other traveled
eastward from Mingzhou (today’s Ningbo) to reach Silla (the Korean
Peninsula) and Japan.
   The first route started from Guangzhou, the largest port in China and
one of the many ports in Guangdong which included the Ports of Leizhou
and Chaozhou. Traveler Sulaiman al-Tajir (CE ninth century) states in his
Journey to the East: “Ships of the Tang Dynasty were very big and only
Chinese ships could sail the dangerous Persian Gulf without hindrance”. At
that time lots of Indians and Persians came to Guangzhou and a zone for
foreigners took shape in the city known as “foreign town” (in the area of
today’s Guangta Road). The foreign town was a gathering place for foreign
businessmen that settled and conducted businesses there and had a “town
leader”. At its peak the number of foreigners living there surpassed
100,000.39 There were numerous shops in the town and the ceramics trade
was one of the most important parts of the businesses conducted there. The
flourishing ceramics trade at that time was mentioned in Zhu Yu’s Ping
Zhou Ke Tan in the Song Dynasty which describes foreign trade ships
berthed in the port being “tens of meters long and deep. Merchants stored
goods in the lower sections of the ship and slept on top of them at night.
The goods were mostly ceramics with the smaller items placed inside the
bigger ones to make the best use of the space”. Jia Dan, a scholar-official
during the Zhenyuan era of the Tang Dynasty, described in detail seven
international routes that connected China with all parts of the world. One of
the routes started from Guangzhou and passed more than 90 countries in the
South China Sea, the Indian Ocean, the Persian Gulf and the coast of East
Africa, making it the most important overseas trade route in the Tang

Dynasty and the longest ocean route in the world at the time. Chinese
porcelain has been unearthed in many places along these routes, such as
today’s Japan, South Korea, Democratic People’s Republic of Korea,
Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines, Iran, Iraq, and Egypt, which
corroborates the historical record that in the Tang and Five Dynasties
porcelain produced in China was sold to Korea, Japan, Southeast Asia and
even the Middle East, Africa and other places.40
   Tang porcelain fragments have been found almost everywhere along the
East Ocean (Dong Yang) and West Ocean (Xi Yang) routes in the Tang
Dynasty. By connecting overseas locations where Tang Dynasty ceramics
have been unearthed with the Port of Guangzhou, we can reconstruct the
Iran and Iraq route that started from Guangzhou, passed through the Straits
of Malacca and then traversed the east and west coasts of India.41
   Another maritime traffic and trade route started from the Port of
Mingzhou (today’s Ningbo) and reached different regions in different
directions:
   To the northeast: the route started from Mingzhou or Yangzhou and
reached modern-day South Jeolla of South Korea by way of Heuksando
Island.
   To the east: the route started eastward from Mingzhou or from
Yangzhou by way of the Yangtze estuary to cross the East China Sea and
reach the Amami Islands in southern Japan, then turned north to pass
Yakushima and Tanegashima, then went further northward passing the coast
of Kagoshima to reach Hakata-ku and Tsukushi, and then arrived at Japan’s
capital region by way of the Seto Inland Sea.
   To the south: there were two routes. One started from the Port of
Mingzhou, passed through the Taiwan Straits, tracked southeast to reach the
Philippine Islands, proceded further south along the west coast of the
islands of Luzon, Mindoro, Cebu, and Mindanao, as well as the Sulu
Archipelago, and reached Java and Sumatra by way of the northwest coast
of Kalimantan. It then passed through the Straits of Malacca, the Nicobar
and Andaman Islands and the Bay of Bengal to reach the east coast of India,
then proceeded south along the east Indian coast, past Sri Lanka, and then
up north along the west continental coastline of India all the way to the
Persian Gulf—or went ashore at Siraf to enter the Iranian inland. Some
went northward to the top of the Persian Gulf and then proceeded up the
Tigris to arrive at Ctesiphon, Sāmarrā and other places. Another route was

to continue along the southern coast of the Arabian Peninsula, and then
enter the Gulf of Aden by way of Oman, or up north through the Red Sea to
reach Aydhab or the Port of Al Qusayr, where the ceramics were unloaded.
It then proceeded westward across the desert to reach the Nile, and then
down the Nile to reach its final destination, Fustat. Some traveled south
along the east African coast, passed Manda Island and reached Kilwa.
Another route, also starting from the Port of Mingzhou, went south along
the coastline of the Chinese mainland, passed Guangzhou and Champa
(today central and southern Vietnam), and then skirted the Malay Peninsula
to reach Sumatra, where it converged with the first route. The rest of the
route overlapped with the first route.
   From the routes described above as well as the travel journals of foreign
travelers in the Middle Ages, it can be seen that the unloading ports or
major trade distribution centers of Yue kiln celadon in Southeast and South
Asia included Palembang and Djambi in Indonesia, Chaiya in Thailand, and
Mantai in Sri Lanka. Major transit ports for Yue celadon to be sold to the
Middle East were Banbhore in Pakistan, Siraf in Iran, and Sohar in Oman,
and major unloading spots for Yue celadon to be transported to Egypt were
Aydhab in Sudan and Al Qusayr in Egypt.42
   The rise and development of the Port of Mingzhou in the Tang Dynasty
stimulated the production of the Yue kilns. It is recorded in A History of
Sino-Japanese Cultural Exchanges that merchant ships departing from
Mingzhou for Japan were “mostly loaded with goods” and that the goods
were mostly “silk, porcelain, spices and medicine…”. After the mid-Tang
Dynasty, the porcelain industry of the Yue kilns saw rapid growth driven by
export need. Shanglin Lake became the central production area for the Yue
kilns, with more than 80 kilns densely distributed around the lake. The over
700 pieces of Yue celadon unearthed during archaeological excavations
from 1973 to 1975 at the Tang Dynasty sea port site on the south bank of
the Binyao River on Heyi Road in Ningbo were ceramics for trade
produced by the Hehuaxin kiln and other kilns around Shanglin Lake that
were prepared for shipping overseas but that were discarded due to damage
in transit.
   The thriving maritime trade in the Port of Mingzhou prompted the Tang
Dynasty to set up an administrative mechanism there in which the
prefectural governor managed the maritime trade industry. The epitaph of
Li Dai, in a collection of the Linhai Museum in Zhejiang Province, records

the historical facts of Li Suli, governor of Mingzhou during the Tang
Dynasty, also managing the maritime trade affairs of Mingzhou and
Taizhou (today’s Linhai).
   During the Five Dynasties, the Qian regime of the Wuyue Kingdom
attached great importance to the Port of Mingzhou. In May of CE 909, in
order to develop overseas trade, Qian Liu set up Wanghai County at the
estuary of Mingzhou. The port construction was subsequently further
improved and overseas trade developed faster, and Mingzhou became the
main port for the foreign trade of the Wuyue Kingdom.43
     It is recorded that in the Tang and Song dynasties, Mingzhou could
manufacture large ocean ships with a carrying capacity which reached
hundreds of thousands of kilograms and leaped to the top of the
shipbuilding industry in China. The Tang and Song dynasties were also the
most prosperous periods for the export of Yue celadon.
    All these factors combined led to the rapid development and great
prosperity of the Mingzhou Maritime Silk Road.
    In 1973, a batch of late Tang celadon was unearthed from the Tang
dynasty seaport site on Heyi Road, Ningbo. The rich variety, large quantity
and high quality of the celadon was rare in the history of China’s ceramics
archaeological studies. Most of the unearthed vessels bore no sign of usage,
indicating that they were goods for export that were loaded onto ships. Yue
celadon accounted for most of the unearthed items, yet there were also a
considerable number of products from the Changsha kilns, which, including
various jars, bowls, handled pots, washers, cases and water jets, were also
of diverse variety and exquisite quality. There was also a very small number
of Wuzhou kiln products. This shows that in the Tang Dynasty Changsha
kiln products were also exported through the Mingzhou Maritime Silk
Road. In fact, the most popular ceramic in Arab countries was the Tang
dynasty Changsha kiln porcelain, which, like Yue celadon, was transported
overseas at least partly from the Port of Mingzhou in the Yongjiang River
estuary.
    Initially the Port of Mingzhou mainly transported Yue kiln celadon
accompanied by some Changsha kiln products. Then with the successful
export of Yue celadon, the influence and prosperity of the Mingzhou
Maritime Silk Road expanded, and as a result, by the Song and Yuan
dynasties, large quantities of export ceramics from a number of major kiln
systems in the country were concentrated in Mingzhou for transportation

and truly made Mingzhou the famous embarkation port for export ceramics
on the Maritime Silk Road.44
   Apart from Guangzhou and Mingzhou, Yangzhou in the Tang Dynasty,
at the juncture of the south and north, the sea and the land, and a major
commercial and wealthy city in China, was also a distribution center of
goods from the north and south and an important port for foreign trade.
Following the dispatch of the eighth Japanese envoy to China in CE 702,
Yangzhou had become one of the arrival and departure points for Japanese
envoys sent to the Tang until the middle of the eighth century. Yangzhou
was also the main port connecting the Tang to West Asia. At the latest by
the latter half of the eighth century, businessmen from Arabia, Persia,
Champa and other countries were able to sail directly to Yangzhou via the
Yangtze River estuary from the coast of the Persian Gulf and the Straits of
Malacca. They used Yangzhou as a commercial base to sell jewelry and
spices, and then shipped from Yangzhou to their native countries Chinese
ceramics, bronzes and other handicraft products, including Yue kiln celadon
and Changsha kiln products. In 1998, the Batu Hitam shipwreck with more
than 50,000 pieces of Changsha kiln porcelain and 200 pieces of Yue kiln
porcelain was raised from the waters of Belitung Island near Java in
Indonesia. The ship departed from Yangzhou, and the Changsha kiln bowl
with the inscription “Baoli Second Year” (CE 826) found onboard indicated
that it was a wreck from the first half of the ninth century. Thus, it can be
concluded that before the rise of the Port of Mingzhou, most Yue kiln
celadon was exported from the Port of Yangzhou together with Changsha
kiln porcelain.45
    After the mid-Tang, great changes took place in politics and the
economy. The Anshi Rebellion delivered a heavy blow to the northern
economy and the land-based Silk Road was blocked, making the south the
main source of income for the country. The Maritime Silk Road became
increasingly prosperous and soon became the link in economic and cultural
exchanges between China and foreign lands. The Port of Quanzhou also
became one of the four famous ports for overseas transportation at that
time.46 American scholar Jean McClure Mudge writes that archaeologists
have found shards of Chinese porcelain in ancient cities in India, Persia,
Palestine, Asia Minor and Egypt. When the Tang Dynasty (CE 618 to 906)
was replaced by the Song (CE 960 to 1279), the road through Central Asia
was blocked by hostile forces. As a result, maritime trade became more

developed. At that time, Chinese porcelain was exported from Quanzhou
and the export volumes were also on the rise.47
   The emergence and growth of multiple ports led the Tang Dynasty’s
ceramic trade to prosperity.
   The prosperity of kilns was often associated with convenient
transportation. For example, the prosperity of the Yue kilns had many
contributing factors, one of which was their proximity to Mingzhou and
Yangzhou. Similarly, the Gongxian kilns were only 40 km away from
Luoyang, the eastern capital of the Tang Dynasty, a metropolis on the
central plains, and also the intersection of key land and water transportation
lines. It straddled the only path that had to be taken for the east and south to
proceed to and return from the capital Chang’an, and also the eastern end of
the Silk Road. Since the Gongxian kilns were in the proximity of the
eastern capital of Luoyang, some of their Tang blue and white porcelain and
Tang tricolor pottery was transported by land to foreign countries by way of
Luoyang and Chang’an. Land transportation mainly relied on camels,
horses, cattle, or even manpower. The transportation volume was small, the
loading and unloading effort-taking, and the transported ceramics were
prone to damage. In fact, most of the export ceramics produced by the
Gongxian kilns were transported abroad by water. The Gongxian kilns
boasted extremely convenient water transport since they were located at the
confluence of the Luoshui and Yellow rivers, which was the center of water
transport for most of China. There were two routes carrying the ceramics
eastward to the sea from Luoyang. One headed eastward along the Yellow
River across the North China Plain and crossed Bohai Bay to reach Koryo
(Silla) and then Japan. The second took the Grand Canal and then sailed
overseas via the Yangtze.48

7.7.2 Export of Yue Celadon
In the early Tang Dynasty ceramics sold overseas were Yue celadon, Xing
white porcelain and Tang tricolor pottery. In the late Tang and Five
Dynasties, the Changsha kilns in Hunan Province rose rapidly to meet the
export demands and the Ding kilns in the north also gradually rose as the
Xing kilns declined. Thus, in the late Tang and Five Dynasties, Yue
celadon, Ding white porcelain and Changsha porcelain were the main
Chinese export ceramics, a fact which is confirmed by overseas
archaeological data.

Yue kiln celadon was a great invention of the ancient working people of
eastern Zhejiang. It had a long history, a wide range of varieties, fine
quality and exquisite craftsmanship combining the arts of carving,
engraving, and sculpting. The brand promotion of the Yue kilns was also
strong as their vessels were often inscribed with the kiln name, artisan
name, and place name. In addition, many literati wrote books introducing it
and poets wrote poems extolling it. The Tang Dynasty poet Lu Guimeng
described the glaze color of Yue celadon as “capturing the greenness of a
thousand peaks”, which became a well-known line. Thus, it was only
natural that for a long time Yue kiln celadon was famous and praised all
over the country and became one of the most influential and well-known
trade commodities in China. This impelled Chinese and foreign
businessmen to regard it as the first-choice commodity in foreign trade.
Overseas archaeological data shows that Yue celadon was exported by sea
in large quantities and the peak periods for the export was from the ninth to
the tenth centuries, that is, late Tang, the Five Dynasties and the early
Northern Song. Relics have been found all over the western coast of the
Pacific Ocean and countries and regions along the Indian Ocean and
Arabian Sea.49
   As for the export route, according to physical evidence unearthed in
China to date, basically no Yue celadon has been found on the northern land
transportation route. Its export was mainly by two sea routes, both departing
from Mingzhou. One route went from Mingzhou to Korea and Japan. The
other passed Quanzhou and Guangzhou, and then proceeded around the
Malay Peninsula to reach Persia, the Mediterranean countries and East
Africa. These export activities were also evidenced by the large numbers of
Tang and Song Yue kiln celadon ready to be sold overseas that have been
unearthed in the ancient Port of Mingzhou since the 1970s.
    Existing overseas archaeological data indicate that in the Tang Dynasty,
the Five Dynasties and the Northern Song Dynasty Yue celadon had
developed wide international sales channels and markets. Its trade covered
important coastal ports and cities of Asian and African countries, including
medieval capitals, hub ports, trade centers and religious monasteries that
formed a huge international trade network across Asia and Africa, reaching
South Korea and Japan in the east, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia and
Thailand in the southeast, India, Sri Lanka and Pakistan in the south, Iran,
Iraq and Oman in the west, and at the farthest, Egypt, Sudan, Kenya and

Zanzibar in Africa. The abundant overseas relics of Yue kiln celadon that
are being discovered is revealing a more and more clear picture of the
overseas trade ports and routes of Yue kiln celadon during the Tang
Dynasty, the Five Dynasties and the Northern Song Dynasty.
    Relics of Yue celadon found in the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia,
Thailand, India, Sri Lanka and other countries were all unearthed in coastal
ports, cities and islands along the shipping routes. This on the one hand
shows that these places were important international trade centers in the
ninth and tenth centuries, and on the other reflects the great demand of
these countries and regions for Chinese Yue celadon.50
   Yue celadon from the Tang and Song dynasties has been unearthed in
more than 20 countries and regions including modern-day South Korea,
Japan, Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India,
Pakistan, Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Syria, Turkey, Sudan, Egypt,
Tanzania and Somalia. In addition, the quantity of Yue celadon remains in
submarine shipwrecks is also considerable.51
   Since Yue kiln celadon entered the export trade in the Tang Dynasty, it
not only circulated around the world as a commodity, but also promoted
cultural exchanges surrounding its production and use, exchanges that
played an important role in the history of human civilization. At the time,
ceramic craftsmen in different countries were competing to imitate Yue
celadon, and the first to master celadon production technology was Korea,
which maintained close relations with the Wuyue Kingdom of China’s Five
Dynasties from the late Silla era. The Wuyue Kingdom abounded with
celadon production and Korea’s communication with it continued into the
Koryo era. The latter at that time was importing porcelain-making
technology along with Yue celadon. After sustained efforts, Korean
craftsmen succeeded in firing Koryo secret-color porcelain, also known as
“jade-color”porcelain, in CE 918 (the Zhenming Fourth Year of the Liang
Dynasty of the Five Dynasties) at a kiln set up in Gangjin. For instance, Xu
Jing of the Northern Song Dynasty wrote in his Notes of a Diplomatic
Mission to Koryo During the Xuanhe Era: “Drinking vessels in Koryo are
mostly painted with gold or silver, while celadon ones are considered the
most precious”, and “there’s a most exquisite incense burner, also in a jade
color, with a lion crouching on top and lotus flower holder below”.

7.7.3 Export of White Porcelain, Tricolor Porcelain and Blue
and White Porcelain
White porcelain sold overseas in the Tang Dynasty was mainly produced by
the Xing and Ding kilns. (Fig. 7.66) Early ceramic types sold overseas at
the beginning of the Tang Dynasty were Xing white porcelain and Yue
celadon, and in the late Tang and Five Dynasties, Ding white porcelain
gradually replaced Xing white porcelain to become a dominant export
category. Nevertheless, as foreign researchers often fail to distinguish
between the products of the Xing and Ding kilns in the Tang Dynasty,
literature on archaeological excavations often mistake Ding kiln products as
Xing kiln products or refer to them collectively as Tang dynasty white
porcelain. Besides the white porcelain produced by the Xing and Ding
kilns, also exported during the Tang Dynasty was Gongxian white
porcelain. So far Tang dynasty white porcelain has been found in many
countries and regions around the world, including Nara and Kyoto in Japan,
the Sāmarrā ruins in Iraq, the Brahmnabad ruins in Pakistan, the
Philippines, Indonesia, Iran, the ancient port site of Mantai in Mannar, Sri
Lanka, the Coromandel Coast of India, Fustat in Egypt, and Tanzania.

    Cultural relics that have been raised from the sea in recent years are
providing a lot of new information for the study of China’s ancient
maritime trade, including for the study of porcelain export in the Tang
Dynasty.
  On the Batu Hitam shipwreck raised from the waters of Belitung Island
near Java, Indonesia in 1998 there were over 60,000 pieces of porcelain,
gold and silver ware, and bronze mirrors of the Tang Dynasty, including
more than 50,000 pieces of Changsha kiln products and hundreds of Yue
and Xing ware and white-glazed green-painting vessels. It is presumed that
the ship departed from Yangzhou, a port that had to be passed by Chinese
ships in the Tang Dynasty heading for West Asian countries. The decorative

patterns of the relics salvaged from the wreck mostly had an Islamic style
which catered to the aesthetic proclivities of West Asia. This indicates that
the goods carried must have been ordered by businessmen from Middle
Eastern countries like Arabia and Persia and were being shipped to the
Middle East for sale.52 The most exciting findings on the wreck are three
complete blue and white porcelain plates, which, based on the
characteristics of the body and glaze, were probably produced by the
Gongxian kilns. The clay of the three plates had reached a high degree of
ceramization.
   The discovery of the three plates confirmed the speculation in academic
circles that the main sales sites of Tang dynasty blue and white porcelain
were Islamic countries and regions. The three blue and white plates have
complete decorations that are different from the simple dot or line
decoration style of the Tang blue and white ware collected by the Hong
Kong Feng Pingshan Museum or that were unearthed in Yangzhou. The
center of the plate was painted with one or two rhombuses surrounded by
bunches of palm leaves. There were four ridges on the inside of the rim that
divided the plate into four sections. The design was fully of the
Mesopotamian art style prevailing in the Middle East at the time. The blue
coloring was low-iron and low-manganese cobalt, a pigment from Persia.53
(Figs. 7.67 and 7.68). This author once viewed an Iraqi-made pottery bowl
with ancient Arabic inscriptions at Berkeley Museum in the U.S. The notes
on the item read: “Its shape and white glaze were clearly inspired by the
porcelain exported from China to the Middle East in the ninth and tenth
centuries. The Abbasid Empire ruled Iraq from CE 750 to 950, during
which the innovative use of cobalt blue on white ground proved to be a
successful combination and influenced Islamic ceramics production for
centuries”. The use of engobe gave the pottery bowl a look that very much
resembles Chinese blue and white porcelain. Following this line of thought
one might surmise that the use of cobalt blue coloring in pottery decoration
in Islamic countries and regions was actually related to the influence of the
blue and white porcelain of the Tang Dynasty, and in turn influenced China
later in the Yuan Dynasty. This is a point worthy of further discussion. (Fig.
7.69).

The Gongxian kiln white porcelain salvaged from the Batu Hitam had a
clean, hard body texture with a tinge of blue color. Its white glaze was very
bright. The three blue and white plates had the body characteristics of
Gongxian porcelain clay. The flowers and plants on the wares were
meticulously painted with a writing brush in the manner of centralizing the
brush tip. The strokes were well spaced, arranged orderly yet free and
unconstrained. Simple, clear and elegant against the backdrop of the
transparent glaze, the paintings were of an artistic effect vastly different
from the indistinct style of ordinary blue glazed ware. The firing technique
of the three plates was also different from that of regular Tang tricolor
pottery. The plates display a high degree of ceramization and give off a
high-pitched sound when struck, indicating that they were fired at a high
temperature above 1,100 ℃. Common Tang tricolor pottery, on the other
hand, was of relatively impure clay and fired at only 700 to 900 ℃,
resulting in a faint and low sound when struck. One article voices the view
that the three blue and white plates can be regarded as pioneering works and
successful models of Tang blue and white porcelain.54
   Besides the Tang blue and white ware, among the objects for export
salvaged from the wreck were also celadon made by Yue kilns and white
porcelain made by Xing and Gongxian kilns. There were also more than
200 white-glazed green-painting vessels, which were probably made by
Gongxian kilns since their body, glaze and shape were all the same as the
Tang tricolor pottery produced by Gongxian kilns.
   Tang tricolor wares were also exported in large quantities. Countries
and regions where Tang tricolor wares have been discovered to date spread
almost all over Europe, Asia and Africa. For instance, large numbers of
shards have been unearthed at ancient cultural sites in Samarkand in
Uzbekistan, Sāveh in Iran, Raqqa and Aleppo in Syria, Sāmarrā in Iraq,
Sudan, Fustat in Egypt, Sumatra and Java in Indonesia, Gyeongju in Korea,
and Okinoshima in Japan. Complete and exquisite Tang tricolor works can
also be seen in museums around the world. Tang tricolor pottery was
mainly exported by land, namely, carried to Central and West Asian
countries via the Silk Road, a situation that is vividly depicted by the Tang
tricolor figurines of loaded camels we see today, and was also partially
shipped by sea to Korea, Japan, and Southeast Asian as well as East African
countries. (Fig. 7.70).

   The Tang tricolor wares unearthed in Japan were brought from China by
Japanese envoys or businessmen at the time. Japan sent the first group of
envoys to China as early as CE 607 in the Sui Dynasty, and subsequently
sent 19 official delegations to the Tang Dynasty. The situation in Korea is
roughly the same as that of Japan, that is, tricolor wares unearthed there
were also mostly brought back by envoys or businessmen from China. In
the Tang Dynasty, tricolor wares were not only treasures sought by people
all over the world, but were also imitated by ceramic craftsmen in many
countries. Among the imitative works, the most successful included the
Nara tricolor ware of Japan, the Silla tricolor ware of Korea, and the tricolor
ware of Egypt and Persia (Fig. 7.71).

The Gongxian kilns were important producers of tricolor ware in the
Tang Dynasty. They started firing white-glazed green-painting vessels and
tricolor vessels in the early Tang Dynasty and began an increasingly large
production scale and more and more new varieties as domestic and overseas
markets expanded and demand surged. The blue and white ware that
emerged in the late Tang Dynasty was produced in response to this demand
and was exported as a new precious porcelain. At that time, Chang’an,
Luoyang, and coastal cities such as Yangzhou, Mingzhou (Ningbo),
Quanzhou, Guangzhou and Jiaozhou (Guangxi) had become international
cities where Chinese and foreign businessmen gathered.
   The export of Tang blue and white ware from the Gongxian kilns to the
Islamic region of the Middle East began in the early eighth century and
increased markedly in the middle and late eighth century, clear proof of
which can be found in the Tang blue and white ware unearthed at ancient
sites from the period in the Philippines, Borneo and Sulawesi in Southeast
Asia and the Islamic region of the Middle East. Tang blue and white ware
and other ceramics produced by the Gongxian kilns have been found over
the years at some ancient sites in Java, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Iran, Iraq,
Egypt, Syria and other countries and regions.55 As early as the late Tang
Dynasty Arab businessman Sulaiman al-Tajir wrote in his Journey to the
East about the sailing of Chinese merchant ships in the Persian Gulf and
was generous with his praise of Chinese ceramics.
   The export of Tang blue and white and tricolor products from the
Gongxian kilns to Islamic countries in the Middle East was on the rise in
the mid-Tang Dynasty and trade activities were booming. At that time the
Islamic region was under the rule of the Abbasid Dynasty, which issued an
order prohibiting luxury, banning or restricting the production of gold,
silver and bronzeware. Replacing the metal ware was high-quality ceramics,
especially the noble and luxurious Tang blue and white and tricolor
products, and this contributed to the large-scale import of Tang blue and
white and tricolor products by the Islamic region from the eighth to ninth
centuries.56
   The large numbers of Tang blue and white ware with elegant shapes and
novel decorations and tricolor ware with bright colors produced by the
Gongxian kilns were sold overseas as precious gifts, expensive ceramics
and trade commodities. They won the adoration of people from different
social strata in the countries and regions they reached and quickly

penetrated their daily lives, religion, marriage and funeral customs,
handicraft industries, culture, arts and other fields. Ceramics became a
special messenger of peace. They served as a channel for and strengthened
the friendly contacts and economic and cultural exchanges between China
and other countries. Some countries even started knowing about China
through the importation of Tang blue and white ware, Tang tricolor ware
and other ceramic products. Today, the tricolor and blue and white products
of the Gongxian kilns unearthed in and collected by various countries, like
other ceramics, have become valuable historical materials and evidence for
study of the foreign cultural, diplomatic and trade exchanges of the Tang
Dynasty.

7.7.4 Export of Changsha Kiln Porcelain
The first porcelains sold overseas during the Tang and Five Dynasties were
Yue kiln celadon and Xing kiln white porcelain, which retained distinct
traditional Chinese styles in terms of shape and decoration. The Changsha
kiln ware that rose rapidly to cater to expanding overseas demands differed
significantly from the above two in that it boldly imitated the Persian style
both in terms of shape and decoration. In fact, Changsha kiln ware took the
needs and preferences of the target countries as the basis of its design and
production. Although was a late starter as an export porcelain, its mass
production soon made it a main category of export porcelain at the time.
According to foreign archaeological data, in almost all the countries where
the Tang Yue kiln celadon and Xing kiln white porcelain were unearthed,
Changsha kiln ware has also been unearthed. The volume of Changsha kiln
ware unearthed at the Siraf site in Iran is even larger than that of the Yue
kiln celadon unearthed at the same site.
    In China, Changsha kiln ware is unearthed mainly at the sites of
commercial hubs and ports in the Tang Dynasty, notably in Wuchang, the
water transport hub in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River. The volume
of Changsha kiln porcelain unearthed in Wuchang is 10 times higher than
that unearthed in Changsha, which on the one hand shows that the
Changsha kilns were built primarily to meet the needs of export in the first
place, and on the other hand gives a clue to the export route of Changsha
kiln ware. Presumably the products were shipped down the Xiangjiang
River, passed through Dongting Lake in Yuezhou to reach Wuchang, then
followed the Yangtze River to Yangzhou, which served as a major

distribution center, and finally were transported to various overseas regions
through Mingzhou. A poem inscribed on a Changsha kiln vessel told about
how the poet had a letter delivered to Yangzhou with the trade ship, offering
evidence of the export route of Changsha kiln ware. In fact, in recent years
thousands of Changsha kiln ware shards have been unearthed at Yangzhou,
covering almost all known varieties of Changsha kiln porcelain. Some
varieties unearthed there have even failed to be seen at the kiln site.57
   Another feature of Changsha kiln ware was the strong exotic style of
many categories; an adaptation to the needs of export. For example, its
celadon boldly adopted brown and green color paintings to enhance the
decorative and color effect, and its products often used West Asian and
Persian style decorative patterns such as dancing foreigners, lions, coconut
groves, grapes, and some birds and magpies.58 From this it can be assumed
that Yue and Xing kiln ware was primarily made for domestic sales yet was
also welcomed by overseas markets, while Changsha kiln ware was initially
produced for export but also had a market in China.
   The popularity and sales of Chinese porcelain in overseas markets in the
Tang Dynasty was further increased by the fact that many countries even
banned or restricted the use and production of gold, silver and copper
utensils and instead purchased large quantities of porcelain from China to
replace them. For example, at the site of Siraf along the Persian Gulf many
Chinese porcelain pieces have been found, most of which are Changsha kiln
ware, apart from the occasional celadon and white porcelain.59
   To date, countries where Changsha kiln ware has been unearthed
include Japan, Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Indonesia, Iran,
Thailand, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Iraq,
Kenya, and Tanzania, among which Japan and Iran have seen the most
abundant relics.

7.7.5 Overseas Dissemination of Chinese Ceramic Technology
in the Tang Dynasty
While exporting ceramic products and ceramic art, China was also
constantly exporting the technologies for making ceramics and for
improving ceramic art. This is a major contribution which China has made
to the world. After the Tang Dynasty started exporting ceramics in the
seventh century, a wave of Chinese porcelain fever rapidly gripped many
countries. Travelling great distances to trade porcelain from China was not

sufficient to meet the demand due to limited transport capacity, so many
countries started competing to imitate China’s porcelain.
   Tang tricolor pottery was the first Chinese ceramic variety whose
production technology was disseminated to the outside world. Many
countries in the world have imitated its production, notably Japan, South
Korea and Egypt.
   Japanese Nara tricolor ware was the most typical example of foreign
imitation of Tang tricolor pottery. The Japanese learnt tricolor pottery
technologies mainly through the envoys they sent to China, who studied the
advanced culture and art of the Tang. Large numbers of Japanese students
and professionals studied various kinds of handicraft in China, some for
several months and some for decades, and they often returned to Japan with
unique skills which they had learnt and spread these skills widely. Nara
tricolor ware was very similar to Tang tricolor pottery not only in terms of
shape design but also in its bright almost-flowing glaze and brilliant and
attractive colors. Nara tricolor ware has been unearthed in the largest
numbers in Nara, Shiga and Osaka. It is presumed that the kiln site must be
in Nara, Shiga or elsewhere. When Tang tricolor pottery declined and
became outdated in China, the popularity of Nara tricolor ware also
declined in Japan.
   The Silla tricolor ware of South Korea, on the other hand, integrated
more Korean national characteristics, probably due to the legendary story
that Silla tricolor ware was made by Silla craftsmen under the instructions
of Tang Dynasty craftsmen who were invited to the capital of Silla.
   Egyptian tricolor ware, also called “Persian tricolor ware,”was made by
firstly applying a layer of engobe to a yellowish-brown body and then
painting geometric or flower patterns with green and yellow glazes. The
glaze was dazzlingly colorful, very similar to China’s Tang tricolor ware.60
   Apart from tricolor pottery, Tang celadon also gained the attention of
many countries. Korea was the first to master China’s celadon making
technology. In the Tang Dynasty, while importing Yue kiln celadon, Korea
also learned its production technology. After a period of learning, Korean
craftsmen succeeded in firing Koryo secret-color porcelain, also known as
“jade-color”porcelain, in CE 918 (the Zhenming Fourth Year of the Liang
Dynasty of the Five Dynasties) at a kiln set up in Gangjin.
   According to South Korean archaeological data, among the more than
1,700 celadon kiln sites found in more than 600 areas of South Korea, the

early ones closely related to the birth of Koryo celadon were in Pongchon
County (South Hwanghae Province), Paechon County (South Hwanghae
Province), Yongin (Gyeonggi Province) and Siheung (Gyeonggi Province).
These kilns shared the following features: “Firstly, they were built on the
hillside just like Yue kilns. Secondly, they were brick kilns that extended 38
to 44 m in length and 1.8 to 2.2 m in width, which was almost the same as
the Yue kilns in the latter period of the Tang and Song dynasties. Thirdly,
the structure of the kilns underwent changes over time, specifically, after
several repairs the kilns were reduced in size and after a certain period of
time, developed towards the form of an earthen kiln.”61 In fact, these
earliest celadon kilns on the Korean Peninsula were similar to the Yue kilns
in almost every respect such as structure, scale, materials, arrangement of
the kiln floor, furniture and tools, method of delivering and placing
greenware within kilns, and the shape and design of the products. During
the Five Dynasties, thanks to convenient sea transport, the Wuyue Kingdom
had close and frequent contacts with Koryo, especially during the reign of
King Qian Hongchu. A direct result of the Wuyue Kingdom’s dissemination
and transplantation of Yue kiln technologies on the Korean Peninsula was
the quick success of Koryo celadon firing. Figure 7.72 shows a Koryo
lidded celadon pot from the first half of the twelfth century that this author
observed in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S. It was extremely
exquisite with glossy glaze and a lotus petal pattern all over with a leaf-
shaped pattern carved in the center of each lotus petal. Though it was Koryo
celadon made in a period equivalent to the Song Dynasty in China, its
technology had been introduced to the Korean Peninsula from the Tang
Dynasty.

Fig. 7.72 Lidded celadon pot,
Koryo period of South Korea, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S

   Yue celadon in the Tang Dynasty also exercised considerable influence
on the ceramics industry of Japan and Egypt. With the constant importation
of Yue kiln celadon, imitation of the ware prevailed in the Japanese
ceramics industry from the ninth century. Taking Yue kiln celadon as the
object of their imitation were many kilns near Kyoto, a kiln in the proximity
of Yamaguchi Prefecture, several kilns in Shiga Prefecture, and the gray
glazed pottery kilns in western Aichi Prefecture. Yet the most successful
imitation works were made by the Sanage kiln to the east of Nagoya. The
jars, bottles, bowls and other objects fired by the Sanage kiln were very
similar to Yue kiln ware in terms of shape design, glaze color and
decorative pattern, but the body texture remained pottery, not porcelain.62

To summarize, since the Tang Dynasty China’s ceramic production
technology, especially porcelain-making technology, was constantly
exported, first impacting Korea and Japan, then Southeast Asian neighbors
such as Vietnam and Thailand, and finally to West Asia and Africa. It can
be said that the history of Chinese ceramics is also a history of continuous
export of China’s ceramic products and technologies.

7.8 Conclusion
7.8.1 An Era of Cultural Assimilation
The Sui and Tang dynasties were not only an era of political unification but
also an era of accelerated cultural integration. While back in the Southern &
Northern Dynasties some foreign cultures, notably Buddhism, had already
infiltrated into northern China on a large scale, the dominant cultural
interaction dynamic at the time was still conflict rather than integration. In
an era featuring frequent wars and isolation between north and south, the
positive effects of cultural integration had not yet been fully released. The
emergence of the Sui and Tang empires later provided an unprecedentedly
broad space for the release of these positive effects. Regarding ceramic art,
although the basic landscape during the Sui and Tang dynasties was
“southern celadon and northern white”, it was not a clear-cut division. For
example, although white porcelain was the dominant product in the north,
the firing of celadon was already beginning in the Yaozhou kilns, and while
in the south celadon was the main product, by the Five Dynasties
Jingdezhen started firing white porcelain.
   The Sui and Tang dynasties saw not only the confluence of northern and
southern cultures, but also the confluence of Han culture and the cultures of
other ethnicities. According to historians’ research, the royal families of the
Sui and Tang dynasties all had strong ethnic minority lineages. It is even
believed by some that the Han nationality in the Sui and Tang dynasties was
a “new Han nationality” with Han as its paternal line and Xianbei as its
maternal line.63 The merging of Han culture and ethnic minority cultures
not only changed people’s way of life, but also changed their spiritual
outlook. Ethnic minorities injected refreshingly bold and heroic elements
into the Han agricultural culture which had long been edified by ethics and
rites, while the Xianbei nomadic culture which had previously been in a
barbaric state for a long time also gradually took on some gentle and refined

spiritual qualities under the influence of the Han culture. In this manner, the
over-refined and somewhat weak culture of the Southern Dynasties and the
overly-fierce and somewhat primitive culture of the Northern Dynasties
both discarded their respective short-comings through cultural integration
during the Sui and Tang dynasties, ushering in a new era with a new
appearance.
   When the Tang Dynasty was at its peak, its territory covered the desert
in the north and An’nan (Vietnam) in the south. Though the northeast was a
bit narrower compared to the Han Dynasty, the western frontier was much
wider. At the time, Emperor Taizong of Tang was respectfully titled the
“Great Khan” by all surrounding countries. In the event of a deceased
general in any of the nomadic regimes, it was the Tang Dynasty that issued
an imperial edict to appoint an heir. It was just like a world federation with
the Tang as the mother country.64 Accordingly, China ‘s ceramic trade at
this time was no longer confined to the domestic market. Ceramics were
traded to Korea and Japan in the east, India, Persia and Egypt at the farthest
to the west, and of course to Southeast Asian countries, which were even
nearer. Amid such trade and cultural exchanges with foreign countries,
Chinese ceramic art developed a new look, different from previous
dynasties. (Fig. 7.73).

Fig. 7.73 Tricolor figurine of camel carrying dancers,
Tang Dynasty, height: 66.5 cm, length: 42 cm, in the National Museum of China

The establishment of the Imperial Examinations system led to the
emergence of civil government in the strict sense in the Sui and Tang
dynasties. Studying became a social fashion since ambitious men aspiring
to public office and a political career had to study Confucian classics and
take the imperial examinations. As the pursuit of natural interest was an
integral part of Confucianism, it was inevitably embodied in the aesthetic
and cultural consciousness of the time, including, of course, in the
aesthetics of ceramics.
   The confluence of northern and southern culture also promoted the rise
of the Chan sect. The Chinese culture at the time still had the Yellow River
basin as its stronghold. Yet eight or nine out of every 10 Chan sect founders
in the Tang Dynasty were born and raised in areas south of the Yangtze
River. Thus, the rise of the Chan sect represented a new wave and new
trend rising out of the influx of Southern Chinese blood and life into the
mainstream of old traditional Chinese culture previously dominated by the
Yellow River basin in the north. This in terms of religion alone already
constituted an earthshaking revolution. With the birth of the Chan sect, the
pessimistic and world-weary Indian Buddhism was transformed into a
Chinese philosophy emphasizing natural interest, liveliness and freedom. In
an instant all aspects of people’s daily lives became associated with
“Heaven” and Buddhism.
   When talking about the history of Chinese culture, people tend to view
the Qin and Han dynasties together with the Sui and Tang dynasties. That is
because the two eras were indeed very important in the history of Chinese
culture and at the same time they were interrelated. As articulated by Qian
Mu, the Chinese culture completed building its primary foundation in the
Qin and Han dynasties, that is, comprehensive institutional systems in all
political and social aspects, and then in the Sui and Tang dynasties it
completed building its secondary foundation, namely, basic systems for all
humanistic creativity in literature and the arts.

7.8.2 Expression of Humanistic Creativity in Ceramics
The foundation for humanistic creativity was built from the various factors
mentioned above and it was expressed in ceramic art in the following
respects.

7.8.2.1 From Animal Themes to Plant Themes

In the Qin and Han dynasties most ceramics were sacrificial ritual objects
or funerary burial objects used in palaces, temples, and tombs and mainly in
the two circles of nobility and religion. By the Wei, Jin and Southern &
Northern Dynasties, celadon had matured and began to be used in daily life,
but was not yet completely free from the restraints of religion. Lots of
celadon vessels in this period still had connotations of primitive religion.
For example, the foot designs and decal decorations of the blue-glazed
decal washers, blue-glazed six-legged washers, blue-glazed tripod
inkstones, etc. of the Western Jin Dynasty were all animal or deity patterns
with religious meanings. The decorations on the shoulders, spouts, lids and
knobs of various jars and pots were also designed after animals with
religious significance. Sometimes entire vessels took the shape of an
animal, such as the blue-glazed toad water pot, the blue-glazed tortoise
inkstone, the frog inkstone dropper, and the blue-glazed sparrow cup. There
were also various other animal-shaped wares, including goat-shaped wares,
tiger-shaped wares, lion-shaped wares, goat-head pots and rooster-head
pots. (Fig. 7.74) During this period, the themes of ceramic decoration were
dominated by animals, myths and religious figures, while plant patterns
were rare. New themes such as the Buddha, flying goddesses, honeysuckle
patterns and lotus petals appeared in the Northern Qi Dynasty and the
Southern Dynasties, nevertheless these also resulted from religious
(Buddhist) influences.

Fig. 7.74 Blue-glazed rooster-head pot,
Sui Dynasty, height: 21.8 cm, top diam.: 6.9 cm, base diam.: 6.7 cm, in the Palace Museum

   When it came to the Sui and Tang dynasties, people turned their eyes
from the empty and boring imperial court to the simple yet vivid
countryside, seeking to spy the beauty and pleasure of life amongst the
mountains, rivers and plants of nature. Accordingly, religious and
aristocratic art styles faded away, giving way to the secular and everyday
style. The subject matter of paintings moved from gods, Buddhism and
human figures to landscapes, flowers and birds, and the format moved from
murals and stone carvings to paper and silk, making it possible for paintings
to be hung in the living rooms and studies of the common people. Porcelain
also entered the homes of ordinary folk as daily utensils. Religious
decorations that had previously dominated ceramic wares decreased and

animal patterns were gradually replaced by plant patterns. By the Tang and
Five Dynasties, porcelain wares were mostly shaped following plants,
giving birth to a series of new models such as melon ridge flagons, water
caltrop flower plates, lotus flower saucers, lotus petal zun (wine containers),
lotus petal candleholders, and crabapple flower bowls. (Figs. 7.75 and 7.76)
Different from the animal-shaped wares of the Three Kingdoms and the two
Jin dynasties, which were mostly burial objects meant to repel evil forces
and demons and thus looked ferocious, animal-shaped wares of the Tang
and Five Dynasties, other than tomb-guarding animals used as burial
objects, were all artistically and aesthetically appealing and were exemplary
works for the ceramic art of later times.

7.8.2.2 From Religious Vessels to Daily Use Vessels
Most intellectuals who passed the imperial examinations to take public
office in the Tang Dynasty came from the bottom of society or the
countryside. In aesthetics they were attached to rural life and landscapes,
and in ideology they were without exception spurred on by the Confucian
creed of “serving society and benefiting the people”. Such preferences were
manifest in ceramic art with the enhanced practicability of porcelain
vessels. The pursuit of porcelain practicality in the Tang Dynasty far
exceeded any previous dynasty. Varieties increased to cover almost all
aspects of people’s lives. There were porcelain tableware, wine vessels, tea
utensils, even stationeries, musical instruments, toys, and almost any other
thing you could imagine. The craftsmanship was also more elaborate and
novel. Innovations were also made in burial objects such as figurines of the
12 Chinese zodiac animals, tomb guarding beasts, warriors (Figs. 7.77 and
7.78), officials, houses, wells, and cabinets. Many varieties close to people’s
daily lives gradually turned from burial objects in the Southern & Northern
Dynasties into practical ones. (Fig. 7.79) A typical example was the tea
vessel. Tea drinking started in China in the Wei, Jin, and Southern &
Northern Dynasties when southern Chinese first turned tea from a medicine

into a beverage. It was later due to the spread of the Chan sect from the
south to the north that tea drinking was brought to the north and gradually
evolved from a religious custom to a social habit. It was in the mid-Tang
Dynasty that tea drinking reached real popularity in northern China. At that
time almost all tea sets were made of porcelain, of which those made of Yue
celadon were the finest. With a hard, fine body texture and a bright, lush
glaze color, Yue kiln celadon was elegant and perfectly suitable for drinking
tea. As Yue kiln celadon developed, the porcelain of other kilns also saw
improvement with greater attention to practicality and the transparency of
the materials. The needs of wine drinking and tea drinking gave birth to a
new variety in the Tang Dynasty, the handled ewer, which evolved step by
step from the rooster-head pot popular in the Wei, Jin, and Southern &
Northern Dynasties. The rooster-head spout turned into the short straight
spout, the dragon-shaped handle was replaced by the small curved handle,
the lug connecting the spout and the handle disappeared, and the plate
mouth turned into the bell mouth. (Fig. 7.80) This evolution from the
decorative rooster-head pot to the practical handled ewer was a giant leap.

7.8.2.3 Pursuit of Natural Interest
The Chinese revere nature and pursue the realm of the “union of Heaven
and man,”which in arts and crafts practice became the “union of object and
soul”. Chinese craftsmen avoid impairing the inner quality of an object.
Rather, they endeavor to bring out the beauty of the object itself and add

radiance to it. Material and human nature are mutually agreeable,
understanding and complementing each other. Such is the ideal common to
all Chinese craft arts.
     It is also why Chinese people often praise craft works as “secret
workings of nature” or “Heaven’s workings through man’s hand”. These
sayings show that the Chinese refuse to tamper with natural objects with
artificial work and do not wish to damage, conquer or replace nature with
human effort. The goal is always to make nature better through human
effort. From this standpoint we can catch a glimpse into the true common
philosophical meaning and inner spirit of all folk arts and crafts in China.
These philosophical ideas were further developed and found particularly
profound expression in the ceramic art of the Tang Dynasty.
   Following their first successful firing in the Eastern Han Dynasty,
Chinese porcelain had been mainly decorated through engraving, carving,
imprinting, sticking, molding, hollowing, etc. on the body surface. After the
Tang Dynasty, decorations focused more on the possibilities of glaze color
itself rather than on external ornament. For example, in the late Tang and
the Five Dynasties Yue kiln celadon led many poets to marvel at its brilliant
green hue. With a hard and fine body texture and bright and lush glaze
color, Yue kiln celadon was extremely elegant and particularly suitable for
use as tea vessels. While ceramic vessels of the early Tang Dynasty were of
a heavy and plain design, after the mid-Tang, Yue porcelain turned to an
elegant style. The attractive shape combined with a bright green color
elevated it to a high aesthetic level. The white porcelain of the Xing kilns in
Neiqiu gained sudden fame, winning people’s admiration with the charm of
its snow or silver-like glaze color alone. Its thick and fine body texture and
clear white glaze gave it a plain yet forceful character and made it perfect
for drinking wine.
   Besides celadon and white porcelain, kilns in the Tang Dynasty also
produced colorful glaze porcelain, brown glaze porcelain, multi-clay glaze
porcelain, black glaze porcelain, yellow glaze porcelain, and more, all
celebrated for their naturally formed glaze color without any artificial
modification. The glaze color was prone to natural and thus quite random
change, and progressed in varying degrees from single color to complex
polychromatic glaze, laying the foundation for the fambe glaze of the Jun
kilns, the oil-spot and hare-fur patterned porcelain of the Jian kilns, and the

tortoiseshell glaze of the Jizhou kilns that were to come in the Song
Dynasty.
   While celadon and white porcelain represented one spirit of the mid-
Tang Dynasty with their simple designs, quiet colors and implicit styles,
and presaged a transition towards the elegance of the late Tang Dynasty and
even the free spirit of the Song Dynasty, Tang tricolor pottery embodied a
totally different spirit, the splendid and magnificent spirit of the peak of the
Tang Dynasty with its bold shapes, heavy colors and loud styles. If we
study it carefully, we will find that although the style of Tang tricolor
pottery was vastly different to celadon and white porcelain, its inner pursuit
had much in common with the two, that is, they all emphasized the beauty
of the material itself rather than ornamentation through external force.

7.8.2.4 Diverse Painting Imageries
Similar pursuits can be found in the literature and art of any period of
Chinese history due to similar cultural and political backgrounds. The Tang
Dynasty was no exception. Literature in the Tang Dynasty was centered on
poetry and prose, which were seldom works that undertake specific
descriptions of life or tell specific stories but were instead light and spiritual
lyrical sketches, mostly drawn from the countryside and nature. Plain and
tranquil, these literary works expressed personal emotion through scenery
depiction. The same is true of Chinese painting at this time. As noted by
Qian Mu, a main characteristic of Chinese painting from the Tang and Song
dynasties was the escape from reality and a tendency to express deep
personal feelings or thoughts using images of external objects. The subject
matter of the then popular landscape and flower-and-bird paintings was
quite detached from real life, but were nevertheless natural, vivid, and
interesting, making them perfect vessels for the Chinese people to express
their aspiration for the ideal peaceful and tranquil life. The simple and
harmonious form of Chinese paintings alone seemed to have cleansed all
the confusion, conflict and tragedy in the world. At that time, every Chinese
household, even those with only basic literacy, would always hang one or
two paintings mounted with paper or silk, some vertical and some
horizontal, in the living room, the study or the bedroom. The occasional
glimpse of them was able to make people relaxed and detached from
secular disturbances. The paintings were in a sense the Peach Garden of
Chinese people’s souls, or a paradise for them.65

This literati-dominated aesthetic preference was also manifest in the
ceramic art of the Sui, Tang and Five Dynasties. Both Yue kiln celadon and
Xing kiln white porcelain placed an emphasis on glaze color as the primary
means of decoration, yet they also attached importance to shape design and
ornamental accessories, which were, unlike previous dynasties, mostly
themed around plants in nature. The new style was most strongly
manifested in the porcelain of the Changsha kilns in the Tang Dynasty.
Before the Tang, Chinese ceramic decoration mainly relied on engraving,
carving, imprinting, sticking, molding, hollowing, etc. on the body surface.
Painting with the writing brush was rare and the decorative images were all
predictable patterns. Free painted images were rare. Changsha kiln products
were the forerunner of Chinese porcelain painting, the other step forward of
which was a departure from religious themes such as mythical beasts,
fairies and Taoist immortals often portrayed in ceramic decoration prior to
the Tang Dynasty to natural landscape, flowers and birds, and fish and
insects. Such a transformation was also attributable to the influence of sister
arts of the time, namely literature and Chinese painting, and was also a
reflection of an agricultural civilization. (Figs. 7.81 and 7.82).

   Embodied in these ceramic vessels was the ideal of Tang dynasty
Chinese to organically combine “practicality” and “nature”. The wares were
on the one hand practical utensils widely and intimately used in people’s
everyday lives, and on the other hand, artworks whose shapes and paintings
were vivid, lively and interesting. This was particularly true of Changsha
kiln products whose paintings encompassed diverse imageries including

natural landscape, flowers and birds, and fish and insects. Such a
connection between porcelain and poetry, prose, calligraphy and painting
actually pioneered the trend to elevate the Chinese porcelain craft to the
heights of literature and fine art. As daily use porcelain became artistic,
people’s everyday lives were also rendered artistic. This trend was also
reflected in other daily necessities apart from porcelain.

7.8.2.5 Poems and Calligraphy as Ceramic Decoration
Another instance of Tang porcelain being influenced by contemporary
literature was the inscription of poems as decoration. Inscriptions on
ceramics already appeared earlier, but to combine the art of calligraphy and
poetry was a decorative means pioneered in the Tang Dynasty. The Tang
Dynasty was a great era for poetry, with the number of poets and the height
of poetics unsurpassed either before or since. The Complete Tang Poems
compiled in the Qing Dynasty comprised 90 volumes that contained some
48,900 poems by more than 2,200 poets. The salient spirit of Tang poetry
lay in its entirely plebeian style, meaning that the poets always took the
position of the common folk to write about the various sentiments and
realms of the daily lives of the common people. Even works concerning the
government and the court were from the standpoint of the common people.
The approximately 50,000 Tang poems in the collection portrayed the
entirety of the plebian society and the life of the 300-year-long Tang
Dynasty. It can be said that the literary form which eulogized the daily life
of the common people reached maturity in the Tang Dynasty.
   This maturity found expression in ceramic art with the rising popularity
of inscriptions, which means that at the time many porcelain craftsmen
were literate, able to and even proficient at writing and reading. Inscriptions
first appeared on porcelain wares of the Changsha kilns in the Tang
Dynasty. The inscriptions included ware names as well as words and poems
promoting the ware, with poems being the most prevalent. For products of
the Changsha kilns, poems were mostly inscribed below the spouts of bell
mouth pots, and some on amphora bellies, saucer centers, or pillow
surfaces. The poems and sentences, mostly originating from folk poetry and
proverbs and rarely containing allusions, were easy to understand. The
inscriptions, engraved by craftsmen for the use of the common people, also
led to the plebeian trend in the written language and calligraphy, the
mastering of which was no longer the privilege of imperial aristocrats and

cultural elites. This makes the following statement of Qian Mu much easier
to understand: “Ancient literature was more used by aristocratic society,
followed by religion; ancient arts were more used in religion, followed by
aristocratic society. This all changed in the Tang Dynasty, when literature
and arts started serving the everyday lives of common people. This was a
major leap forward in the history of Chinese culture”. This statement is
fully reflected in the porcelain art of the Tang Dynasty.

7.8.2.6 New Style Under the Influence of Foreign Cultures
The Tang Dynasty was a highly open era, and porcelain was a major foreign
trade commodity of China at the time. With the export of Chinese porcelain,
Chinese culture was exerting influence in the world. In return, foreign
culture was also influencing China as ceramic craftsmen took into
consideration the aesthetic preferences of foreigners in order to better cater
to foreign markets. Consequently, excellent foreign crafts and decorative
arts were absorbed by Chinese craftsmen and contributed to the new and
unique style of the era.
   For example, the large number of Tang tricolor phoenix-head pots that
have been unearthed had very similar shapes to the silver water pots with
human patterns and bird spouts common in Persia. A bluish gray glazed
handled pot with colorful spots unearthed from a Tang tomb in Shaanxian
County, Henan Province in 1956 was closer in shape to the glassware of
Persia and Egypt, with its lotus leaf shaped mouth, slender neck and oval
belly. In addition, a kind of white-glazed bottle popular in the Tang Dynasty
had a pair of long dragon-shaped handles arching over the mouth and
shoulder and each of the dragons was decorated on the body with three
beads, which was an exotic ornament quite similar to the linked beads motif
common on Persian gold and silver wares, brocades and other art works. In
fact, the shape design of the white-glazed dragon bottle was the result of
combining the domestic rooster-head pot with foreign pots. A Tang white-
glazed long-stem bowl unearthed from the tomb of Duan Boyang from the
Qianfeng Second Year (CE 667) in Hansenzhai in the eastern suburbs of
Xi’an, Shaanxi Province in 1956 was decorated with lotus scrolls and
linked beads all over, another instance of Chinese Tang ware adopting the
Persian motif.66 Yet another case of foreign impact was the use of parrot
motifs, which were often used to decorate Arabian vessels since parrots
were the most loved animal of the Arabs in West Asia. Vessels decorated

with parrot patterns or shaped like parrots in China were mostly from the
Tang Dynasty, dominated by Yue kiln celadon bowls, pots and boxes carved
with parrot patterns, which were sold in large quantities to West Asia or the
Middle East.67
   Yet another example was the Tang dynasty blue-glazed dragon-handle
and phoenix-head pot collected by the Palace Museum. The pot drew upon
the features of Persian gold and silver bird and animal pots in shape and
decoration and was a masterpiece that successfully integrated Chinese and
foreign art. Its belly was decorated with strongly exotic images of foreign
dancers and musicians, a common decoration on gold and silver wares of
the Persian Sassanid Dynasty, and other themes common on Persian and
West Asian works of art such as stars, the moon, floral scrolls, honeysuckle
and grapes, yet its lid in the shape of a phoenix head with a high crest and
eagle beak and its handle in the shape of a highly dynamic flying dragon
had strong Chinese style. Such design integrating different cultures to form
its own characteristics and new style told of the inclusiveness of the Tang
culture and its daring spirit of innovation.
   Camels also became an important motif for ceramics apart from horses
due to the Tang Dynasty’s close contacts with the Western Regions. Two
models of camels carrying musicians, one unearthed in the Tomb of Xianyu
Tinghui in Xi’an and the other found in Zhongbao Village, also in Xi’an,
are classic Tang tricolor works from the peak of the dynasty. One depicted a
camel with a gorgeously colorful felt blanket on its back. On each of the
four corners of the blanket sits a Western musician with high nose and deep
eyes and in the middle of them stands a male dancer gazing into the
distance. The work depicts a lively and noisy scene of traveling while
dancing and singing. The other camel figure was shorter but with similar
designs. Six musicians sit cross-legged on the back of the camel and a
female is dancing in the middle with one hand raised and the other
dangling. Her posture is gentle, and her movement elegant. The seven
human figures are all Han, but each dressed in different clothes. The camel
figures are perfect portrayals of the cultural blending of different countries
and nationalities in the Tang Dynasty, something that could not have been
achieved if not for ample cultural self-confidence and solid national
strength.
   The Buddhist culture imported through the Maritime Silk Road also had
a lot of influence on the decorative art of Yue kiln celadon, which under

such influence came to use decorative patterns with a strong Buddhist
flavor such as Buddha statues, flying goddesses, lotus flowers, honeysuckle
patterns, karma patterns, and the lion. The most typical and also the most
widely used on Yue ware was the lotus flower, the “sacred flower of
Buddhism,”which actually became a prominent feature of Yue celadon
decorative art with its beauty shown to the best advantage in various forms
and methods. Yue celadon jars with piled sculptures was also conceived
under the influence of Buddhist architectural art according to relevant
studies. Yue kiln celadon also bore a lot of marks of cultural exchange
along the Maritime Silk Road, such as paintings and sculptures depicting
many different Western foreigners as decorations on the vessels.68

7.8.3 Emergence of the Scholar Culture in Ceramic Art
Many scholars have accepted the view that Chinese culture built
comprehensive institutional systems in the Qin and Han dynasties and then
in the Sui and Tang completed basic systems for all humanistic creativity in
literature and the arts. This is evidenced by the ceramic development during
the Sui and Tang. The development of celadon in the period suffices to
illustrate. In the Tang Dynasty, while celadon kilns were not as widespread
as they later became, southern kilns represented by the Yue kilns and
northern ones represented by the Yaozhou laid the groundwork for the
emergence of the many celadon kilns, each with their own characteristics,
in the Song Dynasty. In addition, the white porcelain firing technique of the
Xing kilns laid the foundation for the appearance of Ding kiln white
porcelain and Jingdezhen’s qingbai porcelain, egg-white porcelain and
white porcelain after the Song Dynasty. If not for the emergence of the
white porcelain there would not have been the flourishing of polychrome
porcelains in the Yuan, Ming and Qing. The decorated glaze wares and
black glazed porcelain of the Tang Dynasty laid the foundation for wares
featuring glaze patterns that formed naturally during firing in the Song
Dynasty, such as Jun kiln porcelain, hare-fur patterned porcelain, oil-spot
patterned porcelain, and tortoiseshell glaze. Then there is tricolor glazed
earthenware of the Tang Dynasty, which, though not suitable as tableware
since it was low-fired lead-glazed pottery, benefited the development of the
glazed tiles used in later generations for building temples and palaces.
Products of the Changsha kilns deserve special attention because their
underglaze color painting, inscriptions, and decoration combining

calligraphy and painting sowed the seeds for the iron dust decoration of the
Cizhou kilns in the Song Dynasty, for the blue and white porcelain of
Jingdezhen in the Yuan Dynasty, and for the blue and white doucai
porcelain, the wucai porcelain, and the famille-rose porcelain of Jingdezhen
in the Ming and Qing dynasties. From all this it can be seen that the
decorative means and expressive methods of various porcelain types in later
dynasties budded in the Tang Dynasty. The budding was not only in terms
of technology. It also involved the evolution and change of cultural ideas
and artistic aesthetics. Chinese culture before the Sui and Tang dynasties,
featuring bold and heroic values, advocated the bravery of soldiers, while
after the Sui and Tang it moved towards elegance and gentleness and
featured a more literatus temperament. It could be said that though the
ceramics of the Tang Dynasty were not as prosperous as they were in the
Song, the Tang Dynasty, marking the beginning of a new style, was an
important turning point in the history of Chinese ceramic art.
