8.1 Introduction
8.1.1 Dawn of a New Era
After the wars at the end of the Tang Dynasty and the chaos of the Five
Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, China entered a new unified era—the
Northern Song Dynasty. The Northern Song, adopting the national strategy
of “advocating literary grace and inhibiting warlike exploits,” respected
knowledge, encouraged study, and took strong measures to reverse the
unbalanced emphasis on military affairs over civil affairs during the Tang
and Five Dynasties. A Confucian-based imperial examinations system was
established to serve as a new mechanism for selecting civilian officials for
important positions. Of the nine prime ministers serving the reign of
Emperor Taizu of Song, all were civilian officials and six were selected
through the examinations.
    In this period the imperial examinations system reached its peak in
fairness, openness and practicality. It no longer only examined candidates’
mastery of poetry and prose and their word-by-word memory and
understanding of scriptures as in previous dynasties, but mainly focused on
classics interpretation and commentary, and discourse on current affairs.
Official salaries were also increased substantially in an attempt to ensure

incorruptibility. As a result, the impact of family status was further
undermined and a merit-based ancient Chinese bureaucratic system took
shape. According to Roberts, family background records show that of the
jinshi (successful candidates in the imperial examination with the highest
rank) between 1148 and 1256, 60% had no family member appointed as a
government official in up to three previous generations. The imperial
examinations and local prefecture and county school examinations had
become the only way for aspiring men to become government officials.
   The rise of civilian politics was directly related to the revival of
Confucianism. The theories of Sima Guang and Zhu Xi were the most
representative of this revival. They reiterated that basic Confucian thought
should constitute the important principles of governance, made sure these
principles and ideas supported the legitimacy of the monarchy’s power, and
stressed personal moral cultivation, practicing the classics and focusing on
reality. These new ideas pushed Confucianism towards Neo-Confucianism.
Sima Guang’s political ideal was a competent and wise emperor, a peaceful
and prosperous country, officials appointed on the basis of ability, “people
cherished with benevolence” and “ancestor’s codes” abided by. Zhu Xi
advocated exploring the truth and studying the objective world, which
referred to nature, human relations and the words of sages. He also upheld
first knowing and then acting and the unity of knowledge and action. The
new interpretations of Confucian classics by Neo-Confucianism became the
basic content of the imperial examinations. These more enlightened
academic attitudes also promoted new interests and views among scholar-
bureaucrats on art, science and technology, nature, mathematics, politics,
society, and even urban planning. These new interests were manifested in
the increase in wealthy families, the promotion of letterpress printing, the
increase in leisure time and the rapid development of government-run
schools and private academies (at least 124 private academies were
recorded). With these New-Confucianism was widely disseminated. The
movement was a Chinese Renaissance and ushered in a thoroughly new era
of knowledge. Thanks to this the two Song dynasties marked a peak in
China’s history in economic, artistic and scientific attainment. The
porcelain, landscape painting, silk, cartography, shipbuilding, furniture and
interior design in the Song Dynasty were all models for later centuries.
   The society of the two Song dynasties saw the birth of a new class
composed of shopkeepers and handicraftsmen and an urban lower class

made up of shop assistants, servants and other employees (peddlers and
workers). These new classes, who accounted for most of the urban
population, had preferences and a daily life that were obviously different
from those of the upper class (scholar-bureaucrats, nobles and officials). To
cater to these new classes, popular culture and entertainment including
storytelling, martial arts performances, acrobatics and other urban
recreational activities appeared. As a result, wazi and performance areas
compartmentalized with railings appeared in cities of the Song Dynasty,
which constituted new land usages and urban functions not seen previously.
This brought new elements to the urban civilization of the Song Dynasty.1
   The Song Dynasty replaced direct control on commodity prices and
handicrafts with a commercial tax and product tax. Of course, the state still
monopolized the production, circulation and sales of some key products to
raise funds for the army. For instance, during the reign of Emperor
Yingzong there were 271 government-run mining and metallurgical plants.
The handicraft industry was still mainly run by the government, but most
craftsmen were recruited from prefectures and cities whose personal
dependence on government and private landlords was further weakened.
The Song Dynasty was the first regime in China’s history to take the
initiative to promote maritime trade. In addition to sending trade
delegations to Southeast and South Asia, the Southern Song Dynasty set up
maritime trade bureaus, special agencies dedicated to managing maritime
foreign trade and foreign businessmen according to the maritime trade law,
in Xiuzhou (modern-day Huating, Shanghai), Mizhou (near Qingdao
today), Mingzhou (modern-day Ningbo), Quanzhou and Guangzhou. In the
Southern Song Dynasty, ports and trade cities with maritime trade bureaus
included Lin’an (Hangzhou), Mingzhou, Wenzhou, Xiuzhou, and Jiangyin.
More than 50 countries maintained trade relations with China during the
two Song dynasties. The import and export tax collected by the maritime
trade bureaus was about 10–40% of the value of the goods. Records show
that the tax revenue in the year 1189 amounted to 65 million strings (1000
coins per string), more than 10 times higher than the five million strings in
the early Northern Song. Cotterell and Morgan posited that the Song
Dynasty featured a maritime trade volume exceeding that of the whole of
Europe and was the largest trading country in the world in its time.2
   Goodrich states that in the heyday of the Northern Song Dynasty,
Chinese civilization led the world. Indeed, though the territory of the

Northern Song Dynasty was only half the size of the Tang Dynasty at its
largest, the Northern Song was indeed the richest, most civilized and most
urbanized country around the globe at the time, which was made possible
by the new world that was created during the Chinese Renaissance on the
wane of the wars at the end of the Tang Dynasty and the chaos of the Five
Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. As Gernet puts it, compared with the
aristocratic and semi-feudal society of the Tang Empire, “the Song Dynasty
was very different in terms of political atmosphere, social habits, class
relations, military orientation, urban–rural relations and economic
development. A new world with the basic characteristics of modern China
already appeared in the Northern Song Dynasty.”
   By “new world” these scholars refer to the Chinese society built on the
basis of the third Confucian revival in Chinese history. The most prominent
features of the revival were the arrival of Neo-Confucianism and the
formation of a new scholar-bureaucrat class. These scholar-bureaucrats,
called ru (Confucian) or shi (scholar) and mostly from wealthy urban
families, featured rich knowledge, independent thinking, high behavioral
and ethical standards and a strong sense of responsibility towards the
country and the world. These developments were matched with and
contributed to the formation of a new commercial society, a new
urbanization process and a Chinese urban civilization in a new era.

8.1.2 A Prospering Urban Economy
The commercial centers that first appeared in the late Tang Dynasty
flourished in the Song Dynasty, during which there also emerged
commercial towns, a new embryonic form of the city. These commercial
towns were settlements at the county level, some being military towns
abandoned in the late Tang Dynasty and the majority being small un-walled
cities developed at traffic junctions by the handicraft industry or trade.
Their development relied on their own economic functions rather than
administrative functions, and when they developed to a certain size, the
government would endow them with new urban administrative identities.3
   The rapid development of domestic trade and the commodity economy
and the expanding demand for luxury goods such as silk, tea and porcelain
led to the practice of trading local products for imported luxury goods,
resulting in foreign trade. The Song Dynasty’s encouragement of foreign
trade and its advanced shipbuilding and navigation made prosperous

harbors another driving force for urbanization and added another type of
city. In the Tang Dynasty Guangzhou was the only city with a maritime
trade bureau, but by the Northern Song Dynasty these cities increased to
six, and by the Southern Song three more were added, namely, Zhenjiang,
Wenzhou and Jiangyin. The majority of these seaport cities were in the
south, adjacent to the production sites of export commodities.
   Big cities with booming economies and large populations were
concentrated along the Yangtze River and coastal areas. Many major land-
based gateways, also thanks to the government’s favorable policies on
frontier trade, such as tea and horses, developed into important commercial
cities, such as Tianshui (connected with Tubo and Xixia). The Northern
Song Dynasty had more than 40 large cities with a population of over
100,000, while the Tang had only 10. The city scale in the Song Dynasty
surpassed that of Europe in the Middle Ages. Five of the 10 largest cities in
the world at that time were in China.4
   The Song Dynasty was characterized by the appearance of a class
composed of businessmen large and small, much more diverse than in the
Tang Dynasty, the development of large commercial centers, as well as a
substantial increase in populous and active cities which sprang up not only
in the hinterland, especially along the Yangtze River, but also in border
areas (Xiongzhou near modern-day Baoding, Hebei Province, and Qinzhou
near modern-day Tianshui in Eastern Gansu Province) and coastal areas
(Hangzhou and Wenzhou in Zhejiang Province and Fuzhou and Quanzhou
in Fujian Province).
   Urbanization progressed further in the Southern Song when land was
concentrated in the hands of a small number of privileged people, pushing
farmers who were deprived of land or had no source of income to flood into
big business centers. The business centers provided shelter for floating
populations that depended on humble jobs in the city, such as door-to-door
peddlers, street performers, waiters and assistants in small shops, inns,
pubs, and tea houses. Driven by the difficult life in the countryside, drawn
by numerous types and large numbers of humble occupations in cities, and
also attracted by the cities themselves as wealth and entertainment centers,
large numbers of migrants and poor peasants flowed to large settlements.
The prosperity of these settlements accelerated the urbanization and caused
the urban economy to boom in the Song Dynasty.

In the Tang Dynasty, Chang’an and other important cities were first and
foremost administrative cities of the aristocracy. The authorities of these
cities strictly controlled all commercial activities. By the Song Dynasty,
cities, compared with those before the Tang Dynasty, changed
tremendously in both urban structure and population growth. Now
harboring larger proportions of commercial life and recreational activities,
cities were not only centers of politics and power, but also centers of
economic development. In these cities political institutions and their
personnel could have direct contact with typical urban residents, most of
whom were civilians. In the meantime, radical developments in commerce
were breaking all old rules designed to preserve the aristocratic nature of
the city. After 1063 Kaifeng lifted its curfew and residents were allowed to
move freely around the city at night. Marketplaces and entertainment
venues (“wazi,” recreation communities that flourished later in Hangzhou)
were now open overnight. The restriction of commercial and handicraft
activities to certain li or fang (sections of the city area) seemed to have long
been abolished. Shops and workshops could be set up anywhere in the city,
previous walling of li and fang was now removed, and when giving
directions in the city people now used street names instead of li and fang
names. Li and fang were named by the government while streets were
named by the common people and street names had now become common
in China’s new cities. The changes also meant urban areas were vastly
different from the countryside in terms of lifestyle and type of residents.
   From the Song Dynasty the role of cities as economic centers and their
commercial atmosphere strengthened substantially. Take Bianliang, the
capital city of the Northern Song Dynasty, as an example: “Shops and
restaurants were everywhere inside and outside Bianliang City; on the
streets they intermingled with residential buildings, government offices and
temples.”5 Of the commercial industries of Bianliang City, the most
prosperous were catering and entertainment services, with various
restaurants, tea shops, food stores, wasi and brothels scattered along the
streets to receive dignitaries. Large restaurants mainly serving the nobles
and rich merchants were called “proper restaurants,” which according to
records amounted to some 72 in the late Northern Song. The largest of these
restaurants had three stories and were extremely imposing. Medium-sized
and small restaurants, known as “foot restaurants,” were so many that they
“could not be counted.” There were more than 3000 such restaurants in the

reign of Emperor Renzong of Song. In addition, there were numerous
teahouses, food shops and bakeries. The rise of consumption was on the one
hand stimulated by the profligacy and luxurious lifestyle of the feudal
ruling class and on the other, attributable to the thriving commerce and the
development of the merchant class. The daily lives of merchants bore a
close relation to restaurants and food stores since “businessmen often
bought all food and drinks from market stores and did not grow vegetables
in the house.”6 The growth of the catering industry, driven by urban
development in the Northern Song Dynasty, created a huge demand for
household utensils, and this led to the rapid development of the ceramics
industry. Famous kilns sprang up like mushrooms both north and south of
the Yangtze River.

8.1.3 A Flourishing Urban Culture
Cheap and convenient transportation, numerous urban settlements with
diversified functions, as well as accumulated wealth and rich recreational
facilities became the driving force for urban development and created a new
urban civilization in the Song Dynasty. The capitalist class in the new city
composed of large and small businessmen not only had a greater population
base, but their wealth also had a stronger influence than that of the
“scholar” class. Their business was no longer dependent on the demand of
the royal family, the aristocracy and the bureaucracy, but rather was
supported by the great export demand and the needs of the common people.
In terms of luxury goods, the strong demand of the new capitalist class
itself created a large market. These businessmen built lots of elegant private
gardens, displayed exquisite artworks in their households, dressed in
luxurious clothes, and sought out delicious food. All these became part of
China’s new urban civilization featuring a comfortable living environment
and high living standard. Developing in parallel were urban performing arts
for the general public that flourished in response to the needs of the new
urban residents with the emergence of professional folk artists such as
fengshui masters, physiognomy masters, storytellers, opera performers,
chess artists, puppet show performers, acrobats, as well as the employees of
numerous restaurants, tea houses, brothels, bathhouses, taverns and
casinos.7
   By the mid-Northern Song, the Li-Fang unit system had completely
collapsed and the spatial pattern of commercial districts and cities as a

whole changed to an open one, giving birth to many bustling commercial
streets and new services and entertainment industries such as bathhouses,
teahouses, and performance zones with railings. Accordingly, businessmen,
vendors, performing artists and their customers, in other words urban
residents, became the most important part of cities at the time.
    In the history of China’s urban development, Kaifeng of the Northern
Song Dynasty was a typical example of a capital city whose land uses and
functions were dominated by the entertainment needs of large numbers of
citizens and traders. The city areas devoted to comprehensive land use that
met diverse entertainment needs of the general public were called “wazi.”
(Fig. 8.1).8 In the cities of the Southern Song, a new urban civilization
formed by commerce, manufacturing, entertainment and service industries
overrode the cities’ traditional administrative functions and added new
components to the nature, content and spatial pattern of Chinese urban
civilization.

Fig. 8.1 Three-layer structure of the capital Kaifeng in the late Northern Song and distribution of
main markets

Lin’an was the seat of the government of Hangzhou in the Sui Dynasty
and the capital of the Wu Kingdom during the Ten Kingdoms period. By the
Northern Song it had grown into an important industrial and commercial
city and the largest silk, wine and printing center in southern China. In CE
989, the imperial court set up a maritime trade bureau in the city to manage
maritime foreign trade. In 1129, Lin’an became the capital of the Southern
Song Dynasty. Like Kaifeng, Lin’an (now Hangzhou) had thriving
businesses and entertainment services all over the city, especially along
rivers and main roads, with shops large and small “next to one another.”
Southern Song Hangzhou boasted more industrial and commercial sectors
than there ever were in the Northern Song Dynasty, with 414 sectors
altogether. Large markets for agricultural and sideline products were mainly
located outside major city gates, including vegetable markets, fresh fish
markets, firewood markets and crab markets. Many buildings in the city
adopted a street-facing rather than quadrangle style. Limited space led to
the development of multi-story buildings of greater heights. There were in
total 24 “wazi” inside and outside the city, providing performing venues for
a large number of street artists. Hangzhou became a thriving city of
industry, commerce and consumption (Fig. 8.2).9

Fig. 8.2 Distribution of administrative and commercial functions of Lin’an (now Hangzhou) in the
Southern Song

    In large commercial settlements during the Song Dynasty, townsmen
such as craftsmen and small shop owners, and laboring masses including
waiters, home servants and shop assistants formed a new social class,
whose interests and needs differed sharply from those of the upper class. In
contrast to rural areas where entertainment and recreational activities were
carried out only when there were temple fairs or country bazaars, urban life
tended to eliminate the periodicity of entertainment and so the connection
between entertainment and festivals, celebrations and religious activities
also vanished.
    Cities of the Song Dynasty, especially the two capitals Kaifeng and
Hangzhou, as well as Beijing, capital of the Jin and Yuan dynasties, were all
recreation centers with venues providing entertainment on a regular basis
called wazi or washi. The public places of entertainment, different from the
Musical Houses of the Tang Dynasty, which were set up by and affiliated
with the imperial court, were venues where various professional performers
gathered to entertain the common folks. There were storytellers telling
stories on a variety of themes (history, romance, swordsmen, religion, etc.),
mime performers with musical accompaniment, instrument players and
singers, puppet show performers, circus performers, leather-silhouette show
performers, vocal imitation performers, etc. Cities became the birthplace of
new literary forms. From the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries new art
forms developed in parallel with fine literature. The literary and artistic
forms of these cities all retained the folk flavor, taste and interest of their
places of origin. The language was simple, popular, full of dialect terms,
and rich in local style and flavor.
   Paper became a common writing material in China in the late Han
Dynasty (the earliest batch of Chinese paper found within the old borders of
the Han Dynasty was made in the second century BCE). Lithographic
printing using stone plates with characters or patterns came into existence in
the Han Dynasty and was used until the advent of woodblock printing. To
this day one can still obtain cheap and accurate reproductions of carved
patterns or famous calligraphic works using this method. The seal could
also be used to print calligraphy, pictures or religious images. The invention
and development of printing facilitated the propagation of new literature,
new paintings and new decorative patterns.

The Song Dynasty was a perfect illustration of the relations between
literature and art and social reality. From the Southern and Northern
Dynasties to the Sui and Tang, nobles with some nomadic ancestry imposed
their hobbies of strenuous sports (polo, horseback riding, hunting, etc.) on
the common people, while from the Song Dynasty the ruling class
(composed of wealthy and cultured families who resided in cities and often
lived on income from their land) despised physical activities and
intentionally distanced themselves from prairie traditions and folk
entertainment. Military officers that were respected and appreciated in the
early Tang Dynasty lost all their prestige when the army started to be made
up of mercenaries recruited from the bottom of society. Valued instead was
the wisdom, profundity or abstruseness of literature and art, which could be
seen in the upper class of the Song Dynasty, a situation that continued into
and dominated the Ming and Qing dynasties. After that, Chinese literati
became pure intellectuals who despised physical activity with few
exceptions. It was from this time that the Chinese people attached little
attention to physical exercise, a deep-rooted convention that lasted until a
century ago and which was why China was once called the sick man of East
Asia. It was also from this period that Chinese culture and aesthetics began
to change from the masculine to the feminine. The majestic momentum of
the Qin, Han, Sui and Tang dynasties and earlier was gradually replaced by
a gentle and elegant style after the Song Dynasty. Naturally such an
aesthetic preference was also reflected in the ceramic art of the time.

8.1.4 Development of the Ceramics and Crafts Industries
The urban bourgeoisie, composed of landlords and rich businessmen of the
Song, promoted the handicraft industry because as wealthy families
increased in number, increased handicraft workshops supplied luxury goods
not only to the imperial palace and the nobles, but also to the growing
number of urban residents. Urban life in the Song Dynasty was
characterized by magnificent buildings, luxurious furniture, meticulous
clothing and exquisite cuisine. As a result, the craftsmanship and
technologies of all products in people’s daily lives, including ceramics,
architecture and textiles, advanced rapidly in response to the needs of the
market.
   Contrary to many people’s stereotypical impressions that ancient China
was basically an agricultural economy, the main fiscal revenue of the Song

Dynasty came from commerce and the handicraft industry, the value of
which exceeded that in the Han, the late Ming and the eighteenth century.
Frequently traded commodities included ceramics, silk, iron and other
metals, salt, tea, alcohol, paper and books, which were not only traded on
the domestic market, but also exported in large quantities. At that time
foreign countries saw China as a country producing high-end handicraft
products and were strongly attracted to its products. Tea, silk, silverware
and porcelain were among the products traded to Central Asia and the
Middle East through the Silk Road. Silk and ceramics were exported via
waterways from Zhejiang and Fujian ports. Chinese ceramics were exported
to East Asia and the Indian Ocean countries (even to Africa) in such large
quantities that based solely on the samples preserved in Japan, the
Philippines and Borneo it is possible to outline a rough history of Chinese
ceramics.10
   During the Song Dynasty the ceramic handicraft industry made
unprecedented progress. Kilns and workshops could be found in many areas
and especially favored by the royal family and literati at the time were the
five famous kilns, namely, Ding, Ru, Guan, Ge and Jun (Figs. 8.3 and 8.4).
These official kilns produced exquisite wares that were supplied to the royal
family in large quantities. Apart from official kilns, several other famous
kilns also provided products to senior officials and dignitaries. There were
also kilns whose products were popular mainly among the common folks,
such as the Cizhou and Yaozhou kilns in the north, and Jingdezhen and
Jizhou in the south. The porcelain produced by these kilns not only met
people’s needs at the time, but also, with their unique features and free and
unrestrained artistic style, contributed to the future development of ceramic
technologies, and especially, laid the foundation for the polychrome
porcelains of the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties. The kilns distributed all
over the country in the Song Dynasty created a myriad of porcelain types.
Great achievements were made in both the production capacity and quality
of ceramics. Glaze colors further diversified as colored and multicolored
porcelains were created in addition to the traditional blue glazed, white
glazed and black glazed wares. Decoration methods also became richer,
including engraving, printing, sticking, and painting, as well as attaching
leaves and papercuts onto the ware as decoration. At the time, household
goods made of ceramics replaced most metal wares and lacquerwares. The
Song Dynasty could be said to be a peak in the history of Chinese ceramics

with many famous kilns competing with numerous varieties. Kilns and
porcelains in the north and south will be respectively introduced in the
following sections.

8.2 Porcelain Kilns in the North
8.2.1 Northern White Porcelain and the Ding Kilns
8.2.1.1 Northern White Porcelain
During the Song, Liao and Jin dynasties the north was still the main
production area for white porcelain in China. Specifically, white porcelain
production sites in the period were concentrated in a northeast-to-southwest
diagonal pattern along the foot of the Taihang Mountains and their extended
ridges, lying between the Shanxi Plateau and the Hebei Plain starting from
the Juma River valley in the northeast and moving southwestward to reach
the Yellow River at the border of Shanxi and Henan. It can be said that the
Taihang Mountains were the cradle of white porcelain in northern China
during the Song and Jin dynasties. Kilns located in different places shared a
similar style. Typical were the Ding kilns in Quyang (Hebei), the Jingxing
at the foot of Cangyan Mountain (Hebei), and the Pingding, Yuxian, Yuci
(Mengjiajing) and Jiexiu kilns in Shanxi. The whiteness of products was
better at either end of the diagonal pattern and was not as good in the
middle, due to differences in local raw materials and production
technologies. In general, abundant raw materials, fuel resources, skilled kiln
workers and an excellent commodity trading environment at the time
promoted northern white porcelain production to reach its peak. For
instance, the Gangwa kilns, located outside the Shanhai Pass in northeast
China and adjacent to the Zhongjing capital of the Liao Dynasty, drew
lessons from the rich practical experience of white porcelain production on
the central plains and took advantage of its own abundant raw materials and
fuel to produce high-quality white porcelain.11
   Geographical differences determined that different kilns would adopt
different production methods, processes and technologies. The Ding kilns
adopted a large-load quick-firing approach to raise production capacity,
while the Jiexiu kilns loaded less greenware each time and fired more
slowly to reduce the spoilage rate. This is evidenced by the relatively rich
accumulation of defective products at the site of the Ding kilns and less at
the Jiexiu kiln sites.
   The Ding kilns were the first, in the Song Dynasty, to invent the method
of firing round vessels such as plates and bowls upside down as a means of
increasing production capacity. The new method had a vital impact on the
ceramic production both in the north and in areas south of the Yangtze

River, but it seemed to have exerted little impact on the Jiexiu kilns. Before
the invention of inverted firing, one sagger was used to hold each individual
vessel for firing. Now with the new method, saggers combined with cushion
pads, which could accommodate multiple vessels upside down one on top
of the other, replaced previously used regular saggers, and this improved
product quality, reduced firing costs and so reduced overall production
costs. For this important reason, the inverted firing method was soon widely
disseminated. Analysis of material evidence and literature data indicates
that this Ding kiln method became popular around the mid-Northern Song
Dynasty.12 Despite all its advantages, there was still a defect with the new
technology, namely, that the vessels could not be glazed fully to the rim,
which is mentioned in ancient literature: “The imperial court deemed
Dingzhou white porcelain not proper for use because there is an unglazed
rim…” Another reason that the Ding kilns could adopt inverted firing was
the high aluminum content in its raw materials, which could enhance the
hardness of the porcelain body.13
   The firing temperature of Ding kiln white porcelain was 1300 ± 20 ℃
in the late Tang and Five Dynasties, reached its highest in the Northern
Song Dynasty (1320 ± 20 ℃), and then dropped to its lowest in the Jin
Dynasty (1250 ± 20 ℃). Modern products imitating Ding kiln ware have
been fired at a temperature of only 1280 ℃ approximately. It can thus be
seen that during the Song Dynasty the Ding kilns adopted a high-
temperature quick-firing approach to raise efficiency, that is, to fire more
vessels within a fixed period. While the rejection rate was high, the high
output compensated. In contrast, “during the Song and Jin dynasties the
Jiexiu kilns opted for lengthy firing at a relatively low temperature,” i.e.
“the low-temperature long-firing method.” This method did not impose
strict requirements on the construction of kilns and could also greatly raise
product qualifying rates, which was why the accumulation at the site of the
Jiexiu kilns is relatively small. The production at the Jiexiu kilns began in
the early Song Dynasty and lasted for over 1000 years covering the Jin,
Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties, which was quite rare among northern
kilns.14
     It should be noted that during the Song, Liao and Jin dynasties, the main
product of the Gangwa kilns in Inner Mongolia, the Ding and Jingxing kilns
in Hebei, the Pingding, Yuxian, Yuci and Jiexiu kilns in Shanxi was all
white porcelain. Still, occasionally these kilns also adopted diverse glaze

colors and decoration techniques including black glaze, white glaze with
black patterns, white glaze with sgraffito, white glaze with carved patterns,
mold printing, sculpting, shallow relief, and openwork.

8.2.1.2 The Ding Kilns
The Ding kilns are introduced separately because they were the most
representative kilns for white porcelain production in the north.
   The Ding kilns, one of the five famous kiln clusters of the Song
Dynasty, were famous for their white porcelain. The kilns got their name
because they were located in Jianci Village and Yanshan Village in modern-
day Quyang, Hebei Province, and in the Song Dynasty Quyang belonged to
Dingzhou (“Ding” Prefecture). Porcelain production at the Ding kilns had a
long history, originating in the Tang Dynasty, lasting through the Five
Dynasties, and reaching a peak in the Song Dynasty. Back in the Tang
Dynasty, China’s porcelain making had grown into a landscape known as
“southern celadon and northern white.” By the Song Dynasty, the white
porcelain in the north reached a higher level after years of practice, and
representative of this higher level were the Ding kilns, whose advanced
firing methods had a significant impact not only on northern kilns, but also
on kilns in southern China.
   The Ding kilns in the Song Dynasty mainly produced bowls, plates,
cups, boxes, etc. Bottles and pots were few. Bowls and plates were mostly
fired upside down with one on top of the other in order to avoid the
deformation that could easily occur due to their thin bodies and large
mouths. This firing method led to an unglazed rim exposing the body, but
for some wares the rim was delicately edged with gold, silver, or copper.
Early Ding porcelain was mostly plain, yet by the late Northern Song
Dynasty most were decorated with exquisite patterns. Three main
decoration methods were employed, namely engraving, carving and
printing.
   Engraving was the main decoration method of early Song porcelain.
After the rise of engraving, combining it with comb scratching patterns
became popular, that is, outlines of flowers and plants, mostly lotus and
peony, were carved at the center of folded-rim plates, mainly with bamboo
slices and knives, and then multiple parallel lines were carved within the
outlines of the flowers with a comb-like tool. Such tools could carve neat
and natural lines on the surface of greenware, some imitating undulating

water weaves and some emulating the rolling and extending veins of leaves.
It saved labor and had a clever artistic effect. The decoration technique was
also often found on the celadon of the Yaozhou kilns, which indicates that it
was a common feature among porcelains at the time (Figs. 8.5 and 8.6).

    Printed patterns started to be used on Ding ware in the middle of the
Northern Song and matured in the late Song. Mostly seen on the inner
surface of plates and bowls, the patterns were imprinted on pottery molds in

relief when the greenware had not dried. The decorative patterns were
mainly peony, lotus and pomegranate flowers, most of which were
transplanted from the patterns on kesi (a type of Chinese silk tapestry)
works in Dingzhou. The influence of gold and silverware decorations can
also be seen on Ding kiln porcelain. It was for these reasons that the printed
decorations of Ding kiln ware were mature and of high artistic quality from
the very beginning and went on to exert a tremendous impact on both
northern and southern kilns (Fig. 8.7).





Fig. 8.7 Ding kiln bowl with printed pattern,
Song Dynasty, height: 5.7 cm, top diam.: 20.3 cm, base diam.: 4.4 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Some scholars believe the engraving and carving decorations of the
Ding kilns came from local stonecutting. Indeed, stone carvings enjoyed a
long tradition in Quyang. Dingzhou boasted abundant stone materials
suitable for carving and many beautiful works emerged from Huangshan
and Jiashan in Quyang. In 1994 a complete picture of servants and music
players was found inlaid on the No. 34 Tomb Wall of Wang Chuzhi’s tomb
from the Tongguang Second Year (CE 924) of the Later Tang Dynasty in
Quyang. The picture was magnificent, the human figures vivid, the relief
clear and layered, and the image as a whole was properly spaced. It is
plausible to conjecture that masterly stonecutting craftsmanship helped
local potters become more skillful at their craft. Such mutual influence
promoted the progress of the ceramic decoration technology of the Ding
kilns and meanwhile, engraving and carving formed the main decorative
approach of the Ding kilns in the middle and late Song Dynasty.15 The
open-mouth basin and bowl shown in Figs. 8.8 and 8.9 were among the best

ivory white glazed porcelain produced by Ding kilns in the Song Dynasty.
The basin shown in Fig. 8.8, one of the few large vessels produced by Ding
kilns, was decorated with lotus patterns both on the inside and out. The
vessel was fired upside down, so its unglazed rim was edged with a ring of
metal. The small bowl shown in Fig. 8.9 instead was not edged on the
mouth rim and was printed on the bottom with a camellia flower, a
relatively rare pattern in this type of porcelain.

Fig. 8.9 Ding kiln ivory white glaze sunflower-mouth bowl with carved pattern,

   Drawing upon the shallow relief in stone carving, Ding kilns engraved
upward and downward facing lotus petals in multiple layers on the outer
walls of the vessels, sometimes with a circular flower pattern band in the
middle, to form a vertically symmetrical decoration with the upper part of
the vessel corresponding to the lower part. The lotus petal patterns could be
complex and dense, or simple and sparse, albeit all adding decoration to the
otherwise plain vessel surface with concave or protruding strings.16 Ding
ware in the early Song Dynasty mainly featured sunflower petal mouths and
plain surfaces. Engraving Chinese characters on the ware surface was
another decorative method of the Ding kilns, and it was also a means to
record history.17
   Besides the large volume of white porcelain, Ding kilns also fired a
small amount of caramel glazed and black glazed ware, referred to as
“purple Ding ware” and “black Ding ware” in literature (Fig. 8.10). The
caramel and black wares could be rough or fine, the former with a gray
body and the latter with a white body. Moreover, Ding kilns also fired green
glazed ware, which had the same decoration as Ding white ware but only a
small number have been unearthed.

    In the early Song Dynasty, Ding kilns once fired utensils for the
imperial court, evidenced by the words inscribed on the bottom of
unearthed Ding ware, such as “Food Bureau,” “Medicine Bureau,” “Fifth
Prince’s House” and “Mercy and Blessings.” Shards inscribed with “Food
Bureau” constituted the largest number and only one straight-mouth flat-
bottom bowl bore the “Medicine Bureau” inscription. The two bureaus, one
in charge of cuisine and dining, and one responsible for pharmacy and
medical treatment, were among the six bureaus established under the Xuan
Hui Yuan during the Song Dynasty. Still, Ding kiln ware was deemed
unsuitable as food vessels due to its unglazed rim that resulted from the
inverted firing method, which was actually one of the reasons why the Ru
kilns were constructed later. While porcelain made by Ding kilns featured
an unglazed rim that exposed the body, nevertheless the rim was usually
delicately edged with gold, silver, or copper (Fig. 8.11). Therefore, some
researchers believe that the unglazed rim was not the only cause why the
royal palace stopped using Ding kiln porcelain. Another possible factor was
the aesthetics of the time—the Han Chinese regarded white as a taboo color
for it was used only in funerals. Thus, the pure white porcelain produced by
Ding kilns might have lost favor due to its color.

As one of the five famous porcelain producing areas in the Song
Dynasty and once a supplier to the imperial court, the Ding kilns received
special attention from the government, which selected excellent craftsmen
for the kilns and put forward strict requirements on their production in
terms of material selection, use and processing. These measures improved
the quality of Ding white porcelain, which led to neighboring kilns
imitating the products. Some imitated the shape designs, some imitated the
glaze color, some imitated the decoration, and some imitated the firing
method. As a result, the products of these kilns all shared the style or
certain characteristics of Ding kiln ware and a larger Ding kiln system
centered on the Ding kilns took shape. Kilns that have been found to have
been influenced by the Ding kilns or belong to the Ding kiln system
included the Pingding, Yuxian, Yangcheng, Jiexiu, and Huozhou kilns in
Shanxi, the Pengzhou kilns in Sichuan, the Ji’an kilns in Jiangxi and the
Jingdezhen kilns.

8.2.2 The Cizhou Kilns
The Cizhou kilns, located in modern-day Cixian County, Hebei Province,
were one of the most representative folk kiln clusters in the Song Dynasty.
They were so named because the Zhanghe and Fuhe River basins, where the
kilns were located, were under the jurisdiction of Cizhou in the Song, Jin,
Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties. Several porcelain-making centers
including Guantai, Linshui and Pengcheng were towns during the Song, Jin
and Yuan dynasties. Cizhou kiln products were characterized by brush
painting on white glaze with brown, ochre, tea and other colors. A
combination of a variety of techniques such as painting, carving, sgraffito
and filling innovated and added new appearances to the decorative art of
porcelain. It seems that the origin of this style can be traced back to the
many folk kilns in northern China in the Tang Dynasty, which fired not
only white porcelain but also a rich variety of other categories including
black porcelain, colorful porcelain, celadon and low-temperature tricolor
ware. The Cizhou kilns in the Song Dynasty maintained this characteristic
of Tang dynasty folk kilns. In addition, the Cizhou kilns’ underglaze black
and brown painting ware demonstrated an obvious influence from the
Changsha kilns in the Tang Dynasty. Indeed, the underglaze color paintings
and poem inscriptions as decoration in Changsha kiln ware were all
inherited and further developed by the Cizhou kilns. Such features were so

widely adopted by northern folk kilns that a larger Cizhou kiln system
sharing a similar style was formed.
   Cizhou kiln sites that have been discovered over years of investigation
and excavation are mainly concentrated in two areas. One group of sites is
located on both banks of the Zhanghe River, six kilometers west of Guantai
Town, and the other group has Pengcheng Town as its center. Both groups
had densely distributed sites with large quantities of porcelain shards and
remains buried underground.
   The Cizhou kilns started producing celadon as early as the Northern
Dynasties and white porcelain at the end of the Five Dynasties and the
beginning of the Song. In the Song Dynasty, while the five famous kilns,
namely, Guan, Ru, Ge, Jun and Ding, were treasured by scholar-
bureaucrats, the imperial court and the upper classes with their pure
monochrome glaze and elegant and dignified shapes, the Cizhou kilns, with
their unique variety of decorative arts, produced practical life utensils with
a strong folk interest that were deeply loved by people of the middle and
lower classes. Such products of the Cizhou kilns also serve as precious
materials for today’s research since they are artworks with rich folk cultural
connotations. The decorative content of Cizhou kiln ware contains very rich
northern folk customs and is therefore sometimes referred to as a folk
culture museum or “folk culture dictionary.”18
   The body of Cizhou kiln ware was made of the local raw material
“rough blue earth,” which was nowhere near as fine or white as the material
for the white porcelain body of Ding and Xing kiln ware. In response to this
“congenital deficiency,” the craftsmen of the Cizhou kilns first applied a
layer of white engobe on the body, and then used various decorative
techniques, such as carving, engraving, sgraffito, printing, painting, and
glazing, to decorate the products. Especially salient was the adoption of
traditional Chinese ink painting techniques to draw black patterns on a
white porcelain background with a writing brush. The technique, with the
strong contrast between black and white, created a bright, vivid and
expressive artistic effect. An extremely free, unrestrained and rough
painting style was adopted to depict images of traditional folk customs and
interests popular among the people, thus forming the simple, unrestrained,
and bold decorative language and style of the Cizhou kilns, a unique
decorative art that prepared technological and material conditions for the
transition of China’s porcelain decoration from glaze ornament to color

painting and for the emergence and development of blue and white ware,
wucai ware and doucai ware in China.19
   Because the location of the Cizhou kilns had been under the jurisdiction
of Xiangzhou during the Northern Wei and Northern Zhou dynasties, many
porcelain pillows produced there were stamped or inscribed with “ancient
Xiang” plus the family name of the producer, such as “Zhang” or “Chen.”
The inscriptions indicate the pillows were made by old and famous
workshops. The Wang, Li and Chang workshops in the Fuhe River basin
once produced pillows with kiln stamps of their respective family names.
Some of the pillows produced by the Wang workshop were inscribed on the
side “made by Wang by the Fuhe River.” These stamps and inscriptions
signified competition among various workshops in the porcelain pillow
market and today they also serve as a basis for us to identify whether the
pillows were made in the Zhanghe or the Fuhe River basin.20
   The Cizhou kilns in the Zhanghe and Fuhe river basins produced mostly
the same products since the two river basins were both at the eastern foot of
the Taihang Mountains and featured the same raw materials and fuels.
Nevertheless, since they belonged to two different water systems, there
were some differences in the shape and decoration of some of their
products, as well as in the start and end times of their production as well as
its history and development. Previous archaeological investigations and
excavations have arrived at a basic understanding of 17 kiln sites. It was
noted in A History of Chinese Ceramics that “the Guantai kiln was the most
representative Cizhou kiln, with its product lines and varieties being the
epitome of all kilns in the Cizhou kiln system,”21 a comment that was
proven tenable by archaeological excavations of the Guantai and Pengcheng
kilns in 1987 and 1999 as well as many investigations of other ancient kiln
sites.
   Of all the Cizhou kilns, the Guantai kiln produced the richest types of
porcelain. In addition to white glaze ware and black glaze ware, there were
a further 12 types, namely, white glaze with carved patterns, white glaze
with sgraffito (Fig. 8.12), white glaze with green spots, white glaze with
brown spots, black painting under white glaze, caramel painting under
white glaze, caramel painting and carved patterns under white glaze, carved
patterns against a pearl ground, painting under a green glaze (Fig. 8.13),
white glaze with red-green painting, low-temperature lead glaze, and

tricolor ware. The rich varieties made Guantai the most representative kiln
site in the Cizhou kiln system.

   Based on the 1987 excavation report on the Guantai kiln by the
Department of Archaeology of Peking University, we could preliminarily
divide the development of the Guantai kiln into three stages. The first stage,
the founding stage of the Cizhou kilns, was in the early Northern Song
Dynasty. Varieties were mainly daily use vessels such as bowls, plates,
incense burners, water pots, bottles, and pillows. The most common
decoration was white glaze with carved patterns (Fig. 8.14). The patterns

were dominated by lotus flowers, plants with rolled leaves, and water
ripples. In between the patterns, parallel lines were carved with comb-like
tools. Products with carved patterns against a pearl ground were also very
distinctive. In addition to white glaze ware, there were small numbers of
black glaze ware, blue glaze ware and sesame glaze ware.





Fig. 8.14 Cizhou kiln white-glaze large bowl with carved pattern,
Jin Dynasty, height: 8.5 cm, top diam.: 24 cm, base diam.: 6.8 cm, in the Palace Museum

   The second stage, the developing period of the Cizhou kilns, was in the
middle and late Northern Song Dynasty. In this period varieties increased
and incorporated richer changes. There emerged bowls and other utensils
imitating Ding kiln products. Previous decorative techniques were
inherited, white glaze with sgraffito was developed and black glaze with
sgraffito appeared (Fig. 8.15). Sgraffito refers to cutting out the ground
surrounding the patterns so that the patterns appeared in relief. Stamens
were then carved on the flowers and veins on the leaves. Cutting out the
ground revealed the yellowish-brown body color, which highlighted the
white or black decorative patterns. By this time a pearl ground with carved
patterns became a common decorative method of the Cizhou kilns and the
pearl ground of the Guantai kiln was the most beautiful with an orange-red
hue (Figs. 8.16 and 8.17). In addition, a very small amount of underglaze

black painting ware appeared, whose decorative themes included Chinese
characters, human figures, and animals (Fig. 8.18).

   Other decorative approaches of the Cizhou kilns included the following.
Green coloring was dotted on white porcelain, often used on plates, bowls,

pots, flower-mouth bowls, small jars, six-hole bottles, etc. Ware with
caramel painting and carved patterns under white glaze was similar to that
with black painting and carved patterns under white glaze, yet was
generally believed to be occasional products because specimens with
caramel painting were rare. Underglaze green painting was rare among
Cizhou kiln products. The low-temperature three-color glaze of the Cizhou
kilns was a continuation of the Tang tricolor pottery. Wares with red-green
painting on white glaze, unearthed only in a small number from Cizhou kiln
sites, were a precious type in Song porcelain decoration. Besides, in the
Linshui kiln site a number of Bodhisattva Manjusri statues of white glaze
porcelain with red-green color were unearthed, which are assumed to be the
products of the Guantai kilns since Linshui was very close to Guantai.
Specimens unearthed from the Pacun kiln were more numerous, including
bowls whose insides were painted with flowers in red, green and yellow and
whose inner rims were painted with several red circular lines along with
male headed figurines with red and black colors on white glaze.
   Few Cizhou kiln products in the Song Dynasty were marked with their
production date, yet many had labels of their workshop. The labels indicate
that at the time there might have been many small-scale porcelain
workshops in the kiln area, with workshop owners each having their own
expertise and doing porcelain firing as a family business for generations.
   At the time the impact of the Cizhou kilns were significant and wide. A
large Cizhou kiln system took shape covering not only Hebei, but also
Henan, Shanxi and other provinces. For instance, the Dengfeng kiln, a well-
known folk porcelain kiln of the Song Dynasty, was in Quhe Town in
Dengfeng, Henan Province, and was therefore also known as the Quhe kiln.
The kiln started production in the late Tang Dynasty, prospered in the
Northern Song Dynasty, and ceased firing in the Yuan Dynasty. Its
representative product was pearl ground porcelain with carved and color-
filled pattern, which was actually a type of underglaze decorated ware of
the Cizhou kiln system. To make such ware, patterns, usually following
certain themes, were first carved on the body which had had engobe
applied, then small pearl-like circles were stamped with tools to fully cover
the remaining surface of the ware, then a layer of color powder filled in the
concave lines of the theme patterns and the pearl pattern (some wares were
not filled with color powder, revealing the color of the body), and finally a
transparent glaze was applied to the whole body before it was sent for

firing. The pearl ground decoration was conceived under the influence of
the chiseled design technique of the gold and silver ware of the Tang
Dynasty and was unique to the Cizhou kiln system of the Song Dynasty.
   The porcelain pillow shown in Fig. 8.19 was decorated with exquisite
patterns. The main picture depicts a pair of deer surrounded by auspicious
symbols against a backdrop of dense fish-roe pattern, which seems to be
imitating the linked-beads pattern used on gold and silver wares at the time.
The deer symbolized a bright political career because the Chinese character
for “deer” and that for “official’s salary” are homonyms. In the 1920s,
Cizhou kiln porcelain enjoyed a high reputation among British collectors
and provided inspiration for the pottery artists in the British pottery
movement.22





Fig. 8.19 Cizhou kiln deer pattern pillow,
Northern Song Dynasty, in the Victoria & Albert Museum in the UK

   The Duandian kiln in Lushan, Henan also produced pearl ground
porcelain with carved and color-filled patterns in the style of the Cizhou
kiln system, yet the overall workmanship was not as fine as the Xiguan kiln
in Mixian or the Quhe kiln in Dengfeng and color filling was seldom
adopted, probably due to the often large sizes of Duandian kiln products.
Interestingly, most pearl ground products marked with their production date
and workshop name came from this kiln, and it produced more pillows with
inscriptions than other kilns.

The Cizhou kiln inscribed pillow shown in Fig. 8.20 is very precious
because ceramics carrying a production time inscription from the Northern
Song Dynasty are rare. The pillow was inscribed with “Country Forever in
Peace,” “pillow made by the Zhao family,” and “19th of the third month,
Xining Fourth Year.” “Xining” was one of the two reign titles (the other
being “Yuanfeng”) of Emperor Shenzong, the sixth emperor of the Northern
Song Dynasty, who reigned from 1067 to 1085.
