8.3.2 The Guan Kilns in the Southern Song Dynasty
The Guan kilns of the Southern Song Dynasty were newly set up in
Hangzhou after the Northern Song ended and Emperor Gaozong fled to the
south. At that time Lin’an (now Hangzhou) was the center of politics,
culture and the economy as well as the largest consumer city. There were
also Mingzhou (now Ningbo), Yuezhou (now Shaoxing), Wenzhou,
Wuzhou (now Jinhua), and Chuzhou (now Lishui). These cities and towns,
with long histories and an advanced porcelain industry, were both

production centers and markets and distribution centers of porcelain. Yue
ware, Wuzhou kiln ware and Longquan celadon had a long-established
fame for their unique features. The Jingkang Incident marked the end of the
Northern Song regime and amidst the war, the most famous kilns on the
central plains were destroyed. The Song royal family, led by Zhao Gou, fled
southeast, made Lin’an his capital and set up the Southern Song Dynasty.
The Southern Song court established the Xiuneisi Guan kiln on Phoenix
Mountain, Hangzhou, and a new Guan kiln near Jiaotan in the Bagua Cave,
Tortoise Mountain. In the Xiuneisi kiln and the new Guan kiln the best
craftsmen from the north and south gathered to fire celadon required by the
court and dignitaries. These kilns were a continuation of the Bianjing Guan
kilns of the Northern Song Dynasty and were historically called the Guan
kilns of the Southern Song. The earliest record of the Guan kilns of the
Southern Song is found in the Notes in Tan Study by Ye Zhi of the Southern
Song: “During the Zhenghe years the capital established its own kilns to
fire porcelain, called the Guan kilns. After the royal family crossed the
Yangtze River, Shao Chengzhang proposed establishing the Shao Bureau. A
kiln was set up in Xiuneisi to make celadon, called the Nei kiln, inheriting
the legacy of the former capital. Clay was finely washed to be made into
models. The products, extremely exquisite with clear glaze, were favored
by the people. Later a new kiln was set up in Jiaotan, which was quite
different from the old kiln. The others, such as the Wuni, Yuhang, and Xu
kilns, could not be compared with the Guan kilns. As for the old Yue kilns,
they no longer existed.” This description is the earliest written record
discovered to date of the history of Southern Song’s Guan kilns and has
been used as textual research materials by subsequent researchers.
According to the text, the Guan kilns were set up back in the Northern Song
Dynasty and the Guan kilns of the Southern Song Dynasty inherited their
technology and production methods. The text classified Southern Song’s
Guan kilns into “Xiuneisi” and “Jiaotan,” the former “called the Nei kiln”
and the latter “the new kiln,” and explicitly pointed out that the new kiln
“was quite different from the old kiln.” It is mentioned that the Xiuneisi kiln
was also named the “Nei kiln,” that it used finely washed clay to make
models, and produced extremely standard products that were cherished by
the people for their clear and transparent glaze. According to the Ge Gu Yao
Lun, an early Ming manual on ceramics by Cao Zhao, “Products fired by
the Song Dynasty’s Xiuneisi (Guan kiln) were made from fine clay, had a

blue color with a pinkness of differing shades, and featured a crab claw
pattern, purple rim and iron feet. The wares of fine color were similar to Ru
ware. Those made from black clay were called Wuni wares. Fake ones were
fired by the Longquan kilns and had no pattern.” Here the characteristics of
the porcelain fired by the Xiuneisi kiln were described in detail. As for the
location of the kiln, Gao Lian of the Ming Dynasty wrote in his book Zun
Sheng Ba Jian that “the Guan kiln was at the foot of Phoenix Mountain,”
yet for many years people only found a lot of scattered porcelain shards and
fragments of kiln furniture in the area and had not really discovered the
exact location of the kiln site.
    In September 1996, the Tiger Cave kiln site near the Southern Song
imperial city site on Phoenix Mountain was discovered by chance when
flooding exposed large numbers of celadon shards and kiln furniture. In
November that year, the Hangzhou Institute of Cultural Relics and
Archaeology conducted a one-month-long archaeological survey of the site
and named it the Tiger Cave kiln site following the place’s name as used by
the local people. The geographical location of the kiln site is very special
because it coincides perfectly with the location of the Southern Song
Xiuneisi Guan kiln as recorded. From then until 2001, archaeological
departments comprehensively inspected the celadon kiln site which spanned
the Southern Song and Yuan dynasties with three excavation and
investigation works. The large number of site remains and physical
materials excavated from the Southern Song Dynasty strata showed
conclusively that the site was once an important part of the Guan kilns of
the Southern Song Dynasty.46 (Fig. 8.48).

Fig. 8.48 Southern Song Guan dragon kiln site in Hangzhou,
picture provided by Ms. Feng Xiaoqi

   During excavation, the Hangzhou Institute of Cultural Relics and
Archaeology unearthed a large number of Guan kiln porcelain shards and
kiln tools. The main varieties were bowls, plates, cups, jars, saucers, pots,
washers, lamps, chopstick shelves and other daily utensils, as well as
decorative wares such as gu (goblets with broad lips, long narrow stems,
and flared bases), cong-style bottles, incense burners, pedestals, and
flowerpots. Body color might be incense ash color, dark gray, purple, or
black. Purple rims and iron feet were common. Thick bodies and thick
glaze layers dominated while thin bodies or thin glaze layers were rare.
Glaze color was mainly greenish blue and beige yellow, as well as emerald
green, grayish blue, light purple, and yellow. Most glazes had ice cracks
(Fig. 8.49). Some of the porcelain shards were found to have the words
“Xiuneisi” and “Guan kiln” written in brown under the glaze.

Fig. 8.49 Guan kiln vase with string pattern,
Song Dynasty, height: 33.6 cm, top diam.: 9.9 cm, base diam.: 14.2 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Following the Xiuneisi Guan kiln, the Southern Song Dynasty built a
second Guan kiln called the Jiaotan Guan kiln, whose site is located in the
area of Tortoise Mountain in the southern suburbs of today’s Hangzhou.
The site was discovered at the beginning of the twentieth century and
porcelain shards had subsequently constantly flowed into the antique
markets of Hangzhou and Shanghai and thus attracted the attention of
ceramics researchers at home and abroad. In the 1950s the Zhejiang
Provincial Cultural Relics Management Committee carried out a small-
scale trial excavation of the site, cleaned up a dragon kiln, and excavated
some of the shard accumulations beside the kiln. Then a Lin’an
archaeological team officially excavated the site in 1985 and conducted
supplementary excavations in 1988 to support the building of the Southern

Song Guan Kiln Museum. These excavations offered a clear understanding
of the Southern Song Jiaotan Guan kiln. Of the unearthed porcelain shards,
23 varieties of wares were complete or restored. In addition to daily utensils
which were unearthed in the largest number such as bowls, plates, bottles,
jars, pots, and basins, there were also a number of decorative objects such
as gu, cong-style bottles, incense burners, pedestals, and flowerpots. The
decorative objects were mostly for ceremonial use and imitations of bronze
and jade wares of the Shang, Zhou, Qin and Han dynasties (Fig. 8.50).
Wares can be classified into thick and thin based on body thickness, and
glaze color was mainly greenish blue and beige yellow, though shades of
yellowish-brown and earthy yellow were also common.47 Daily use utensils
accounted for the largest number of the wares unearthed, yet among the
Song Guan wares collected by the Palace Museum and the Taipei Palace
Museum, daily use utensils are fewer while display ceramics account for
the majority, which is probably because the former suffered a high rate of
damage while the latter enjoyed better preservation. This also shows the
important position of display ceramics as ceremonial wares in the
production of the Southern Song Guan kilns.

Fig. 8.50 Guan kiln flat vase with double pierced handles,
Song Dynasty, height: 23 cm, top diam.: 9.4 × 6.4 cm, base diam.: 6.3 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Southern Song Guan celadon excelled mainly through its jade-like
mellow glaze color, its archaic, simple and dignified shape design, along
with its crack pattern, and therefore it did not require any rich decorative
themes. Besides common plant and animal patterns, there were also various
string patterns, Eight Trigrams patterns, yunlei patterns, square spirals,
double circles, and bump patterns. Commonly used decorative techniques
were engraving, molding, stacking, kneading, hollowing out and openwork;
engraving was mostly used on daily use utensils such as bowls and plates,
molding was used on a wide range of varieties, stacking was mostly used on
wares imitating ancient vessels such as bottles, pots, stoves and gu, and

openwork was mostly used on lids, pedestals and stoves. The rich
decorative techniques, the improvement in firing technology and the
diversity of kiln tools for loading and firing on the one hand reflected the
attention the Southern Song Guan kilns were receiving in terms of
production technology and on the other hand explained the reasons behind
the excellent quality of their products.48
   Guan kiln craftsmen who migrated south in the Southern Song Dynasty
brought technology to Hangzhou. The conditions in the south for porcelain
firing were relatively superior to those in the north. At that time the south
already had a solid foundation with the Yue kilns, secret-color ware and the
Longquan kilns and it would have been easy and quick for the south to
learn to fire Guan wares. In the early years of the Southern Song Dynasty
the products still demonstrated a heavy influence from the Northern Song
Guan kilns, mainly in their thin body, thin glaze layer and the use of prop
nails for firing. For instance, the samples unearthed at the Jiaotan kiln site
had a thin, fine body which could be light gray, gray or deep gray. The outer
surface had a thin layer of greenish blue, bluish gray or beige yellow glaze
applied. The commonality of beige yellow glaze indicates that the porcelain
firing technology of potters in this period was still in the exploratory stage.
The circular feet of bowls, plates and washers were high and flared. Nails
were used to prop the wares during firing, leaving needle-like marks on the
glaze of the outer bottom.
   As the Southern Song regime consolidated its power, the imperial court
required higher quality porcelain. Consequently, the technology of the Guan
kilns was constantly improved. The technique of multiple firing and
multiple glazing was adopted to achieve an improved jade texture of
celadon, and the mouth and belly wall of wares, especially of small wares
such as bowls, plates, washers and saucers, was thinned down to make the
wares more lightweight and graceful. The greatly thickened glaze layer also
prompted kiln workers to reform kiln tools, such as replacing prop nails
with cushion pads to avoid the nails getting stuck to the thick glaze during
firing and rendering the products defective. The adoption of cushion pads
allowed the circular foot of wares to take on the function of bearing the
weight of the ware, prompting previous flared circular feet to be gradually
replaced by straight ones.49
   The Southern Song Guan ware not only inherited the simple yet
dignified shape design and thick glaze texture of famous northern wares

such as the Northern Song Bianjing Guan and Ru wares, but also
assimilated the thin body combined with thick glaze, bright, clear glaze
surface and exquisite shapes of famous southern wares such as Yue and
Longquan wares. Cao Zhao of the Ming Dynasty described Southern Song
Guan ware in his Ge Gu Yao Lun as: “Products fired by Song Dynasty’s
Xiuneisi (Guan kiln) were made from fine clay, had blue color with
pinkness of different shades, and featured crab claw patterns, purple rims
and iron feet.”
   The characteristics of Southern Song Guan ware could be summarized
as “purple rim and iron feet,” “greenish blue glaze,” “ice crack patterns”
and “thin body and thick glaze.” Of the seven major glaze colors of Guan
ware, namely, beeswax yellow, pale blue, greenish blue, light greenish blue,
deep greenish blue, crab color and putty color, greenish blue was the finest.
Repeated polishing and firing of the greenware achieved an extremely thin
body while the glaze thickness was more than three times that of ordinary
ceramic glaze. It can be seen that the attraction of the Southern Song Guan
celadon lay not in its decoration, but mainly in its jade-like, dignified,
elegant and mysterious natural beauty.

8.3.3 The Ge Kilns
The inclusion of the Ge kilns among the celebrated kilns of the Song
Dynasty was first seen in the Ming Xuande period publication Manual of
Xuande Ritual Vessels (Xuande ding yi pu), which noted: “the Chai, Ru,
Guan, Ge, Jun and Ding wares [were] collected by the imperial storage.”
That Ge ware was ranked after Ru and Guan and before Jun and Ding
indicates that the Ge kilns were regarded as famous kilns of the Song
Dynasty and their products were important items for collection. Most Ge
wares handed down from the Southern Song Dynasty have been collected
by the Palace Museum, Shanghai Museum and the Taipei Palace Museum,
except for some that were scattered abroad. Varieties included various
bottles, burners, washers, plates, and jars. The body might be thick or thin,
the body texture fine porcelain or sandy, the body color blackish gray, deep
gray, light gray, earthy yellow, etc., and the glaze color greenish blue, pale
blue, putty color, bluish yellow, etc. The glaze surface had ice crackles, fine
crackles, Hundredfold crackles or a fish-roe pattern (Fig. 8.51). The crack
patches were large (ice) or small (fish-roe) and the crevices could be thick
(iron wire) or thin (silk). The crevices were often filled with black, gold or

red colorings, so the patterns were called “golden threads and iron lines.”
(Fig. 8.52).

   There is little archaeological data available to corroborate the Ge wares
which survive today because the Ge kilns have not been found in literature
from the Song Dynasty and their site has not been located. This has given
rise to a number of different views about the Ge kilns. Some believe “they
were one of the official kiln clusters in the Song Dynasty”50 on the grounds
that common Ge ware varieties such as tripod burners, fish eared burners,
double-eared nipple-footed burners, zhi-style bottles, gallbladder bottles and
folded-waist plates mostly imitated ancient bronze ceremonial ware, were
all of the style of court use porcelain, and shared common designs with Ru
and Guan ware while being quite different from folk porcelain (Figs. 8.53
and 8.54).

   Also supporting this view is the record in Zun Sheng Ba Jian that “the
character of Guan ware is roughly the same as that of Ge ware,” that “the
kiln is under the Phoenix Mountain in Hangzhou,” and that “Ge kilns were
managed by the private sector and sourced all the clay used locally.”
Records of Jingdezhen Ceramics quotes the similar view of Tang Bingjun in

his Wen Fang Si Kao Tu Shuo that “(Ge kilns)…called Gege kilns (“elder
brother kilns”), also used clay from Hangzhou.” From these records some
deduce that the Ge kilns were the “Gege kilns” near Hangzhou and were
probably the “Guan kilns” run by Xiuneisi or civilian kilns supervised by
the government and under the charge of Xiuneisi.51
   The earliest record concerning the Ge (elder brother) and Di (younger
brother) kilns is found in the Comprehensive History of Zhejiang compiled
during the Jiajing era of the Ming Dynasty. The book records the legend of
two brothers, Zhang Shengyi and Zhang Shenger, who came to Liutian at
the foot of Liuhua Mountain in Chuzhou, where most of the inhabitants
took pottery as their occupation, to make the best greenware of the time
each with his own kiln. But the book also states, “the time of the two
brothers is unknown.” The Sequel to Qi Xiu Lei Gao published in the
Jiajing 45th Year further states: “Both the Ge kilns and Longquan kilns
were in Longquan County in Chuzhou. In the Southern Song two brothers,
Zhang Shengyi and Zhang Shenger, each fired one kiln, and those made by
Shengyi were Ge ware…those made by Shenger were Longquan ware,
named after the place. The color was blue of different shades and the feet
were an iron color also of different shades. Previously there was said to be
purple feet, which are rare nowadays. Wares made from fine clay with pure
glaze color are the most precious. Ge ware has more fragmented cracks,
called Hundredfold crackles…” Published five years later than A
Comprehensive History of Zhejiang, the Sequel to Qi Xiu Lei Gao states
that the two brothers were from the Southern Song Dynasty and also points
out that they made porcelain in Longquan County in Chuzhou. This is the
earliest literature known so far indicating that the two brothers were from
the Southern Song, and later literature on the Ge and Di kilns after the
Jiajing years of the Ming Dynasty mostly relies on this.
   However, tests on Ge ware specimens show that the chemical
composition of their body and glaze, the color of the cracks and the
polishing method of the feet are all different from those of the Longquan
black-body celadon unearthed, and are instead similar to the crackled glaze
wares produced in Jiangxi that imitated Guan ware. So some people think
that Ge wares were imitations of Guan wares (Fig. 8.55).

Fig. 8.55 Ge kiln chrysanthemum petal plate,
Song Dynasty, height: 4.1 cm, top diam.: 16 cm, base diam.: 5.6 cm, in the Palace Museum

   The Shanghai Institute of Ceramics of the Chinese Academy of
Sciences tested the Song Dynasty Longquan black-body celadon samples
and came to the following conclusion: “the view of some that they were
imitations of Guan ware is well based since their body composition is very
close to that of northern kiln products but quite different from that of
general Longquan ware.”52
    Still some believe that the Ge wares passed down to the present are
imitations of Guan wares but were not fired by Longquan kilns, and that the
place of production was somewhere near Jingdezhen in Jiangxi. Besides,
Ge Gu Yao Lun makes reference to a crackled glaze ware kiln that was in
Yonghe Town in Ji’an. Since crackled glaze ware was similar to Ge ware
with cracks, it is likely that the two were related.53
     If a summary is to be made, accounts differ, and opinions vary about
many issues surrounding Ge ware and to find the truth requires further
exploration by cultural relic archaeologists.

8.3.4 The Longquan Kilns
The Longquan kilns were located in the southwestern part of Zhejiang
Province. Neighboring counties such as Qingyuan, Yunhe, Lishui, Wuyi
and Jiangshan, as well as Pucheng and Songxi counties of Fujian Province
were all important celadon producers, yet Longquan was the most thriving.
Specimens unearthed from the kiln site indicate that the Longquan kilns
started production in the early Northern Song Dynasty, reached their zenith

in the late Southern Song, developed further in the Yuan Dynasty, and
declined after the mid-Ming Dynasty as craftsmen gradually dispersed to
other places. From beginning to end the Longquan kilns’ porcelain
production lasted for six or seven hundred years.
   The rise of the Longquan kilns in the Song Dynasty was directly related
to the decline of the Yue kilns. In the early and middle Northern Song
Dynasty, the Yue kilns, after almost one thousand years of glory,
experienced a decline due to fuel shortage, rising artisan salaries and heavy
kiln industry taxes in the Ningshao area, transiting from large-scale
commercial production to small-scale production only for local sales.
Craftsmanship also became rough and crude, probably in order to reduce
costs. Of the Yue wares unearthed in various Asian and African countries,
those of the mid-Northern Song Dynasty were of the latest period, which
indicates that as the Yue kilns declined their products were no longer
exported.
   The decline of the Yue kilns broke the supply and demand balance of
celadon, providing a perfect opportunity for the rise of the Longquan kilns.
The huge profits domestic and foreign markets had to offer were a natural
driving force for folk kilns devoted to commodity production. Moreover,
the decline of the Yue kilns drove some craftsmen to other places, one of
which was the mountainous Longquan kiln area, to make a living, and this
added to the technical strength of the Longquan kilns, contributed to their
rapid rise in the late Northern Song Dynasty, and enabled them to almost
completely inherit the traditions of Yue kiln porcelain making. It is worth
noting that in this early period of the Longquan kilns, their products were
sold not only in nearby areas, but were also found in trade ports and foreign
countries. This shows that porcelain for export started occupying an
important position in the Longquan kilns’ production from their early
period.54
   The decline of the Yue kilns after the mid-Northern Song Dynasty led
celadon technology to shift to other places suitable for its development.
Historical records state: “celadon originated from Liutian (刘田).” 刘田 was later
written as 琉田 (also pronounced Liutian), and this was the central production
area of the Longquan kilns. The production capacity of the Longquan kilns
was small in the late Northern Song and reached a larger scale only in the
late years of the Northern Song after a period of development.55

Early products of the Longquan kilns were mainly plates, bowls and
pots, and a small number of jars. The main decorative technique was
engraved patterns, supplemented by comb points or comb-carved waves,
banana leaves, clouds and lotus petals. These early products of the
Longquan kilns bore similarities with Yue, Ou and Wuzhou wares in terms
of shape, decoration and glaze color, suggesting associations between the
Longquan kilns and the other kilns and reflecting the common local and
temporal characteristics of celadon in Zhejiang. After the mid-Northern
Song Dynasty, as the Yue and Ou kilns fell into decline, the Longquan kilns
gradually formed their own style. Varieties increased to include stoves,
bottles, plates, cuspidors and sculptures, each with diverse designs.
Decoration was still dominated by the engraved pattern (Fig. 8.56). Comb
patterns decreased and auspicious words such as 金玉满堂 (“Gold and jade fill
the hall”) and 河滨遗范 (“Good example set by predecessors at riverside”)
appeared on the wells of bowls. Decorative patterns included waves, clouds,
banana leaves, peonies, elaborate blossoms, and children at play. The shape
design and decorative patterns of a kind of shallow flat-based saucer were
quite similar to those of similar saucers produced by the Yaozhou kilns in
Shaanxi of the same period, both often with a swimming fish or a lotus
flower carved at their centers. This provided evidence for the judgement
that in the same period, porcelain kilns in different places often shared a
common style in terms of shape and decoration. In the late Northern Song
Dynasty lotus relief patterns became popular. They were often used to
decorate the outer surface of bowls. The petal tips were rounded, and the
petals were all carved with lines (Fig. 8.57).

   Longquan kiln products from the Northern Song Dynasty used local
porcelain stone with a high silicon and iron content, resulting in a thick,
heavy and steady-looking body. The body was mostly gray or light gray and
the glaze was relatively thin with a yellowish blue color (Fig. 8.58). The use
of lime glaze led to an excellent glaze surface luster because lime glaze has
a relatively low viscosity and good fluidity at high temperature. Glaze was
commonly troubled by yellow shades because kiln workers at the time had
not well mastered the skills of controlling reducing atmosphere.





Fig. 8.58 Longquan kiln double-fish washer,
Song Dynasty, height: 6 cm, top diam.: 13.5 cm, base diam.: 13 cm, in the Palace Museum

   By the Southern Song Dynasty, Hangzhou became the new political
center and the rise of the Guan kilns there also led to rapid development in
the Longquan kilns. Around the middle and late Southern Song Dynasty the

quality of Longquan celadon improved quickly and significantly. In
addition to the kilns located within modern-day Longquan County that fired
celadon, many kilns in nearby areas, such as in Qingyuan, Suichang and
Yunhe and also in Jiangxi and Fujian also fired celadon following the
Longquan kiln style.56 In this period, Longquan kiln products were well-
made and sophisticated, and the varieties also increased. In addition to daily
utensils such as bowls, plates, pots and jars, new varieties of display objects
and sacrificial vessels emerged, many of which imitated ancient copper,
jade and lacquerware. The incense burner shown in Fig. 8.59 was a
Longquan celadon ware that imitated bronze incense burners back in the
Shang and Zhou dynasties. The ware shown in Fig. 8.60, called a “mallet
bottle”, also known as “kinuta” in Japan, usually employed in pairs as
burial objects or household sacrifices, took its shape design also from
similar bronzewares with large mouths and double fish ears. These celadon
wares imitating antique bronze vessels became the aesthetic fashion of
scholar-bureaucrats in the Southern Song Dynasty and this fashion in turn
promoted the development of Longquan celadon. Besides ancient bronzes,
Longquan ware also imitated Guan kiln ware and produced two different
types of Guan-style products, namely Dayao ware and Wayaoyang ware.
Dayao ware was white-bodied celadon with a thick body and glaze. Glaze
colors included greenish blue, plum green and pea green. Surface
decoration that were popular previously, such as engraved or printed
patterns, decreased because thickened glaze would conceal them and
compromise the effect. Instead more effort was spent on shape design.
Decorations included relief, bulging veins and decals, which appeared
simple, elegant and dignified against the backdrop of thick glaze.
Wayaoyang ware was back-bodied celadon with a thin body and thick glaze
and bore a remarkable resemblance to the thin-bodied thick-glaze products
of the Southern Song Guan kilns, not only in appearance, but also in
production technologies from body and glaze formula to firing method. The
Southern Song imperial family’s preference for celadon had a significant
impact on the trends of the upper class at the time, but the products of the
Guan kilns were strictly forbidden to be used by the common people.

Fig. 8.59 Longquan kiln blue-glazed double-eared incense burner,
Southern Song Dynasty, in the British Museum

Fig. 8.60 Longquan kiln blue-glazed fish-eared bottle,
Southern Song Dynasty, in the Victoria & Albert Museum in the UK

   The Longquan kilns were the largest folk celadon producer in Zhejiang
at the time. With a long porcelain-making history and rich experience,
skilled craftsmen, and the best techniques in firing products similar to Guan
ware, the Longquan kilns naturally became the go-to place for court
officials and rich businessmen to order “Guan-style” celadon. In fact,
quality Longquan celadon was prevalent among the daily use utensils of the
upper class in the Southern Song Dynasty. It has been found in large
quantities in officials’ tombs and in the ruins of the Lin’an capital, as well
as in the ruins of the imperial city of the Southern Song and in the
Cuangong Palace cemeteries for the six Song emperors in Shaoxing, which
indicates that at the time the court was also using Longquan celadon as
funerary objects. Though in general the quality of Longquan ware was not
as meticulous or exquisite as that of Guan ware, the folk nature of the
Longquan kilns allowed them more freedom in terms of the variety, shape

and decoration of their products. Not as restricted as the Guan kilns in many
ways, craftsmen of the Longquan kilns were able to make much more
diverse products according to customer needs as well as accommodate their
own techniques and preferences. Particularly notable was the plum green
glaze color that was unique to this period. Bright, soft and mellow, the glaze
color lifted celadon production to a new height (Fig. 8.61).





Fig. 8.61 Longquan kiln flowery mouth bowl,
Song Dynasty, height: 4.9 cm, top diam.: 13.6 cm, base diam.: 4 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Craftsmen of the Longquan kilns in the Southern Song Dynasty took
great pains to innovate technologies in order to give celadon the beauty of
jade and emerald. They firstly replaced the lime glaze (calcium glaze) used
in early celadon production with lime-alkali glaze (calcium potassium
glaze). Early celadon was often only semi-glazed because lime glaze had a
low viscosity and was prone to flowing at high temperature, resulting in a
generally thin glaze layer and a high surface glossiness resembling the
appearance of glass. Lime-alkali glaze, in contrast, had a high viscosity and
thus low fluidity at high temperature, allowing wares to be fully and thickly
glazed to realize a softer glaze gloss. The replacement of lime glaze with
lime-alkali glaze by craftsmen of the Southern Song Longquan kilns
realized a more elegant and lustrous celadon glaze and was a great
innovation in the history of ceramics. Secondly, Longquan kiln craftsmen
increased the thickness of the glaze layer through multiple applications of
glaze, which added to the richness of the glaze color just as depth adds to

the mysterious color of water. The ancient Chinese interpreted the color
celadon (in Chinese, 青, “qing”) in so many ways that the word encompassed
almost all green and blue shades from the palest to the darkest bordering on
black. Normally, at least two or three layers of glaze were applied to give
the celadon glaze a deep green tone. The glaze thickness of Southern Song
Longquan celadon specimens surviving today exceeds 1.5 mm, which is
really the key to their “plum green” color, comparable with emerald.
Thirdly, Longquan craftsmen altered the color of the body by changing the
raw material composition of the body. The tone of the body affects glaze
color. Usually a lower iron content in the raw material of the body was
desired because a high iron content would undermine the whiteness of the
body. Yet Longquan kiln craftsmen intentionally added a certain amount of
zijin (reddish purple) earth into the clay to raise its iron content, because
with the gray tone that this brought to the white body, the glaze color of the
celadon looked even more attractive. Still another technological change of
Southern Song Longquan celadon was the adoption of a strong reducing
atmosphere during firing. The higher the temperature in the kiln, the
stronger the reducing atmosphere, the more thorough the melting of the
body and glaze, and the better the texture of the glaze. It is recorded that the
temperature for firing plum green celadon in Longquan kilns of the
Southern Song Dynasty ranged from 1250 to 1280 ℃.57 (Fig. 8.62).

Fig. 8.62 Longquan kiln tripod burner,
Song Dynasty, height: 12.4 cm, top diam.: 14.5 cm, base diam.: 9.2 cm, in the Palace Museum

    After the mid-Southern Song Dynasty, some of the kilns in Dayao and
other places, under the heavy influence of the Guan kilns, started producing
two types of high-grade thick-glazed products clearly imitating Guan ware,
namely black body celadon and white body celadon. Such high-grade
products were confiscated as court porcelain and the more predominant of
the two—the white-body thick-glazed celadon—was sold to overseas
markets such as Japan. The Longquan kilns made major innovations in the
shape design, body and glaze formula, glazing technique and decoration
approaches of celadon to produce products with a generous glaze layer,
exquisite workmanship, beautiful shapes and rich diversity. The invention
of a light bluish blue glaze and plum green glaze pushed celadon making
technology to a new height. As sales of Longquan ware increased at home
and abroad, the Longquan kilns completely usurped the historical position
of the Yue kilns, became the central production area for celadon in southern
China, and rose to global fame.58

8.3.5 The Jizhou Kilns
The Jizhou kilns were in present-day Yonghe Town in Ji’an, Jiangxi.
Today’s Ji’an was Luling County in the Han Dynasty and the Three
Kingdoms period, and was renamed Jizhou through the Sui, Tang, Five
Dynasties and Song. In the Song Dynasty the Jizhou kilns were one of the
famous folk kiln clusters south of the Yangtze River. They fired a rich
variety of porcelains with strong local characteristics.
   Researchers have conducted several investigations at the Jizhou kiln site
since the 1950s and found the site to be 2.5 km long and one kilometer
wide, with some of the piles more than 20 m high. There are 22 kiln piles in
total and most of them were formed in the Song Dynasty (especially the
Southern Song). Researchers thus inferred that the kilns were created in the
Five Dynasties and flourished in the Southern Song Dynasty. Wares from
the Five Dynasties unearthed from the site included caramel-brown glazed
bowls, jars and pots and white glazed bowls and cups, which had similar
features to those unearthed from the tombs of the Five Dynasties in other
places. The Jizhou kilns developed significantly when it came to the Song
Dynasty, especially the Southern Song. Products in this period included
black glazed ware, caramel glazed ware, blue glazed ware, white glazed

ware, white glazed ware with brown painting, green glazed ware, and
caramel-yellow glazed ware, of which black glazed and white glazed
vessels accounted for the majority, followed by white glazed ware with
brown painting, and then green glazed ware, while the other types were few.
   The most distinctive among Jizhou kiln products in the Southern Song
was black glazed ware, which was previously rarely produced but started to
be fired in large numbers by many kilns in the Song Dynasty because the
fashion of observing tea color and the popularity of the “tea fight” created
the need for black glazed teacups. Many black glazed teacups, bottles and
jars have been unearthed at the Jizhou kiln site. Jizhou kiln black glazed
porcelain was not only produced in large quantities, but it also had a variety
of decorative techniques, such as the leaf pattern, the paper-cut pattern (Fig.
8.63), color painting, glaze sgraffito, glaze sgraffito plus color filling, and
tortoiseshell glaze, all of which, being novel and unusual with a strong local
flavor, set the Jizhou kilns apart from other porcelain kilns in the Song
Dynasty (Fig. 8.64). It is worth mentioning that from quite early times,
Chinese potters had learnt that plant ash could be directly mixed into the
glaze. With ingenious imagination they placed a leaf under the black glaze
of a bowl, and firing brought out rich colors and retained the shape of the
leaf (Fig. 8.65).

   The porcelains produced by the Jizhou kilns bore the obvious impact of
the northern kilns, which on the one hand was brought about by the mutual
assimilation between the southern and northern kilns, and on the other, was
due to the northern porcelain-making technologies being brought by
northern potters as they moved to and settled in the south along with the
Song imperial family. The inverted-fired printed white porcelain mass
produced by Jizhou kilns in the Southern Song Dynasty had a distinct Ding
kiln style and was clearly influenced by former Ding kiln craftsmen who
migrated to the south. In addition to imitating Ding white porcelain, the
Jizhou kilns added color painting to the white wares, specifically, black and
brown paintings in the Cizhou kiln style, and this gave the Jizhou kilns the
name “southern Cizhou kilns.”59 (Fig. 8.66). The underglaze painting
technology of the Jizhou kilns was basically the same as that of the Cizhou
kilns, which also used iron-based coloring. Yet the Jizhou kilns innovated
the technique of the Cizhou kilns by not first applying engobe on the
greenware but rather painting the coloring directly onto the greenware. This
is because the porcelain body of Jizhou painted ware was light beige
yellow, whiter than that of the Cizhou kilns, thus eliminating the need for an
engobe. It was perhaps due to this technical difference that Jizhou painted
porcelain ware took on more of a caramel-red color after firing and was not
as bright as Cizhou ware, thus constituting a unique archaic and simplistic

style (Fig. 8.67). The painted patterns were mostly vines, peonies, lotus
petals, butterflies, geese and fish. For the background pattern, Cizhou ware
often used “pearl ground” while Jizhou ware mostly used a ripple pattern.
Cizhou ware used lots of human figures and inscriptions of poems as
decoration, both of which were rarely found on Jizhou kiln products. Jizhou
underglaze painted porcelain mostly used patterns as decoration. Words
were seldom used, and even if there were words, they were only to
supplement the decorative patterns. Jizhou kilns also fired small quantities
of low-temperature green-glazed and caramel-yellow-glazed pottery, which
were also produced by Cizhou kilns. Unearthed wares include green glazed
pottery pillows, green glazed printed fish, small bowls with vines and
chrysanthemum patterns, and caramel-yellow glazed pottery. Their firing
technology shared the characteristics of the northern Cizhou kilns. For
instance, the Cizhou Guantai site, which produced low-temperature lead-
glazed pottery in large numbers, adopted a twice-firing process, meaning
that the greenwares were first fired, and then the better pieces were selected
to be glazed and fired in a low-temperature furnace. Unglazed plain wares
fired only once were also found at the site of the Jizhou kilns, indicating
that these kilns used the same firing process. But the shape design and
decorative patterns of green-glazed pottery pillows differed between the
two kilns, and the arranging of wares in the kiln was also different (Fig.
8.68).

   Northern kilns sharing similar traits with the Jizhou kilns were not

Yaozhou kiln late Tang Dynasty short-spout pots, thick-lipped bowls and
black-glazed bowls with hare’s fur pattern were similar to those of the
Jizhou kilns, and the layout of fish-swimming-in-water and vine and
chrysanthemum patterns on Jizhou kiln green-glazed small cups was

kiln Hundredfold crackles and the Jian kiln black glaze, especially the latter,

glaze wares fired by the Jizhou kilns were derived from the Jian kiln system

on absorbing and fusing the technical advantages of various northern and
southern kilns. Of course, in certain cases such absorption was mutual, such
as the Jizhou kilns’ interaction with Jingdezhen. The qingbai (bluish white)
porcelain with jade-like color which Jingdezhen produced in large
quantities in the Northern Song Dynasty have also been found in a Jizhou
kiln site, and in the decorative patterns of Jingdezhen blue and white
porcelain that rose in the Yuan Dynasty we can also see many influences
from the underglaze paintings of Jizhou kiln wares.

8.3.6 The Jian Kilns
Fujian’s porcelain industry reached a peak in the Song Dynasty, with a large
number of large-scale kilns and a complete range of ceramic products of
good quality. Often one kiln fired several kinds of porcelain at the same
time, which contributed to the prosperous porcelain industry landscape of
three major types of porcelain—black glazed ware, celadon and qingbai
ware—all thriving at the same time in Fujian. In the meantime, Fujian kilns
which were adept at absorbing the advanced ceramic technologies of other
kilns, conceived such decorative techniques as brown glaze, green glaze,
yellow glaze, underglaze brown painting and sgraffito-engraving, which
enriched Fujian’s porcelain production and assisted with the export of
Fujian ceramic products.
    In the Song Dynasty, the tea fight became a social fashion and for that
black cups were the most suitable. The preference of the upper-class society
for black teacups led to a rapid development of black-glazed porcelain. It
was in this period that Fujian black-glazed ware reached its peak,60 and the
most representative producers were the Jian kilns.
   The Jian kilns were located in modern-day Houjing and Chizhongcun in
Shuiji, Jianyang, Fujian, adjacent to Jian’ou in the south. From the large
area of ancient kiln sites, we can imagine the spectacular scene back then of
furnaces burning red and smoke curling upwards.

In the Song Dynasty, Jian kilns were famous for producing hare-fur
black-glazed teacups. “Hare’s fur” was a kind of strip-shaped crystalline
black glaze. Also famous were two other kinds of black glaze pattern,
namely the partridge feather and oil-spot. Hare’s fur and oil-spot were both
precious varieties of traditional black glazed ceramics in China. Hare-fur
cups were deeply loved by people in the Southern Song Dynasty and
sentences praising them were often found in ancient poetry. Emperor
Huizong of Song commented in Da Guan Cha Lu (Treatise on Tea):
“Bluish black color is better for cups, and those with fur-like strips are the
best.” Such favor for hare-fur cups was due to the popularity of the “tea
fight” in the Song and Yuan dynasties, which, also called “trying tea” or
“tea competition,” was a form of entertainment of the upper class at the
time. Tea fanciers in the Song Dynasty used semi-fermented tea bricks for
the tea fight. They ground the brick into a fine powder, placed the powder
into a cup, and then poured in boiling water so that a layer of white foam
would float to the water’s surface. Using black teacups made it more
convenient to observe the white tea foam. Cai Xiang states in The Record of
Tea: “White tea color calls for a black cup. Cups made by Jian’an are deep
black with a hare-fur pattern. The body is slightly thick. When backed, the
cups stay hot for a long time before cooling down, making it the most
suitable for use. No cups produced in other kilns are as good.” The teacups
used by Emperor Huizong of Song, Zhao Ji, in tea competition were hare-
fur cups made by the Jian kilns. The social trend to follow the preference
and interest of the emperor promoted the Jian kilns’ mass production of
black-glazed teacups and led many other kilns to follow suit (Fig. 8.70).

Fig. 8.70 Jian kiln black glazed bowl,
Song Dynasty, height: 6.3 cm, top diam.: 12 cm, base diam.: 3.6 cm, in the Palace Museum

    In the late Northern Song Dynasty, owing to the special needs of the
upper class for tea competitions, the Jian kilns fired not only daily-use folk
porcelain but also black cups exclusively for the use of the court. At the
Luhuaping kiln site, a number of support plates inscribed with “for the
imperial court” were unearthed, along with cups with the same inscription
on the bottom. This was physical evidence that proved that the Jian kilns at
the time were producing tributary wares for the court of the Song Dynasty.
It is recorded in Remnant Affairs of the Xuanhe Reign that in the Zhenghe
Second Year of Emperor Huizong’s reign in the Northern Song Dynasty
(1112), “Huishan Mountain Spring water and the Jian kilns’ special fur cup
were used to brew new Taiping Jiarui tea to be presented to Cai Jing.”61
This documentary record corroborated the historical fact that Jian kiln cups
were made as tribute to the court.
   Black glazed porcelain began to be produced very early in China’s
history, but its output had been very limited because of its monotony,
rigidity and lack of change. To break the monotony of black glazed ware,
potters ingeniously took advantage of the coloring mechanism of oxidized
metal in the glaze at different kiln temperatures to create varied crystalline
glazes with strip or oil-spot crystals, and fambe flower glazes that looked
like tortoise shell. Some potters burnt paper-cut patterns in the glaze.

Potters also carved, engraved, picked out and printed patterns on black-
glazed wares to further enrich the decorations. All these helped make black
porcelain, which had not been afforded much attention previously, become
one of the most popular porcelain types in the Song Dynasty. The black
glazed wares with silver-bright hare-fur crystals fired by the Jian kilns
became one of the most distinctive black glaze products of the time.
   “Hare-fur glaze” refers to blackish blue or light brown streaks on the
black base of cups that resembled the fine fur of a hare. Hare-fur glazes
could be gold, gray, yellow, silver, etc. Golden hare fur was found on a
brownish-black glaze backdrop. The “fur” protruded slightly on the glaze
surface and glistened gold. Gray hare fur was found floating in brownish
black glaze and the strands were extremely thin. Yellow hare fur which was
in fact dull yellowish-brown, was found densely covering brownish black
glaze. Silver hare fur refers to a white mist-like pattern found on a bluish
black glaze base. There was yet another kind of fur pattern which glittered
with iridescent silver reflections and showed no sign of crystallization, and
that was true “silver” hare fur (Fig. 8.71).





Fig. 8.71 Jian kiln hare-fur bowl,
Song Dynasty, height: 6 cm, top diam.: 11 cm, base diam.: 3.5 cm, in the Palace Museum

   There were basically two mechanisms for the formation of Jian kiln
hare-fur glaze. The first involved anorthite crystallization and liquid–liquid
separation as ferric oxide crystallized on the surface. The ferric oxide
crystals were relatively complete and well-developed, but because the
crystallization was irregular and the crystal grains extremely small, there

would be diffuse reflections with light emanating from one direction, and
this gave the golden light to the crystal streaks, thus forming the golden
hare fur. The second mechanism involved no crystallization in the glaze and
only liquid–liquid phase separation. A thin layer of ferric oxide crystals
formed on the upper glaze. If the crystals were complete and smooth and
the reducing atmosphere was strong, the crystals would carry a strong
regular reflection and weak diffuse reflection, thus giving off bright white
light and forming silver hare fur. In contrast, if the crystals were small, that
is, mostly of submicroscopic size, and the atmosphere more oxidizing, the
miniature streaks would not reflect light and therefore take on a dull earthy
yellow color, forming the yellow hare fur.62 To summarize, the hare’s fur
was composed of many hematite microcrystals. The iron content of the
body of Jian kiln hare-fur cups was as high as 9%, and at high temperature
some of the iron in the body would blend into the glaze, which also
contributed to the formation of the hare-fur streaks. During firing the air
bubbles generated in the glaze layer brought the iron to the surface. When
the temperature reached 1300 ℃ and the glaze started flowing, the iron-rich
parts would form stripes, and when it cooled down small hematite crystals
would form (Fig. 8.72).





Fig. 8.72 Black-glazed hare-fur bowl,
Song Dynasty, height: 7.5 cm, top diam.: 18 cm, base diam.: 5 cm, in the Palace Museum

Another typical pattern of Jian wares was oil spots, in other words,
many small silver metallic dots on a brownish black glaze surface. The dots
looked like oil droplets and were of varying sizes, some reaching several
millimeters in diameter and some only the size of a needle tip. These small
spots with a silver-gray luster were actually massive microcrystals or dense
groups of granular hematite and in some cases magnetite. They were
formed when iron oxides collected at these spots during firing and then
crystallized as hematite and magnetite during cooling. The collection of
iron oxides into certain spots took place through the following process.
When the temperature exceeded 1200 ℃, ferric oxide in the glaze
decomposed and produced air bubbles. Places with richer ferric oxide
would produce more air bubbles and similarly around these air bubbles the
content of ferric oxide was higher than other parts of the glaze. As the
decomposition reaction continued, air bubbles grew, small bubbles merged
into larger ones, and the ferric oxide content surrounding the bubbles
increased. When a bubble reached a certain size, it rose to the surface of the
glaze and was discharged, in the meantime bringing the iron-rich matter
around it up to the surface. As the bubble was discharged the iron-rich
matter gathered at that place and later during cooling formed an “oil spot.”
This also explains why oil spots were larger at places where the glaze was
thick while in places of thin glaze, they were small or nonexistent: a thick
glaze layer was conducive to the growth of bubbles so that more iron oxide
would accumulate around them.

8.3.7 The Dehua Kilns
When introducing or describing the Dehua kilns, previous works on
ceramic history mostly began with the Ming Dynasty because the Ming was
the peak period in the Dehua kilns’ development. In recent years, the large
number of ceramic products salvaged from the sea revealed to us the
importance of ceramic production in coastal areas as well as the fact that
while China’s overseas ceramic trade reached its peak in the Ming and Qing
dynasties, it had developed considerably in the Tang and Song dynasties.
Wide overseas markets promoted the development of ceramic production in
coastal areas, especially the Dehua kilns, which lay to the northwest of
Quanzhou, a famous historical and cultural city in central Fujian Province.
The area featured an abundance of high peaks, deep valleys and meandering
streams. The many streams and small rivers flowed in all directions with

Daiyun Mountain at the center. Those which eventually merge into the
Minjiang River include the Chanxi, Leitan, Houting, Xiaoyou, Dazhang,
Shuanghan, Lingjiao, Xiadian, and Qiongxi Streams, and those flowing into
the Jinjiang River include the Daxi and Sheliao Streams. Water flowing
down the mountains created abundant hydraulic power for the Dehua kilns’
ceramic production. Kiln workers used streams and waterways or
constructed small canals from rivers to divert water artificially to power
waterwheels to crush and process porcelain clay.
  A favorable climate and suitable soil for forest growth made Dehua one
of the famous forested areas in Fujian with rich forest resources. Natural
coniferous and broad-leaved mixed forests abounded, along with natural
broad-leaved forests, followed by natural masson pine forests. By 1949
small areas of primitive and secondary forests still remained. Abundant
forest resources provided sufficient fuel for the large-scale production of the
Dehua kilns. Highly flammable masson pine leaves were the main fuel for
firing fine porcelain while coarse porcelain was fired with pine branches.
   Dehua boasted rich mineral resources, especially porcelain clay and iron
ore. “People there are simple and diligent. The resources are enough for
self-sufficiency.” “Ceramic firing reached a high level.”
   Celadon was the main porcelain produced in the early period of Dehua.
According to the latest archaeological literature, a number of deposits of
imprinted soft pottery, imprinted hard pottery and primitive blue-glazed
porcelain were found on the hills around Liaotianjian Mountain on the
border between Dehua and Yongchun, and a remnant section of a kiln
furnace was found in a citrus orchard south of Liaotianjian Mountain. From
the shards of imprinted soft pottery, imprinted hard pottery and primitive
blue-glazed porcelain collected from the deposit layer of the site, experts
from the Fujian archaeological team confirmed that the site was from the
Shang and Zhou dynasties. In the Dehua Ceramics Museum this author was
able to view a number of Tang dynasty celadon wares which were very
similar to Jingdezhen’s celadon in the Tang Dynasty.
    In history, Dehua had long been subordinate to Quanzhou, a port city
with a highly developed foreign trade. The Fujian Maritime Trade Bureau
was established in Quanzhou in the Yuanyou Second Year of the Northern
Song Dynasty (1087). The prosperity of the Port of Quanzhou exerted an
extremely important influence on Dehua’s porcelain industry development
and people’s livelihoods there. Dehua was connected by water to the ports

of both Fuzhou and Quanzhou. Making it more convenient was Dehua’s
proximity to Yongchun; in other words, porcelain products from Dehua
could be loaded onto ships and carried by river to the Port of Quanzhou as
long as they were carried to Yongchun.
   During the Song Dynasty many parts of Southeast Asia were still in a
relatively primitive state as far as the use of domestic utensils are
concerned. It is recorded in the Zhu Fan Zhi (“Annals of Foreign
Countries”) by Zhao Rukuo of the Southern Song Dynasty that in the
Dengliumei Kingdom (modern-day Nakhon Si Thammarat in Thailand)
people “used sunflower leaves as bowls to eat, did not use spoons or
chopsticks and instead used their hands to put food into their mouth,” that
in Sujidan (modern-day Sukadana on the western coast of Kalimantan)
people “used tree leaves instead of vessels to hold food and discarded the
leaves after meals,” that in the Boni Kingdom (near modern-day Brunei in
northern Kalimanta) people “had no vessels and used bamboo-woven
containers for food, which they abandoned after eating,” and that in Persia
only the king “had food contained in porcelain ware.”63 These records
reflected the simplicity of local dietary utensils in these areas before the
importation of porcelain. The mutual corroboration between the large
number of specimens unearthed from most Dehua kiln sites of the Song and
Yuan dynasties and the ancient porcelain wares discovered in Southeast
Asia lead us to believe that the Dehua kilns became one of the production
centers of daily-use porcelain at the time precisely because their products
followed the needs of the people of Southeast Asia.64
   At this time, Jingdezhen was famous for producing yingqing and
qingbai porcelain. Kilns in southern Fujian all imitated these wares, and the
Dehua kilns were no exception. Most products of the Dehua kilns in the
Song Dynasty were qingbai wares similar to those of Jingdezhen. Yet there
were still differences. Dehua qingbai wares in the Song Dynasty used
support pins during firing and were therefore left with pin marks in the
bowl, while Jingdezhen qingbai porcelain bowls were devoid of such
marks. Another difference was that Dehua qingbai porcelain featured
simpler decorative images than Jingdezhen qingbai porcelain (Fig. 8.73).

Fig. 8.73 Dehua kiln qingbai funnel-shaped bowl,
Northern Song Dynasty, in the Dehua Ceramics Museum in Fujian

   Most qingbai wares from the Dehua kilns used engraved or printed
decorations. Patterns of the Northern Song Dynasty were rich, mainly
clouds, thunder, cloud combs, peonies, floral scrolls, clouds and water,
elaborate blossoms, lotus petals, flowing clouds, lotus flowers,
chrysanthemum, orchids, Malan orchids, duckweed, grass and flowers,
flowers and birds, bees, fish, and inscriptions. In the Southern Song
Dynasty Dehua wares, besides continuing the decorative style of the
Northern Song, made new breakthroughs in the expressive forms of
religious art, such as by highlighting the religious connotations of the lotus
motif in the decoration of lotus mouthed vases, lotus petal bowls, kundikā,
etc. By the Yuan Dynasty the shape design of Dehua wares featured distinct
edges and corners, and decorative patterns went beyond various flowers and
birds to include auspicious words such as “blessing,” “longevity,” “gold and
jade fill the hall,” and the Buddhism-related symbol “卐” and the Chinese
character for “Prajna.” The predominant use of the lotus motif among all
flowers reflected an organic combination of decorative art and religious art
and helped the products win the favor of overseas markets.65 (Figs. 8.74
and 8.75).

Fig. 8.74 Dehua kiln white-glazed sunflower-mouth plate,
Southern Song Dynasty, in the Dehua Ceramics Museum in Fujian





Fig. 8.75 Dehua kiln white glazed powder case,
Southern Song Dynasty, in the Dehua Ceramics Museum in Fujian

    After being set up in 1978, the Chinese Underwater Archaeological
Team carried out several investigations in the coastal waters of China and

made important achievements, among which was the salvage of a large
number of qingbai wares produced by the Dehua kilns. The batch of Dehua
qingbai wares salvaged from the Huaguang Reef No. 1 Shipwreck site had
a white body and grayish white or bluish white glaze. Varieties included
powder cases, ewers, bottles and double-gourd vases.66 From the site of the
Nanhai No. 1 Shipwreck in Guangdong a batch of Dehua qingbai wares
were also salvaged. The body color was white or grayish white, with
qingbai glaze applied inside and out, and with the foot and bottom unglazed
exposing the body. Varieties included bowls, cups, plates, cases, bottles and
ewers.67 Porcelain products of Dehua kilns were also found on the
Quanzhou Fashi Song/Yuan Shipwreck, including some white porcelain.68
   The Nanhai No. 1 Shipwreck was a Song dynasty sunken ship
discovered by the Chinese Underwater Archaeological Team in the

over 4000 precious porcelain pieces, including a large number of Dehua

glazed double-gourd vases, white-glazed small round powder cases, white-
glazed melon-ridge powder cases and white-glazed small bottles.69 (Figs.
8.76 and 8.77).

8.4 Ceramics of the Liao Dynasty
The Liao Dynasty was a regime established by the Khitan peoples in the
north of China in CE 916 (the Zhenming Second Year of the Later Liang of
the Five Dynasties) that then successively coexisted with the Five Dynasties
and the Northern Song Dynasty. Its territory was broad, even larger than
that of the Northern Song, reaching the Sea of Japan in the east, the Altai
Mountains in the west, the Kherlen River in the north, and modern-day
northern Hebei and Shanxi in the south. Moreover, the Liao was the first
frontier ethnic minority regime in Chinese history to be included in the

official histories of China. Before the Liao Dynasty, many minority regimes
on China’s northern frontier, such as the Xiongnu and the Tujue, had once
unified the desert and had a great impact on the history of China, yet
previously these ethnic minority regimes were regarded as “foreign” states
outside China by the central plains dynasties, a situation that changed from
the Liao Dynasty. Although Liao was still hostile to the central plains
dynasties, it was considered no longer external to China. In fact, of Liao’s
territory, only the Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun and its southeastern
section were within the area traditionally understood as “China”. Even the
capital of Liao was not in traditional “China.” Yet it is precisely these small
parts of Liao territory within traditional “China” that brought the Liao
Dynasty into the official discourse of China’s history and even made Liao
territories outside traditional “China,” such as its northeastern section and
north of the Gobi desert, part of China. Therefore, while introducing the
porcelain production of the Song Dynasty, we should also pay attention to
that of the Liao Dynasty, for this was an area where ethnic minority ceramic
art blended with Han ceramic art.
   Before and after its establishment, the Liao constantly attacked the
central plains, used the Han captives to establish new prefectures and
counties, and named these prefectures and counties after the names of
places where these captives came from. Most of these Han people engaged
in agricultural production as slaves or in handicraft work as craftsmen.
These craftsmen brought central plains technologies to the Liao and,
together with local people, promoted the development of the Liao’s
handicraft industries, including the porcelain industry of course.
   Since the Tang and Five Dynasties, the porcelain industry appeared
successively in three prefectures in northern China, namely, Xing Prefecture
(today’s Xingtai in Hebei), Ci Prefecture (today’s Cixian in Hebei) and
Ding Prefecture, and the Ding Prefecture was the northernmost and closest
to the Liao. The History of Liao recorded in several biographies of how
Khitan peoples “attacked Yan and Zhao” and “conquered Ci Kiln Town” or
“seized the Ci kiln business.” This led some researchers to acknowledge the
possibility of potters in Ci Kiln Town being repatriated to Liao.70 In
addition, during the period from Emperor Taizu to Emperor Shizong of the
Liao regime, the Liao assaulted Dingzhou many times, and it is plausible
that among the population captured from Dingzhou by the Liao there were

Ding kiln workers. Thus, porcelain craftsmen of the Liao Dynasty would
mostly have come from Ci Kiln Town and Ding kilns in the central plains.
   Ceramics of the Liao Dynasty, having inherited the traditions of the
ceramics of the Sui and Tang dynasties and assimilated the influence of the
culture of the central plains, formed a unique national style of its own.
Archeological investigations over the years have discovered many kiln sites
of the Liao Dynasty, which were distributed in all of the then five circuits of
Liao’s territory, namely, Shangjing (the Supreme Capital, Linhuang)
Circuit, Zhongjing (Central Capital, Dading; today’s Ningcheng) Circuit,
Dongjing (Eastern Capital, Liaoyang) Circuit, Nanjing (Southern Capital,
Xijin, today’s Beijing) Circuit and Xijing (Western Capital, Datong) Circuit.
There were, for example, Liao Shangjing kilns, Nanshan kilns and
Baiyingele kilns in Lindong Town in Shangjing Circuit, Gangwa kilns in
Chifeng in Zhongjing Circuit, Gangguantun kilns in Liaoyang in Dongjing
Circuit, Longquanwu kilns in Beijing in Nanjing Circuit, and Qingciyao
Village site in the western suburbs of Datong in Xijing Circuit.
    Porcelain kilns in the five circuits will be respectively introduced in the
following sections.

8.4.1 Shangjing Circuit
Three porcelain kilns have been found in Shangjing Circuit, namely, the
Liao Shangjing kilns, the Nanshan and Baiyingele kilns, all in Lindong
(Fig. 8.78).

Fig. 8.78 Liao Shangjing site in Inner Mongolia,
picture provided by Ms. Feng Xiaoqi

   The Liao Shangjing kilns were located in the imperial city of the then
Supreme Capital of Liao, Linhuang, now one kilometer south of Lindong
Town in Baarin Left Banner, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The
kilns produced porcelain during or around the Dakang (Taikang) era of the
reign of Emperor Daozong of Liao (1075–1084). The kiln yard was small,
and production lasted for a relatively short time, but the products were of
good quality. The kilns could be inferred to be official kilns in the late Liao
Dynasty because their products were of fine quality and they were set up
inside the imperial city. Technically heavily influenced by the Ding kilns,
the Liao Shangjing kilns mainly produced white porcelain and black-glazed
porcelain, along with small quantities of green-glazed pottery. The white
porcelain had a pure white thin glaze layer with a bright, mellow luster.
White wares included cups, bowls, plates, saucers, bottles, jars, yu, pots,
and boxes, among which plate-mouthed long-necked pots (Fig. 8.79),

crabapple flower long plates, square plates, long-handled ewers, and others
were the most popular with the Khitan peoples and were often engraved
with various marks on the bottom. The Liao Shangjing kilns’ black
porcelain had black glaze with shades of dark green. Where the glaze was
thick, there were effects resembling drips from a burning candle or massed
fat. Heavy, warm and lustrous, this kind of black glaze was not found in
other Liao ware, nor among the products of any Song dynasty kiln, and thus
must have been created by the Liao Shangjing kilns themselves. The black
wares included only a few varieties, including bottles, jars, pots, yu, and
tiles. Green-glazed pottery had a white body and was made only in two
varieties, namely bottles and jars.

Fig. 8.79 White glazed pot with sgraffito,
Liao Dynasty, height: 32.8 cm, top diam.: 8.4 cm, base diam.: 8.2 cm, in the Palace Museum

   The Nanshan kilns were one kilometer southwest of Linhuang, Supreme
Capital of the Liao at the time. The kiln yard was not large, and its
establishment also seemed to be during or around the Dakang (Taikang) era
of Emperor Daozong’s reign. Folk kilns in the late Liao Dynasty, the
Nanshan kilns mainly fired tricolor glazed pottery, as well as monochrome
glazed pottery and low-temperature white glazed pottery, all of a relatively
poor quality. The body was a uniform light red and had engobe applied.
Then a combination of yellow, green and white glazes or a monochrome

glaze was applied to the engobe, but the glaze color was not very bright,
and the glaze layer was highly prone to peeling. Low-temperature white
glazed pottery had an opalescent white glaze that was not mellow. Some of
the white or yellow glazed wares were also painted with some green
coloring. Most products were small utensils, such as plates and saucers.
   The Baiyingele kilns were located in Baiyingele which was about two
kilometers west of Lindong Town. From their products and similar wares
unearthed from Liao dynasty tombs it can be inferred that they must have
started production from the early years of Emperor Jingzong’s reign to the
time of Emperor Shengzong or later. They were folk kilns with a large kiln
yard. Specializing in firing large coarse porcelain wares with Chayemo (tea-
dust) glaze and black glaze, their products all had a coarse, thick and
yellowish body with high hardness and strength (Fig. 8.80). Chayemo (tea-
dust) glaze was grayish green with a yellow tone. The glaze was thick yet
with poor glossiness. Chicken-leg shaped vases were the most common
varieties using such a glaze. Black glazed wares were of a pure black color
yet lacked luster. Such wares were mostly urns and jars, especially double-
eared jars, while basins or bowls were rare.

Fig. 8.80 Tricolor yuhuchun vase with engraved pattern,
Liao Dynasty, height: 30 cm, top diam.: 7.5 cm, base diam.: 8 cm, in the Palace Museum

8.4.2 Zhongjing Circuit
The main kilns found in Zhongjing Circuit were the Gangwa kilns located
in today’s Gangwa Kiln Village sixty kilometers southwest of Chifeng City
in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The kiln yard was very large.
Production began during the reign of Emperor Taizong or Emperor
Shizong, and lasted for a long time until the Yuan Dynasty, which might be
attributed to the convenient import of the products of the central plains to

the frontier areas thanks to the rapid transportation development and
frequent trade exchanges from the Yuan Dynasty.71
   Records of the Song and Yuan dynasties indicate that the Gangwa kilns
were important official kilns of the Liao Dynasty, which was later
corroborated by the propping tools and furniture inscribed with the Chinese
character “Guan” (official) regularly found in the kilns later. The kilns fired
a relatively rich variety of porcelains. The white porcelain used ganzi soil
(similar to porcelain stone) as raw material to make a yellowish body with
black impurities. White engobe was applied to some of the white wares to
improve the texture of the products and to conceal the originally bluish gray
color of the ganzi soil. The best among the Gangwa kilns’ white porcelain
products reached a high degree of ceramization comparable to that of the
white porcelain of the Ding kilns. Engraved wares usually had the patterns
picked out with a bone blade. There were picked-out patterns on white
glaze and picked-out patterns on caramel glaze (Fig. 8.81). This decorative
method represented the mainstream of Liao dynasty decoration. Imprinted
wares were mostly bowls with the “wheel chrysanthemum pattern” on their
wells. There were many kinds of small sculptures and ceramic toys.72
Besides white porcelain, the Gangwa kilns also fired white wares with a
black pattern, Chayemo (tea-dust) glazed wares, tricolor wares and
monochrome glazed pottery. White wares, including those with black
patterns, had a white yet grayish yellow body, often with black impurity
spots, which were especially prevalent in large utensils. White porcelain
products were mostly cups, bowls, plates, saucers, pots, and jars, while toys
were few. White glazed wares with black patterns might have appeared in
the late Liao Dynasty. Tricolor and monochrome glazed pottery had a soft,
fine body texture that was light red in color. Tricolor wares had yellow,
green and white paintings. Attractive and bright, they were comparable to
the tricolor wares of the Tang Dynasty. Monochrome glazed wares, either
yellow or green, had thick and graceful glazes. Tricolor and monochrome
glazed pottery were mostly printed plates and saucers and yellow-glazed
spherical-body round-handled cockscomb pots, and a small number of
phoenix-head bottles, tricolor printed pottery ink slabs, and small Buddhist
pagodas. Chayemo (tea-dust) glazed wares had a coarse, hard and yellowish
body, frequently troubled by black impurities, and a grayish green and in
some cases yellowish glaze that was turbid and opaque. Chayemo glazed
wares were mostly chicken-leg shaped vases carved with the Chinese

characters for the surnames “Sun” and “Xu” on their shoulders. All of the
Gangwa kilns’ products, apart from the Chayemo glazed wares, had engobe
applied to the body. Among the kilns’ products there were also a small
number of fine black glazed porcelain wares.





Fig. 8.81 Gangwa kiln white glazed jar with black painting,
Liao Dynasty, height: 39.5 cm, top diam.: 19.8 cm, base diam.: 15.8 cm, in the Palace Museum

8.4.3 Dongjing Circuit
The Gangguantun kilns were the main kilns in the Dongjing Circuit of the
Liao Dynasty. Located in Gangguantun on the south bank of the Taizi
River, 15 km east of today’s Liaoyang, Liaoning Province, the kiln yard
was very large but has now been washed away in large portions by the Taizi
River. From their products it could be inferred that the kilns were relatively
large-scale folk kilns at the time. They started firing porcelain in the late

Liao Dynasty, and thrived in the Jin Dynasty. Their products were mainly
white-glazed porcelain, small numbers of white-glazed black-pattern
porcelain and black-glazed porcelain, along with still fewer tricolor wares.
White-glazed porcelain had a coarse, white body texture that often
contained red and black impurities. Varieties included cups, bowls, plates,
saucers, bottles and jars, among which there were, albeit a very small
number of, fine products. The body texture of the white-glazed black-
pattern wares was basically the same as that of the white-glazed wares
while the black-glazed wares were rougher and coarser. All the kilns’
products used engobe. The white glaze could have subtle yellow shades, the
black glaze was pure black, while the pattern of the white-glazed black-
pattern wares was actually yellowish black. The black-glazed wares were
mostly rough, large vessels for daily use, while there were also small
numbers of more exquisite wares such as teacups, small bowls, small jars
and small bottles. Small toys such as various human figurines, beast-head
flutes, dogs, horses and camels could either have black or white glaze.

8.4.4 Nanjing Circuit
The main kiln yard in Nanjing Circuit in the Liao Dynasty was the
Longquanwu kilns in today’s Beijing. The kiln site was discovered near
Longquanwu Village in Junzhuang Commune in Mentougou in 1975 by the
archaeological team organized by the Beijing Municipal Administration of
Cultural Relics in cooperation with the “Learning Agriculture from Dazhai”
movement. Lying 20 km from urban Beijing, Longquanwu Village is
surrounded by mountains on three sides and has good natural conditions for
firing porcelain. The kiln yard, about 200 m in length from east to west and
300 m in width from north to south, was on the west bank of the Yongding
River to the north of Longquanwu Village.73 It started production from
around the Huitong era of Emperor Taizong of Liao. It was the most
important kiln site from the Liao Dynasty found in Beijing and the second
largest kiln yard in the territory of the Liao Dynasty next only to the
Gangwa kilns in Chifeng. A large number of its products were unearthed at
the site and also from tombs nearby, of which white-glazed porcelain
accounted for the majority. Some of the wares unearthed from the kiln site,
such as lotus pattern jars, chrysanthemum petal mouthed plates, and stoves,
were similar in shape and decoration to those produced by the Ding kilns
found in the tomb of Han Yi, the base of the Jingguang Stupa, and the tomb

of Wang Ze, and were obviously made and fired under the influence of
Ding wares.74 The white porcelain wares of Longquanwu can be classified
into fine and rough, the former with a bright white, firm body and the latter
with a body texture that was less pure and delicate. Fine items had a white
glaze with slight blue shades that appeared translucent, while the glaze of
the rough items was white yet lacked mellowness. Some of the rough white
wares, while few, even had heavy yellow tones and were turbid and opaque.
Black-glazed and other wares had generally the same body conditions as the
white-glazed items (Figs. 8.82 and 8.83).
