   Three common points can be identified in the decoration of black and
white porcelain pillows in the Jin Dynasty: 1. for pillows of all different
shapes, the top surface was encircled following its outline and then theme
images were painted in the encircled space; 2. since the pillows were often
only about 30 cm long, leaving a relatively small area for painting, the
images were mostly simple and concise sketches and small scenery
paintings with common themes being flowers and birds, animals, children
at play, horses, bears and poetry; 3. most pillows had all sides decorated
with floral scrolls of the same style, and a small number with single grass or
with no decoration at all. If these three common points are taken as the
criteria for a large category, a high proportion of black and white pillows
would fall into it. The earliest pillow with year markings that belonged to
this category discovered so far is the Dading Second Year (1162) oval
pillow with bird pattern found at the Guantai second kiln site in 1987. Also
belonging to the category are the Dading Fifth Year (1165) bean-shaped
pillow with the pattern of a sea beast carrying fish in its mouth (Fig. 8.94)
in the Handan Institute of Cultural Relics Protection, the Dading 18th Year
(1178) bean-shaped pillow with chess playing pattern in the Philadelphia
Museum of Art in the US, and the Taihe First Year (1201) bean-shaped
pillow with double ducks in water pattern in the Seikadō Bunko Art
Museum in Japan (Fig. 8.95). The book Pillows Donated by Yang Yongde
Couple contains one black and white octagonal pillow with goose carrying
grass in beak pattern (the Cixian Institute of Cultural Relics Protection has

in its collection one such pillow) (Fig. 8.96). The pattern of goose carrying
grass in beak on the pillow is also found in a Taihe First Year (1201) red
and green bowl belonging to a Japanese private collector. The Taihe Fifth
Year (1205) tiger-shaped pillow with brown glaze and black painting in the
Hebei Museum also has a goose pattern drawn in the clearing on the top
surface. Thus, the pillows, often painted with goose carrying grass in beak,
found in the Jin dynasty stratum of the Guantai kiln site could be inferred to
also be from the Taihe era. From the above pillows with year marks it could
be deduced that Jin dynasty porcelain pillows of the same category must be
approximately from the Dading era (or slightly earlier) to the Taihe era
(early thirteenth century).106

   Beginning with the Tongguan kilns in Changsha in the Tang Dynasty,
Chinese potters started writing poems and other texts on porcelain as
decoration to complement the pictures, which is a unique style of Chinese

ceramics, a style that was further developed by the Cizhou kilns in the Jin
Dynasty, especially on porcelain pillows as the pillow surface, flat and
large, was perfectly suited to text decoration. Text decoration on porcelain
pillows was very rich and can be classified into the following categories:
1.
   Phrases

Phrases on porcelain pillows are often auspicious words or words to
exorcise evil spirits. One example is the white glazed carved oval pillow
inscribed with “Spring, summer, autumn, winter” unearthed from the Jin
dynasty stratum of the Guantai kiln Phase II site. Pillow contains a black
and white ruyi-head-shaped pillow, a collection of the Museum of the
Nanyue King Mausoleum in Guangzhou. In the ruyi-head-shaped circled
space on the pillow surface two Chinese characters meaning “repelling
ghosts” are written. Thus, the pillow was presumably used to exorcise
ghosts and ward off evil spirits (Fig. 8.97).107 The Tokyo National Museum
has in its collection a Cheng’an Fifth Year (1200) yellow-green glazed
carved ruyi-head-shaped pillow whose one side is embossed with a deer
carrying the character “blessing” on its back. The meaning is “blessing and
good fortune” since the Chinese character for “deer” and that for “salary”
are homonyms. This pattern is also seen on the black and white pillows of
the Jin Dynasty and the unglazed pillows unearthed from the Guantai kilns.
In the collection of the China Cizhou Kiln Museum in Cixian County there
is a black and white octagonal pillow with bamboo pattern and the Chinese
character for “flower.” In the pillow surface area outlined by two lines, one
thick and one thin, a piece of bamboo is painted and above the bamboo is
written the word “Flower.” The pattern is a celebration of a wedding night
because the Chinese character for “bamboo” and that for “candle” are
homonyms, and so “Flower” and bamboo in combination means “flower
candle,” or painted candle, which is used to light the nuptial chamber. The
pattern is an early auspicious image making use of homophonic sound that
appeared on porcelain (Fig. 8.98).108 Other kilns in the Cizhou kiln system
in the same period also produced wares with characters such as “Blessings,”
“Blessings and Virtue,” “Eternal peace for family and country,” and
“Blessing, Virtue, Longevity,” which were mostly used on pearl ground
pillows. The phrases are mostly short, containing only a few characters,
which are mostly auspicious words and words of blessing. At the end of the

Song Dynasty and the beginning of the Jin text appeared mostly on wares
decorated with comb scratching, painting, and black sgraffito. Common
phrases included “Endurance” and “Moral calmness,” with pillows
inscribed with “Endurance” being the most numerous, which was probably
related to people’s mental state given the turbulent social environment of
the late Song and early Jin dynasties. The considerable change from
“Blessing, Virtue, Longevity” and “Eternal peace for family and country” to
“Endurance” was a true portrayal of the social transition from stability and
prosperity to turbulence and poverty.109

2.
   Couplets

A couplet is a pair of antithetical lines written on paper or cloth or carved
on bamboo, woodwork or pillars. Concise, well-organized and coordinated,
they are a unique artistic form of the Chinese language made possible by
the language’s feature of each character having one and only one syllable.
Many folk couplets have rich philosophical meaning and everyday life
interest and are therefore widely used on porcelain pillows in the Jin
Dynasty. For instance, one black and white ruyi-head-shaped pillow
collected by the China Cizhou Kiln Museum in Cixian County, Hebei is
inscribed with “One trellis of green cucumbers, a garden of white and black
beans,” (Fig. 8.99) and a green-glazed black-pattern ruyi-head-shaped
pillow collected by the Hebei Museum carries the words “On the waterfront
wind blossoms age, under the moon dew leaves yellow.” (Fig. 8.100). Most
of these folk couplets were written on pillows by Cizhou kiln craftsmen
who described the scenery that they saw or experienced. Other instances of
such couplets on porcelain pillows include: “The wind blows the bamboo in
the front courtyard, rain beats the flowers in the back courtyard;” “Fish
jump in the drizzling rain, swallows fly in the wind;” and “To appreciate

flowers one rises early in spring, to cherish moonlight one sleeps late at
night.” Some of the couplets are famous lines from poems that are revised
by craftsmen. For instance, the “At moonset cry the crows, streaking the
frosty sky, dimly lit fishing boats ‘neath maples sadly lie” (translation by
Xu Yuanchong) by poet Zhang Ji of the Tang Dynasty is modified by the
Cizhou kiln craftsmen to read: “As leaves fall the apes cry, streaking the
frosty sky, by the riverside the fishermen sadly lie.”

3.
  Poems

Many may regard writing poetry an elegant cultural activity for elites to
express their aspirations, ideas and feelings and think that ceramic
craftsmen with little education and little literacy were not up to the task of
writing poetry. Yet in fact poetry is the oldest and most basic literary form
in the world that originated from the production activities of the common
people. Its earliest forms included the labor chants (which later developed
into folk songs) and the sacrificial eulogies of ancient times. It is stated in
the Book of Rites (Liji), Book of Music that “poetry speaks the mind, songs
exercise the voice, and dance expresses feeling: the three spring from the
heart and then musical instruments follow.” Poems, combined with music
and dance, are collectively known as poetry (in Chinese “Shige,” literally
“poem song”). Poetry originated from the common people and is an
expression of their voice and feelings. The words are the plainest language
of the common people and folk craftsmen at the time, and do not inevitably
require a certain level of education. Examples include the five-character

poem Old Man on a black and white octagonal pillow in the Linzhou
Culture Museum in Henan and the seven-character poem Ode to
Chrysanthemum on a green glazed carved ruyi-head-shaped pillow in the
collection of the Tianjin Museum of Art.
4.
   Ci

Ci is a type of lyric poem that is sung with musical accompaniment. It
originated in the Tang Dynasty, developed mature patterns in the Five
Dynasties and flourished in the Song Dynasty. Like poetry, ci also
originated from the common people. The many musicians who made a
living in cities by singing, wrote or adapted lyrics containing long and short
sentences based on the patterns of the musical rhythm, and these lyrics, the
earliest ci, gained wide currency with the spread of the music. Still, in the
Tang Dynasty the literati believed these lyrics were not elegant enough to
be regarded as real poetry. It was in the Song Dynasty that ci won the
attention of the literati and refined scholars and became a literary form
equal in status to Tang poetry. Thus, it is not difficult to understand that ci
composed by the common people appeared years earlier than those written
by the literati.
   Due to its folk and popular nature, ci naturally became a source of text
decoration for the Cizhou kilns, which were primarily folk kilns. Potters
chose to write many ci works on porcelain pillows in line with the tastes of,
and thus proving popular with, the ordinary folk due to their easy-to-
understand, simple and natural nature. Examples include the black and
white octagonal pillow inscribed with a Rumengling (tune name, literally
“Like a Dream”) collected by the Cizhou Kiln Museum in Cixian County
(Fig. 8.101) (this particular Rumengling was written by Su Shi in memory
of Dongpo in Huangzhou), the black and white bean shaped pillow
inscribed with a Rumengling collected by the Fengfeng Mining Area
Cultural Relic Preservation Center (Fig. 8.102), the yellow-green glazed
fan-shaped pillow described in Pillow, now in the collection of the Museum
of the Nanyue King Mausoleum in Guangzhou, which is printed with floral
scrolls and beast face patterns on the front, back and two sides, and carved
with Huanxisha (a tune name, literally “Silk-Washing Stream”) on the top
surface in an area encircled by double lines,110 the black and white
octagonal pillow (Fig. 8.103) that has in the octagonal area encircled by

slightly inward-arcing broadband and thin lines Pusaman (tune name,
literally “Buddhist Dancers”) by Su Shi written in Xingkai (a style between
running script and regular script),111 and the black and white octagonal
pillow collected by the Handan Institute of Cultural Relics Protection in
Hebei (Fig. 8.104) carrying the work Wuyeti (tune name, literally “Crying
Night Crow”) in Xingcao (a style between running script and cursive
script).112 It can be seen that the ci decorations on Jin dynasty Cizhou
porcelain pillows is extremely rich. Some from ordinary folk, some from
the works of Song dynasty literati and poets, yet mainly reflecting the
aesthetic preferences of the common people at the time, these ci works are
valuable data for examining not only the folk ceramic art but also the folk
culture of the Jin Dynasty.

8.5.4.4 Red and Green Porcelain
Red and green porcelain appeared in the Jin Dynasty. Its appearance was
significant in the history of Chinese ceramics because it was the pioneer of
the later world-famous polychrome porcelains of the Ming Dynasty such as
red and green ware, blue and white doucai ware, and blue and white wucai
ware. However, in the past, due to entrenched Han-centrism, it was seldom
referred to as Jin red and green porcelain, and was instead mostly called
“Song multicolor ware” or “Song red and green ware,” which is a
misunderstanding that needs to be corrected with the advent of many new
archaeological discoveries.
   The Japanese scholar Hasebe Gakuji posits that red and green porcelain
started to be produced in the thirteenth century based on inscribed remains
from the Taihe First Year (1201) and Zhengda Seventh Year (1230), but
such remains were few among unearthed cultural relics from the Jin and
Yuan dynasties. A red and green bowl with the word “Qing” written in the
center was unearthed from the Hou Majin tomb in Shanxi Province. The
bowl could be deduced to be produced in the first half of the thirteenth
century because the bricks used in the tomb are the same as those in a tomb
nearby inscribed with Chongqing First Year (1212). Many shards of Song

red and green bowls and dishes were unearthed at the Kalake’ermu Site in
Inner Mongolia. The site was where the second Mongol monarch (Ögedei
Khan) first built a city in early 1235, and then soon after 1260, when
Emperor Shizu of Yuan Kublai moved the capital to Beijing, became a
small regional city. Thus, the peak time of this site was the mid-thirteenth
century, but shards of Yuan dynasty blue and white porcelain and celadon
recognized as fourteenth century products have also been unearthed here.
Consequently, the latest production time for the Song red and green ware
unearthed at the site cannot yet be determined, although it can be
determined that they were produced in the first half of the thirteenth century
at the earliest and were in all likelihood produced in the thirteenth
century.113 In addition, it is recorded that red and green porcelain was found
in all three archaeological excavations of the Guantai site, with red and
green porcelain sculptures of “ladies” and “small persons” unearthed in the
first and second excavations and red and green small figurines and shards of
vessel covers with red lines and yellow dots unearthed during the third
excavation, which all belonged to the third stage of the Guantai kilns, in
other words, the Jin dynasty stratum. Nevertheless, the best red and green
porcelain products from the era were produced not by the Guantai kilns in
Cizhou, but by the Linshui kilns. In 1989, a Jin dynasty tomb inscribed in
intaglio with the epitaph “Cui Xiannu deceased on 13th of the eighth month
in the Taihe Second Year” was discovered in Linshui Town and from the
tomb dozens of red and green child figurines of different sizes (25 cm
maximum and 10 cm minimum) and postures (Figs. 8.105 and 8.106) were
unearthed.114 In May and June 2002, the cultural relics preservation
departments at both prefectural and district levels of Handan jointly
conducted remedial excavation of the ancient kiln site newly discovered at
the Shuntian Shopping Mall construction site in the Sangong District of
Linshui Town in the Fengfeng mining area where they discovered ancient
porcelain kiln workshops, material pools, water wells and a large volume of
kiln furniture of the Tang, Song, Jin and Yuan dynasties, and unearthed over
30,000 pieces of remnant vessels and shards of celadon, black porcelain,
white porcelain with engobe, black and white porcelain, red and green
porcelain, engraved and carved wares, imprinted wares, and products
imitating Jun ware. The findings indicate that the Linshui kilns not only
produced in large quantities porcelain types that were the most
representative of the Cizhou kiln system such as black and white ware, but

also fired red and green porcelain and imprinted white porcelain that are
superior to those made by the Guantai kilns.115 History of Chinese
Ceramics has the following record: “From a cellar in Linshui County a
batch of Bodhisattva Manjusri statues sitting on elephant and lion backs in
white glaze porcelain with red, green and golden colors were unearthed.
The statues are 20–50 cm high… The statues are tall and in bright colors.
The application of the color gold to a large area is especially rare.”116 (Figs.
8.107 and 8.108). These red and green statues were obviously produced by
the Linshui kilns, but because when the book was written it was not known
that there were ancient Song and Yuan kilns in Linshui, the book mistakenly
stated that the statues “must be the products of the Guantai kilns since
Linshui was very close to Guantai.” At present, the unearthing of large
numbers of red and green wares and shards (presently in the collection of
the Fengfeng Mining Area Cultural Relic Preservation Center) at the
ancient kiln site in the Sangong District of Linshui Town and the discovery
of a coloring workshop there indisputably proves that the Linshui kilns
were the main producers of Cizhou kiln red and green porcelain. Besides
the Cizhou kilns, kilns producing red and green porcelain in the Jin Dynasty
also included the Bayi kilns in Changzhi, Shanxi, the Pacun kilns in
Yuzhou, Henan, the Hebiji kilns in Henan, the Quhe kilns in Dengfeng,
Henan, and the Dezhou kilns in Shandong.

   Red and green porcelain, created by the Cizhou kilns, was the first
above-glaze painted porcelain in China. The combination of underglaze
black color with above-glaze red, yellow and green colors created
multicolor porcelain painting techniques. There are three basic techniques.
1. Doucai (Fig. 8.109). The so-called doucai method, mostly used for
sculptures, is a combination of high temperature decoration and low
temperature glaze painting. First, black color is painted on white engobe (to

draw eyebrows, eyes and clothing lines, or to color the pedestal), then a
layer of white transparent glaze is applied, and then the ware is fired at high
temperature into porcelain complete with the preliminary decoration. Then
red, green and other colors are added before the ware is sent to the kiln for
the second time to be fired at a low temperature. After the second firing
some further colors are applied. 2. Red outlines with coloring (Fig. 8.110).
First, iron red is used to draw the outlines of the image, and then green and
yellow colors are painted within the red lines, sometimes also outside the
lines if the image so requires. The lines are simple, stylized and smooth
with a strong sense of motion and urgency, and the colors are bright. Images
drawn with this method are mostly found on bowls, plates, jars, bottles and
other vessels. 3. Black covered by other color (Fig. 8.111). This is a type of
doucai. Underglaze black pattern fired at high temperature is covered by
another layer of low-temperature coloring, transparent green or transparent
yellow, to create the effect of black pattern against a green or yellow
background. The method is mainly used to paint the lace of the costume of
red and green figurines.117

   The red and green porcelain wares found so far are mainly plates,
bowls, basins, jars, bottles, cups, figurines and Buddha statues, mostly daily
use utensils and sculptures, along with porcelain for ornamentation and
display. The main decorative themes are phoenix, peony, lotus, and
waterweeds (Figs. 8.112 and 8.113). Red and green porcelain shared many
similarities with black and white porcelain in terms of painting style. While
the development of black and white porcelain laid the foundation for the
emergence of Jingdezhen blue and white porcelain in the Yuan Dynasty, the

development of red and green porcelain prepared for the emergence of
Jingdezhen red and green ware in the Yuan and Ming dynasties and of
Jingdezhen blue and white doucai ware and blue and white wucai ware in
the Ming Dynasty, playing an important transitional role in the history of
Chinese ceramics.

8.6 Foreign Trade in Ceramics During the Song
Dynasty
8.6.1 Maritime Ceramics Export Routes
The Maritime Silk Road was mentioned in records as early as the Han
Dynasty, when Chinese ships sailed from ports in Guangdong, Guangxi,
Vietnam, etc. along the eastern coast of the Indochina peninsula to finally
reach Southeast Asian countries. After the Tang and Song, with the progress
of navigation and shipbuilding technologies, the routes of the Maritime Silk
Road were greatly expanded, and trade became more and more prosperous.
There was no more convenient or safer means of transportation than by
water for China’s porcelain, and so the routes are also known as the

“Ceramic Road.” Before important archaeological discoveries were made,
this prosperous Maritime Silk Road existed only sporadically in literature
and little was known about the trade routes and modes. It was not until the
twentieth century when Chinese porcelain and other cultural relics were
discovered in ports along these routes that people were able to gradually
piece together the details of these routes. Now it is known that these routes
went beyond Southeast Asia. They went through the South China Sea
across the Indian Ocean to reach countries along the Persian Gulf. Even
many ports on the east coast of Africa have seen the unearthing of Chinese
porcelain.
    In the Song Dynasty, with the development of agriculture and the
handicraft industry in southeastern China and the progress of maritime
transport, the Song regime attached great importance to maritime trade,
which was also due to the fact that the land-based foreign trade transport
routes in the northwest were successively blocked by the Liao, Xixia and
Jin regimes. The progress in the shipbuilding industry provided further
favorable conditions for overseas trade in the Song Dynasty and for the
further improvement of the “Maritime Ceramics Road”. Many new
archaeological discoveries are also providing us with abundant research
materials to understand the Maritime Ceramics Road in the Song Dynasty.

8.6.2 Overseas Trade in the Song
During the Northern Song Dynasty, the imperial court attached great
importance to Mingzhou’s overseas trade. The same year that the Wu Yue
area submitted to the rule of the Song regime (CE 978), the Northern Song
court established the Zhejiang Maritime Trade Bureau in Hangzhou to
govern the shipping affairs of Hangzhou and Mingzhou. It was stipulated in
the Duan’gong Second Year of the reign of Emperor Taizong of Song (CE
989) that: “From now on those who travel to foreign countries for trade
must register at the Zhejiang Maritime Trade Bureau for official approval so
as to be allowed to travel abroad, and those who violate this rule shall have
their goods confiscated.” In the Chunhua Third Year (CE 992), the Zhejiang
Maritime Trade Bureau was moved to Dinghai County in Mingzhou
(present-day Zhenhai, Ningbo), and in the Xianping Second Year (CE 999)
the imperial court set up a separate maritime trade bureau in Mingzhou. In
Yuanfeng Third Year (1080) Emperor Shenzong of Song gave an order
explicitly designating the Port of Mingzhou as the only port that the

Northern Song regime would endorse for the issuing of visas for shipment
to Japan and Koryo and stipulating that any attempt to travel to Japan or
Koryo without obtaining approval from the Mingzhou Maritime Trade
Bureau would constitute a violation.118
   The Song Dynasty set up a maritime trade bureau in Guangzhou to take
charge of overseas trade only four months after it conquered the Southern
Han regime and achieved sovereignty over Guangzhou in the Kaibao
Fourth Year (CE 971). Guangzhou remained the largest port in China until
the Northern Song Dynasty. By the Southern Song Dynasty, the status of
the Port of Quanzhou rose as the political center moved southward to
Lin’an (now Hangzhou). The Port of Chaozhou in eastern Guangdong was
also a major port at the time. Meanwhile, the trade routes still followed
those of the Tang Dynasty and remained the longest ocean routes in the
world at the time. The main exports were silk, ceramics and tea.119
   Written at the beginning of the twelfth century, Ping Zhou Ke Tan
contains specific descriptions of maritime ceramics transport at the time.
The second volume of the work carries the following record: “(Foreign
trade ships of the day) were tens of meters long and deep. Merchants stored
goods in the lower section of the ship and slept on top of them at night. The
goods were mostly ceramics with smaller items put inside larger ones to
make the best use of the space. When at sea the ships are not afraid of the
wind or waves, but only of getting stranded in shallow waters, in which
case it would be difficult to get away again. If a ship leaks and cannot be
repaired from on board, frogmen who are good at swimming are instructed
to repair the ship externally. The navigator is versed in geography. He tells
the direction by the stars at night, by the sun in the day, and by the compass
in bad weather. Alternately, he takes a mud sample from the bottom of the
sea with a hook rope dozens of meters in length and smells the mud to
know where the ship is.”120
   The Southern Song regime placed more emphasis on overseas trade as
its territory shrank to cover only the south, and fiscal revenue declined
sharply. Gu Yanwu, a famous scholar at the end of the Ming Dynasty, once
summarized the situation thus: “after the southward migration (of the Song
royal house), there was a shortage of funds and everything depended on
overseas trade.”
     It is recorded in Important Annual Records Since the Jianyan Era that in
the 10th month of Shaoxing Seventh Year, Lian Nanfu, scholar of the

Baoxing Pavilion and Governor of Guangzhou, “reported to the throne the
disadvantages of maritime trade, basically advising that the maritime trade
bureau only relied on trade with foreign businessmen, and that Pu Yali, a
big businessman, arrived in Guangzhou the day before and that he did not
return because a military officer exchanged women for his fortune.” After
hearing this, Emperor Gaozong immediately instructed: “Let Nanfu
persuade him to return to his country and continue to transport goods.” The
Emperor also continued: “Foreign trade brings rich profits, and this could
be millions if the trade was conducted properly. Wouldn’t this be better than
to levy the people? That is why I pay attention to foreign trade; in other
words, to spare the people some effort.” In the ninth month of Shaoxing
16th Year, Emperor Gaozong again talked about foreign trade: “Profits from
maritime trade could be beneficial to the country. It is advisable to follow
the old practice to attract people from afar and open ports for trade.” It can
be seen that at the time the government attached great importance to
overseas trade. The Song Dynasty also formulated a series of preferential
policies to promote foreign trade. Foreign businessmen who repeatedly
imported large quantities of merchandise and who attracted other foreign
merchants to come and trade were awarded official posts as a reward;
Chinese businessmen who attracted foreign merchants to conduct trade
were also granted certain official posts, and officials in charge of managing
foreign trade who performed well in promoting trade were promoted as a
reward. Reception centers for foreign merchants were set up in trade ports
such as Hangzhou, Mingzhou, Wenzhou and Quanzhou. An order was
given in the Shaoxing Third Year of the Southern Song Dynasty that the
government shall hold a banquet to see off Chinese maritime merchants
when they put to sea and hold banquets to welcome foreign merchants upon
their arrival. Protective measures were taken in favor of foreign
businessmen and merchant ships. “If a drifting foreign ship is spotted along
the coast, if the ship is damaged or the owner absent, the government shall
conduct a rescue, register the goods on board, and return them to the next of
kin of the owner.” Tax could be exempted if the ship suffered damage due
to bad weather at sea. If extorted by local officials, foreign merchants were
allowed to appeal directly to government authorities of higher ranks.
Government officials who impaired overseas trade should be punished.
With these encouraging polices in place, the overseas trade of the Southern
Song naturally became more and more prosperous.121

8.6.3 Kilns Producing Export Ceramics in Coastal Areas in the
Song Dynasty
Export goods in the Song Dynasty were mainly comprised of silk and
porcelain. Silk accounted for the majority in the Northern Song, but by the
Southern Song, porcelain exports increased significantly with the reduction
in silk sources from the north. Porcelain, as one important foreign trade
commodity, was sold to many countries and regions against this historical
background.
   At the time, Chinese porcelain was a high-grade commodity in
Southeast Asia and was in short supply, while imports from abroad were
mostly primary native products such as tortoiseshell, pepper, spices,
medicinal materials, ivory, wood, and natural jewelry, which were all raw
materials. Therefore, the overseas porcelain trade brought huge profits. The
encouraging polices of the Song dynasty rulers for porcelain export, the
government fiscal revenue increase that could result from the taxation
involved, and the absence of adverse elements such as the long-term war in
the north, all drove the southern porcelain industry to develop on a larger
scale. Porcelains that were mass exported at the time included qingbai
porcelain from the Jingdezhen kilns, celadon from the Longquan kilns in
Zhejiang, and black glazed porcelain from the Jian kilns in Fujian. Driven
by these kilns, many folk kilns which imitated their products solely to
export for profit emerged. Most of these kilns were located on transit routes
near rivers and waterways.
   As a result, many kilns firing products that imitated Longquan ware,
Jingdezhen ware and Jian ware appeared in Fujian along the coast.
Specifically, kilns that imitated the qingbai porcelain of the Jingdezhen
kilns included Pucheng, Chong’an, Zhenghe, Guangze, Jian’ou, Jianning,
Minqing, and Minhou, kilns that imitated the celadon of the Longquan kilns
included Pucheng, Songxi, Chong’an, Guangze, Zhenghe, Jianyang,
Jian’ou, Jianning, Jiangle, Fuqing, Minqing, Minhou, Lianjiang and
Fuzhou, and kilns in the Minjiang River reaches that imitated the high-
quality black porcelain of the Jian kilns in Shuiji Town, Jianyang, which
were once selected as imperial suppliers to the Song court, included
Pucheng, Chong’an, Guangze, Shaowu, Jianyang, Jian’ou, Shunchang,
Nanping, Taining, Jiangle, Sanming, Youxi, Minqing, Minhou, Fuqing,
Lianjiang and Fuzhou. The products of these folk kilns were transported
down the Minjiang River together with the products of the Jingdezhen,

Longquan and Jian kilns to be exported via Fuzhou. That is why in many
remains of the Song and Yuan dynasties, porcelain relics produced by these
different kilns often coexist.
   Besides the above kilns in Fujian, kilns producing export porcelain also
appeared in Guangdong from the time of the Tang Dynasty, and by the
Song Dynasty, thanks to further development of the Maritime Ceramics
Road, such kilns in Guangdong continued to increase. In excess of 600 kiln
sites have been found, distributed across over 40 counties and prefectures
including Chenghai, Chaozhou, Jieyang, Meizhou, Xingning, Huiyang,
Boluo, Longchuan, Dongguan, Shenzhen, Shaoguan, Shixing, Nanxiong,
Lechang, Ruyuan, Guangzhou, Panyu and Foshan. Export porcelains of the
Song Dynasty discovered along maritime routes in foreign countries and
along China’s border are mainly products of the Xicun kilns in Guangzhou,
the Bijiashan kilns in Chaozhou, the Huiyang kilns, the Qishi kilns in
Foshan, the Suixi and Haikang kilns, of which the Xicun kilns in
Guangzhou and the Bijiashan kilns in Chaozhou boasted the largest scale
and richest products.122
   This author once viewed a qingbai glazed phoenix-head pot in the
Metropolitan Museum of Art in the US as shown in Fig. 8.114, with a note
saying that it was produced in “the Tang or early Song Dynasty, about the
tenth century.” It is an excellent qingbai porcelain work with the phoenix
head minutely and vividly carved. The earliest porcelain pot or bottle-
shaped water jar with phoenix head can be traced back to the Tang Dynasty
and was inspired by the gold and silver phoenix-head pots imported from
the Persian Sassanid Dynasty. “The maritime trade between China and the
Philippines and Indonesia in Southeast Asia expanded greatly in the early
Song Dynasty (the end of the tenth century), and many qingbai porcelain
wares like this phoenix-head pot were exported to those areas.” From this
description by the Metropolitan Museum of Art it can be largely confirmed
that the pot was produced for export, yet it is hard to tell whether it was
produced by the Jingdezhen kilns or by coastal kilns imitating Jingdezhen
ware since Jingdezhen once produced the same qingbai glazed phoenix-
head pots yet with a more delicate style and slightly different glaze color.

8.6.4 New Information Introduced by Ancient Ceramics
Recently Raised from Sea
In recent years more attention has been paid to the production of ceramics
in coastal areas, for one because scholars are doing more research on export
ceramics in different dynasties and for another because new archeological
discoveries around the world are bringing to people’s attention not only
newly unearthed ancient ceramics but also many ancient ceramics which
have been newly salvaged from under the sea on the Maritime Ceramics
Road. The discovery of these ancient ceramics from the seabed helps us
further understand the production and export of ceramics along the coast of
China in different dynasties as well as the Maritime Ceramics Road itself.

Regarding Song dynasty ceramics raised from the sea, the first findings
to gain our attention are the four underwater excavations carried out by
archeologists on the “Baijiao No. 1” shipwreck site in the Dinghai Sea at
Lianjiang, Fujian respectively in the spring of 1990, at the end of spring and
the beginning of summer in 1995, in the summer of 1999 and in the summer
of 2000. Most ceramics raised from the shipwreck are black glazed small
cups of similar design, specifications and size. They are most probably
imitations of the hare-fur cups made by the Jian kilns. During the Song and
Yuan dynasties there were many kilns firing black glazed cups in Fuzhou,
notably the Dongzhang kilns in Fuqing, the Pukou kilns in Lianjiang, the Yi
kilns in Minqing, the Changbing kilns in Tingjiang, and the Nanyu and
Hongwei kiln sites in Minhou. Analysis and comparison of body texture,
glaze color and shape led to the preliminary conjecture that the black glazed
cups from Baijiao No. 1 are closer to products of the Fuzhou area and are
especially similar to those made by the Changbing, Nanyu and Hongwei
kilns. Therefore, it is preliminarily presumed that the age of the Baijiao No.
1 shipwreck was Southern Song, that is, from the late twelfth century to the
early thirteenth century. Also raised from the sea during the underwater
excavations of Baijiao No. 1 shipwreck were a number of qingbai porcelain
bowls which might have been produced by kilns in the surrounding areas,
such as the Yi kilns in Minqing, the Changbing kilns in Tingjiang, and the
Huanxi kilns in Fuzhou.123
     It is conjectured that the destination of Baijiao No. 1 might have been
Japan because the shipwreck is on the northward route from the Minjiang
River estuary. The ceramics salvaged from the wreck are mainly black
glazed cups. From the South Korea Sinan Shipwreck a small number of
cups produced by the Jian kilns in Fujian and some black glazed cups made
by the Chayang kilns in Nanping were raised, and a considerable number of
black glazed cups from the Jian and other kilns have also been discovered
and unearthed in Japan.124
   Also worth noting is the “Nanhai No. 1” Shipwreck that was found in
the Yangjiang Sea of Guangdong Province in 1987. Overall salvage
operations began in 2007 and have so far raised from the wreck more than
2,000 pieces of intact porcelain in over 30 varieties. The objects were the
finest works of famous Song kilns such as the Dehua, Cizao, Jingdezhen
and Longquan kilns. Most of the works can be classified as national first-
class or second-class cultural relics. They exhibited a distinct exotic style

and were therefore considered to be produced by Song dynasty potters
based on designs that had come from overseas orders. Specifically, they
include qingbai glazed ware from the Jingdezhen kilns such as bowls, small
cups, and plates with patterns such as lotus petals, lotus flowers, peony,
yunlei, flying phoenix, children at play, and twining flowers, qingbai glazed
ware from the Dehua kilns such as bowls, cups, plates, cases, bottles, jars,
and handled ewers with such patterns as lotus petals, lotus flowers, peony,
floral scrolls, yunlei, and twining flowers, qingbai glazed ware from the Yi
kilns in Minqing including bowls, cups, and handled ewers with mostly
engraved and carved patterns such as lotus petals, lotus flowers, and floral
scrolls, qingbai glazed ware from the Longquan kilns including bowls,
plates, and tight-mouth bowls with engraved and carved decorations such as
chrysanthemum petals, lotus petals, lotus flowers, and curling clouds, and
caramel-black glazed ware and green glazed ware from the Cizao kilns in
Jinjiang, Fujian, mostly cups, water caltrop flower saucers, bottles, double-
gourd vases, and stoves.
   The site of the “Nanhai No. 1” wreck is on the route of the “Maritime
Ceramics Road” mentioned earlier. Traveling northeast from the wreck area
through the Chuanshan Islands one can reach multiple ports including
Yangjiang, Hailing Island, Guangzhou, Chaozhou, Quanzhou, and Xiamen,
and traveling west one can proceed to the Leizhou Peninsula and
Qiongzhou Strait to reach Guangxi and then cross the Nanhai Sea to reach
more distant destinations. Some scholars judged from the direction of the
shipwreck’s nose, that is, 240° southwest, that the cargo ship had just sailed
from a Chinese port heading for overseas destinations. Similarly, the
Guangzhou Daily on February 1, 2007 has the following news: “According
to experts, the nose of the ‘Nanhai No. 1’ points 240 degrees southwest, and
from this and the wreck’s location it could be surmised that the ancient ship
was heading for Singapore, India and other Southeast Asian regions for
overseas trade.”125
    Archaeologists believe that the significance of the discovery of the
“Nanhai No. 1” lies not only in the finding of a ship carrying tens of
thousands of rare treasures, but also in the invaluable information it has to
offer and its extraordinary academic value. For one, “Nanhai No. 1” is on a
route of the “Maritime Silk Road” (Maritime Ceramics Road), and for
another, the “treasures” on board are extremely rich and valuable in both
number and variety. Thus, the wreck is able to provide the most credible

data for the study of this period of history. Exploration and excavation of
these underwater cultural relics could restore and fill the historical gap
concerning the ancient Chinese “Maritime Silk Road.” Just as the two
major discoveries in the cultural history of modern China, in other words,
the “oracle bones” and “Dunhuang,” led to the birth of oracle bones studies
and Dunhuang studies, the finding of “Nanhai No. 1” is likely to bring
about the rise of “Maritime Silk Road Studies.”126
    In any case, the discovery of “Nanhai No. 1” and other shipwrecks is of
very important, even epoch-making, significance for the compilation of the
history of Chinese ceramics.
    In the Song Dynasty, the shipbuilding industry usually used local
materials, and the wood of “Nanhai No. 1” was masson pine, which was
produced in Guangdong and Fujian. Thus, some experts believe that the
ship was most likely manufactured in Guangdong or Fujian.127 If it was
made in Fujian, it probably departed from the Port of Quanzhou and if it
was made in Guangdong, it might have departed from the Port of
Guangzhou.
   But was it the Port of Quanzhou or Guangzhou? Some scholars believe
Nanhai No. 1 and some other sunken trading vessels must have departed
from the Port of Quanzhou, based on the location of the shipwrecks, the
geographical locations of the kilns that produced the ceramics on the ships,
and wares similar to those on board that have been discovered overseas.
Geographically speaking it makes the most sense that ceramics produced by
the Dehua and Cizao kilns would have been shipped from the Port of
Quanzhou. Besides, historical records mention that the cargo loaded in
Quanzhou at the time included “Rao ware” (Jingdezhen ware) and “Chu
ware” (Longquan ware).128 Water was usually the most economical and
convenient mode of transport for ceramics in the Song Dynasty. The
northeastern part of Fujian is bordered by Zhejiang and Jiangxi. So,
products of the major producing areas of the Longquan kilns could enter the
upper reaches of the Minjiang River system after a short land route.
Jingdezhen belongs to the Xinjiang River system, which is adjacent to the
upper reaches of the Minjiang River system. Thus, Jingdezhen products
could also enter the Minjiang River after a relatively short land route and
then proceed down the river to enter the sea at the Minjiang River estuary.
For both Longquan ware and Jingdezhen ware, this was the nearest passage
to the southern coast of China and then overseas. The other routes (such as

through the Yangtze River estuary or the Port of Ningbo) would be much
longer. In addition, on other shipwrecks from the Song and Yuan dynasties,
instances of Jingdezhen ware loaded together with ceramic products from
kilns in the Minjiang River basin in Fujian have been found (for example,
black glazed porcelain made by the Chayang kilns in Nanping, Fujian, and
qingbai ware by the Yi kilns in Minqing have been found on the South
Korea Sinan Shipwreck). All these point to the conclusion that the Minjiang
River waterway was probably a very important ceramics export route that
traditionally connected the Jingdezhen, Longquan and Minjiang River basin
kilns together.129
   During the Song and Yuan dynasties, large numbers of Chinese
ceramics were exported through various ports along the coast. Among the
relics on sunken ships, ceramics of the Jingdezhen and Longquan kilns and
kilns in Fujian are frequently seen. Compared with the same kind of
porcelain produced in Fujian, Jingdezhen and Longquan ware were high
quality products that were in short supply. To meet the huge demand of the
overseas markets, the Jingdezhen kilns, which were in the hinterland, tried
their best to transport their products through waterways to large ports to be
sent to sea, and one of these major routes was via the Minjiang River
waterway to be transshipped from Fujian.130 Another reason that Quanzhou
was probably the departure port of the sunken ships was the rise of the
port’s status in the Southern Song Dynasty as the political center moved
southward to Lin’an (present-day Hangzhou) and the shipping center
moved from Guangzhou to Quanzhou.
   Convenient transportation would often promote the development of a
porcelain industry. The rapid development of the Longquan kilns in the
Song Dynasty can be attributed to the improvement in transport,
specifically, the rise of the Port of Quanzhou in the Song Dynasty, the
establishment of maritime trade bureaus in Wenzhou and Ningbo by the
Song regime, and the location of the Longquan kilns adjacent to Wenzhou
and Ningbo with quick access to the upper reaches of the Minjiang River
system via short land routes. The Longquan kilns developed especially
rapidly after the mid-Southern Song Dynasty. Under the heavy influence of
the Guan kilns, the Longquan kilns began to produce two types of high-
grade thick glazed product: black body celadon and white body celadon,
which bear clear signs of imitating Guan ware and were confiscated as
products for court use. The predominant type of the two, white-body thick-

glazed celadon, was exported to overseas markets such as Japan. The
Longquan kilns made major innovations in the shape design, body and
glaze formula, glazing technique and decoration approaches of celadon to
produce products with a generous glaze layer, exquisite workmanship,
attractive shapes and rich diversity. The invention of light bluish blue glaze
and plum green glaze pushed celadon making technology to new heights.
As overseas sales of Longquan ware increased, the Longquan kilns totally
assumed the historical position that once belonged to the Yue kilns to
become the central production area for celadon in southern China and
Longquan ware became the main export porcelain of China at that time.
   Archaeological data show that Chinese ceramics were first exported to
Japan in the Nara period. Celadon from the 12th to thirteenth centuries that
have been unearthed in Japan is basically all Longquan ware. They were
unearthed in over 40 Japanese counties and cities distributed in both coastal
and central areas of Honshu, Kyushu and Shikoku. Analysis of the wares’
shape designs, glaze colors and decorative patterns indicates that most of
them were produced in the Northern Song to the early Yuan Dynasty. Early
products were mainly bowls and plates, including lotus flower bowls, bowls
with vertical cloud pattern, carved bowls with comb pattern, and large
plates with phoenix pattern, which generally feature a thick body wall,
broad, short and shallowly dug out circular foot, and thin, bright glaze. The
firing process is similar to that of Yue ware. Products of later periods
differed remarkably from earlier ones with the firing process greatly
improved. One type of later product is bowls with a thick body, thin glaze
and broad lotus petal pattern carved on the outer wall, and the other type is
thin-body thick-glazed products after the mid-Southern Song Dynasty
called “Kinuta” and regarded as a treasure in Japan. Besides Japan, Song
dynasty Longquan celadon is also frequently found in Vietnam, the
Philippines and other places.131
   Longquan wares also accounted for the majority of the ancient Chinese
Song and Yuan porcelain found in Africa. For instance, of the large number
of porcelain shards produced in China from the 10th to sixteenth centuries
unearthed from the site of Fustat (ancient Cairo city) in Egypt, the celadon
shards from the 12th to fourteenth centuries are all products of the
Longquan kilns in the late Northern Song Dynasty, the Southern Song
Dynasty and even the Yuan Dynasty. Common varieties are lotus flower
bowls, bowls with vertical cloud pattern, bowls with lotus petal pattern and

large plates with phoenix pattern. These varieties are also the most common
among relics found at Song dynasty Longquan kiln sites in China. Also
discovered have been celadon shards with thin body and thick glaze that is
light greenish blue in color, which are typical utensils in the middle and late
Southern Song Dynasty. Varieties include shallow belly washers, plate-
mouthed bottles, powder cases and lotus petal bowls.132
   Of course, we can see from relics raised from shipwrecks that besides
Longquan ware, accounting for quite an important proportion of the
porcelain exported in the Song Dynasty is also qingbai ware produced by
the Jingdezhen kilns as well as various qingbai porcelains, celadon,
caramel-black glazed porcelain and green glazed porcelain produced in
coastal areas in Fujian and Guangdong. This author believes that the export
porcelain production in Fujian and Guangdong is an integral part of the
history of Chinese ceramics and that with the salvage of many shipwrecks
and porcelains from the sea, the topic will attract more attention and in-
depth study among academic circles.
    In addition, it is noteworthy that the export porcelain of the Song
Dynasty found in distant locations is mainly southern kiln ware and little is
from northern kilns, which suggests two points. Firstly, the export porcelain
must be mainly from the Southern Song period rather than the Northern
Song period, because otherwise there should be northern kiln ware among
the export porcelain if porcelain could be easily exported to foreign
countries. In the Northern Song, all kilns across China, north and south
alike, were ruled by the Song regime. Secondly, during the Southern Song
the restrictions on trade between the Southern Song and the Jin in the north
meant porcelain produced by northern kilns seldom circulated in the south,
which might have contributed to the result that the export porcelain at the
time was mostly produced by the Longquan, Jingdezhen, and kilns in
coastal areas in Fujian and Guangdong, which belonged to the territory of
the Southern Song.

8.7 Conclusion
8.7.1 Characteristics of the Northern Kilns
The Song Dynasty marked a peak in China’s porcelain industry
development with kilns all over the country from north to south, with
various porcelain types and glaze colors contending, and with many new

achievements made in porcelain-making technologies. Achievements made
in the northern kilns’ porcelain-making technology may be summarized into
six aspects:
   The first was the discovery and application of copper red glaze. The use
of copper oxide as a glaze colorant in China began in the Han Dynasty and
continued without interruption through the Wei, Jin, Southern and Northern
Dynasties and the Sui and Tang dynasties. By the Tang Dynasty, white
glazed porcelain with green speckles was made. At the Jiaocheng kiln site
in Shaanxi Province not only were many specimens of white glazed ware
with green coloring unearthed, but a small number of specimens of white
glazed ware with red speckles were also found. The appearance of red color
on porcelain is a major innovation because this would enable craftsmen to
realize that copper oxide turned green under general conditions yet could
also turn red in specific conditions. If the appearance of the red speckles on
the white glazed ware found at the Jiaocheng kiln site in Shaanxi was only
coincidental, the successful firing of the purplish red glaze of Jun ware
indicates that potters of the Yuzhou kilns had fully mastered the rule that
copper oxide could turn purplish red when fired in a suitable atmosphere.
This was a great achievement which facilitated the successful firing of red
glazed porcelain by Jingdezhen in the Yuan Dynasty.
   The second achievement was the creation and promotion of upside-
down firing or inverted firing. Ding kiln workers changed the traditional
single piece saggers for containing plates and bowls to be fired face up into
saggers combined with cushion pads to fire the wares upside down. The
new sagger and the inverted firing method greatly increased production
capacity under the same firing conditions and costs such that unit cost was
reduced, market competitiveness was raised and the daily needs for plates
and bowls, which were the mostly commonly used wares of the common
folk, were better met. Wares fired in this upside-down manner had an
unglazed rim, and the Ding kilns’ success in adopting this method was soon
copied by other kilns. The southward advance of the Jin Dynasty and the
southward migration of kiln workers passed on this new method to many
kilns in Jiangxi, Zhejiang, Fujian and Sichuan.
   The third achievement was in the use of printed decoration. Printing
was a traditional ceramic decoration method in China, and by the Song
Dynasty the method was greatly improved with the Ding kilns being the
most representative. Ding kiln white porcelain that has survived to the

present includes a large number of printed plates, bowls, and saucers, which
are decorated in the well with relief patterns of peacock, peony, dragon in
clouds, carp lotus pond, flowers and other images. The patterns exhibit a
high artistic level with dense yet orderly layout and slender, neat lines. In
the Song Dynasty Dingzhou produced not only white porcelain, but also
kesi (a type of Chinese silk tapestry). Craftsmen transplanted suitable
patterns from kesi works onto pottery models used to print patterns onto
porcelain, which was also why the printed patterns of Ding kiln ware were
of a high artistic level from its inception. Besides Ding ware, Yaozhou kiln
celadon also used printed decoration extensively and featured rich themes,
of which children at play was particularly vivid and interesting.
   The fourth achievement of porcelain decoration in the Song Dynasty
was the progress made in carved decoration, which is represented by the
Yaozhou kilns. The Yaozhou kilns started using carving decoration in the
early Northern Song Dynasty and reached a peak in the Southern Song
Dynasty. The carved patterns featured a variety of themes, sharp, smooth
lines, skilled use of the blade, and vivid, powerful images, which was a
showcase of the superb skills of the potters. The Yaozhou kilns’ carving
decoration was not only the best among the northern kilns, but also ranked
top in the whole country at the time (Fig. 8.116).

Fig. 8.116 Yaozhou kiln small pot with carved pattern,
Jin Dynasty, height: 13 cm, top diam.: 4 cm, base diam.: 6 cm

   The fifth achievement was the rise of black and white decoration, which
was popular among northern folk kilns represented by the Cizhou kilns.
Taking black coloring as ink and porcelain greenware as paper, it was an art
that combined Chinese ceramic technology with traditional painting. It won
the admiration of the people from its first appearance and developed
rapidly. These black paintings on a white backdrop are mostly themed on
things familiar to and popular among the common folks. Typical examples
are the pillows produced by the Cizhou kilns with images of bears at play,
circus, Cuju (an ancient Chinese football game) and children at play. The
pictures not only vividly decorated the utensils, but also left a trove of
precious information for later generations to learn about the folk life of the
times. They also laid the “painting skills” foundation for the emergence of
Jingdezhen blue and white porcelain in the Yuan Dynasty.
   The sixth achievement was the creation of overglaze red and green
decoration, which appeared in the Jin Dynasty and was the earliest
overglaze decoration in China. Kilns firing such wares were concentrated in

the north, such as the Cizhou kilns in Hebei, the Pacun kilns in Yuzhou,
Henan, the Changzhi kilns in Shanxi and the Zibo kilns in Shandong. At the
sites of all these kilns, bowls decorated with red, yellow and green
colorings have been found. The red, yellow and green decoration in the Jin
Dynasty pioneered multicolored decoration and inspired the emergence of
Jingdezhen wucai wares later.

8.7.2 Characteristics of the Southern Kilns
The above description is about the achievements of the northern kilns in
porcelain-making technologies in the Song Dynasty. Next, let us look at the
achievements of the southern kilns. During the Song Dynasty, many new
achievements were made in porcelain-making technologies in the south,
which raised product quality and expanded sales. The achievements may be
summarized in the following manner.
   The first was the use of high-quality porcelain clay, a major advance in
the porcelain-making process made in areas south of the Yangtze River in
the Song Dynasty. Many porcelain works produced by Song dynasty kilns
found so far boast pure white body, which was a major step forward from
the gray or grayish white body of previous dynasties. Ancient porcelain
making was carried out by hand and it was difficult to reduce the iron
content in the raw materials. Hence, an important and almost the only way
to raise porcelain body quality was to find and use high-quality porcelain
clay as raw material. It was by discovering high-quality porcelain clay that
many kilns in the Song Dynasty were able to fire top quality porcelain, such
as the qingbai porcelain with pure white body produced by the Jingdezhen,
Nanfeng, Tong’an and Chaozhou kilns. The body was so thin that they were
almost translucent and fully met the standard of modern porcelain.
   The second achievement was the enlargement of kiln volume. All kilns
in the south in the Song Dynasty were dragon kilns, built on hills that were
quite large with the short ones some 50–60 m in length, the longer ones 70–
80 m, and the longest reaching 100 m. The lengthening of the kilns
increased their capacity by several orders of magnitude and was an effective
measure to meet the increasing demand for porcelain both at home and
abroad.
   The third was the new height reached in the firing of blue glaze. Blue
glaze has a long history in China. In the Southern Song Dynasty, Longquan
kiln potters, after repeated practice, abandoned the traditional lime glaze

back in the Northern Song Dynasty and creatively fired lime-alkali glaze,
which enabled the application of a thicker glaze layer thanks to its high
viscosity at high temperature. This is impossible with lime glaze because
lime glaze has a low viscosity at high temperature and in order to avoid
flow in the glaze only a thin layer could be applied. Besides, kiln workers at
the time were more skilled at controlling the firing temperature and
reducing atmosphere and were thus able to produce light greenish blue and
plum green glaze color, which raised celadon firing technology to a new
level.
   The fourth achievement of the southern kilns in the Song Dynasty was
the many innovations made in glaze surface decoration. Black glaze was a
typical example. Black itself was a dull and unpopular color, but after a
certain processing technique, kiln workers were able to produce rich and
colorful decorations with those of the Jian kilns in Fujian and the Ji’an kilns
in Jiangxi being the most distinctive. The Jian kilns mainly produced black
porcelain and innovated the spot or streak crystals on the glaze surface, the
former termed oil spots and the latter hare’s fur, and the Jizhou kilns, which
produced many kinds of porcelains and its black porcelain remaining the
most representative, transplanted the popular paper-cut art to porcelain and
created a new decorative style by combining paper-cuts and porcelain
making. Other examples are the tortoiseshell glaze which featured infinite
changes with yellow and black as the main tone and was the most
frequently used on teacups, and the qingbai porcelain, a new porcelain type
Jingdezhen craftsmen created by imitating the bluish white jade color and
called “false jade” due to its remarkable resemblance with bluish white
jade. A variant of qingbai porcelain was the yingqing (shadow blue) ware
featuring carved patterns on translucent porcelain that resulted in
transparent light and shadow effect, hence its name (Fig. 8.117).

Fig. 8.117 Qingbai glazed melon-ridge handled ewer,
